Developing machine learning models that operate in real-time, providing precise and efficient predictions is a top priority. Real-time predictive models are heavily utilized in the aerospace and automotive industries, among others. Our research focuses on the theoretical framework of real-time collaborative filtering, an essential algorithm for real-time predictive models. We have created two new RTCF algorithms, based on differential equations and a probabilistic approach, which are both easily integratable into graph neural networks. Our experimental results show that these RTCF models are feasible and can be effectively integrated into graph neural networks.

A Slim Sidon sequence, specifically of weight w and width q, can be thought of as a combination of two elements, u and v, whose discrete Fourier transform has nonvanishing absolute values for at least $q^2$ many input possibilities. It has been proven that any subset of a Slim Sidon sequence, of weight less than $2^{5/3}$ and width less than $2^{2/3}$, cannot produce a nonlinear Boolean mapping, as this would contradict a long-standing conjecture known as the hyperplane conjecture. Additionally, the fastest known algorithm for determining if a given element belongs to a Slim Sidon sequence of weight less than 4000 and width 768, has a running time of $n^{1.293}$.

A technique for randomly selecting subsets of binary vector arrays with a specified minimum guaranteed magnitude is described. The proposed method generates these subsets at a faster rate than existing methods, particularly when the desired subsets have low dimensionality. It can also efficiently identify if such a subset exists with a specified minimum margin for lower-dimensional arrays.

I propose a theoretical model for adjusting parton distribution functions (PDFs) based on numerical calculational methods like next-to-leading-order (NLO) and beyond NLO orders. This will serve as the foundation for the xFitter framework, which will be discussed in detail. xFitter calculates adjusted PDFs using data from various experimental outcomes.

This document outlines the official launch of the ELKI data mining platform, consisting of over 800,000 lines of source code, showcasing a complete data mining pipeline encompassing clustering, feature extraction, and outlier detection across various data types. Developed by Sebastian Schaffstein, the open-source framework empowers users to conduct comprehensive data analysis and supports comparative evaluations of algorithms and methodologies, as evidenced in the accompanying handbook. Additionally, the framework addresses challenges commonly encountered in real-world datasets, such as dealing with missing and uneven data.

We've developed an efficient technique, parametric sowing, for creating a strong and robust array of optical frequency fluctuations within a microresonator. This innovative approach begins with a initial pump power that is below the threshold for nonlinear lattice effects in the microresonator. As a result, an initial pattern of fluorescence emerges due to linear loss mechanisms in the device. Applying the parametric sowing principle, we increase the pump power while maintaining a constant power level throughout the microresonator. This action causes the initial fluorescent points to evolve into a highly stable and regular pattern of optical frequency fluctuations that can be maintained over extended periods for an incredibly wide range of adjustment capabilities. This phenomenon is accompanied by minimal thermal loading and is thus ideal for generating stable and consistent patterns of optical frequency fluctuations.

We establish a key concept - stochastic subgroups - to investigate a specific type of atypical subgroup, X, within acylindrically hyperbolic groups. It's inherent that such a subgroup, X, remains infinite and has only finitely many conjugates. Our research focuses on determining the full set of stochastic subgroups within any given acylindrically hyperbolic group and, in addition, finds necessary and sufficient conditions for a subgroup, X, to be both stochastic and loyal - a distinct category of subgroups, Y, within G. Essentially, this involves finding common group actions for both X and Y via an algorithmic process, thereby enabling the creation of a natural probability measure on X that is invariant under the action of Y.

Quantization in neural networks has been shown to have various benefits, primarily stemming from its memory and processing costs being significantly lower. A more unanticipated advantage of quantization is improved model generalizability, which has piqued researchers' interest. This study delves into the relationship between quantization and generalizability by analyzing binary weight neural networks, specifically those using the Sign-Sum Product (SSP) activation function. Through our examination of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), we identify key factors contributing to the generalizability enhancements afforded by quantization. These factors can be categorized into activation function properties, weight initialization methods, and network architecture characteristics. By combining these insights, we propose a initialization method for binary weight neural networks that integrates empirical observations from the training process. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the generalizability enhancements resulting from quantization can be attributed to the broader weight initialization range made possible by quantization. This effect is particularly pronounced in networks featuring multiple layers. However, our proposed new initialization method is shown to yield generalizable performance on large-scale text classification datasets, such as those involving extensive documentation. Additionally, our analysis also addresses the influence of activation functions on Neural Network learnability, a topic that has received scarce attention thus far.

We have extended quantum extremal surfaces from fields to any type of field configurations in any higher-order derivative theory. This involves defining an appropriate 'energy' density called $\mathcal{E}$, which can be a complex function. Quantum extremal surfaces are then found by minimizing the Lagrangian density over all possible trajectories in the field space. This leads to an expression for the leading logarithmic correction to the entropy in theories with a specific type of higher-order derivatives, resulting in an expression dependent on the number of derivatives.

Research on simple models for biological systems that can be represented as lattices has gained significant interest recently.  There are various models that employ different types of mathematical functions to represent the growth of organisms within the lattice.  In this study, we establish a universal method to calculate the speed of spread of these models by using a complex analysis technique called the multiplicative intersection index.  This method allows us to develop a general formula for the spread rate in the asymptotic limit.  Additionally, we apply our method to two specific models, the d-dimensional contact process and the d-dimensional voter model, and derive exact expressions for the spread rate in the asymptotic limit in both cases.  Our method also provides insight into the phase transition in these models.

Various stabilization techniques can be applied to ensure convergence and achieve precise results for iterative compressed sensing algorithms. This report examines techniques such as regularization, constraint enforcement, and residual-based adjustments that can be incorporated into the iterative process. By adding these stabilization methods, the algorithms can produce high-precision results even in problematic cases. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods on compressed sensing-based imaging techniques used in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging. The techniques were successfully applied to SAR imaging data and the results indicate that stabilization is essential to achieve precise images, particularly in data with noise and multiple scatterers.

A combined image is formed by integrating multiple original images, each with a unique orientation and weighing them differently. This process is heavily reliant on the Point Spread Function (PSF) of the detector, as well as any applicable convolution kernels. Theoretical frameworks exist for determining the PSF of a combined image when its components are aligned, but these are largely unknown for misaligned configurations. This study presents a novel approach for calculating the PSF of a combined image when its components exhibit arbitrary orientations and varying weights. The proposed method utilizes a convolution matrix based kernel to achieve this. Additionally, specific formulas are developed for the PSF of a combined image when the weights and orientations of its components are constant, as well as for the situation where the images being combined are unweighted and unaligned. To verify the efficacy of the proposed method, numerical simulations were conducted comparing the calculated PSF with the PSF of a directly observed image from a simulated galaxy galaxy. The study finds that the linear approximation holds surprisingly well, even at relatively low signal-to-noise ratios (as low as 1000). The study concludes by presenting a practical technique for determining the PSF of a combined image through iterative simulation of the observed image until the stop condition is satisfied. The study also presents a practical technique for determining the PSF of a combined image by applying a convolution matrix based kernel which simplifies significantly as the number of original images approaches infinity.

Gaussian free fields (GFFs) are a fundamental concept in probabilistic theory, closely related to numerous other random phenomena. In conformal perturbation theory, they serve as primary fields driving the propagation of conformal field theories. On the other hand, they have a strong connection to multiple SLE (Schramm-Loewner evolution) via two distinct linking mechanisms: one being the impact of Liouville fields in conformal field theory and another resulting from interactions with the stochastic log-gas model. This paper demonstrates the establishment of these connections between GFFs and multiple SLE, achieving this by simplifying and refining existing approaches to the stochastic log-gass model, in the process uncovering novel relationships between GFFs and the generalised multiple SLE framework of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class.

This research demonstrates that for any given smooth initial data for the Navier-Stokes equations in three-dimensional space, there exists a singular solution or a non-physical solution. To define this class of singular solutions, we use the concept of the utmost norm and a priori estimates for certain mathematical operators. Our work expands upon the findings of Demmel and Trefethen, who initially formulated these estimates in a more general context and speculated about their practical applications, ultimately leading to a new understanding of the nature of singular solutions in the context of the Navier-Stokes equations.

In 2021, the community adopted the 'Quantum Algorithms for Linear Algebra' validation process, and in 2022, the validation process was adapted for Quantum Linear Regression and Multi-Layer Perceptrons. However, the existing validation process poses significant challenges, primarily due to the considerable size of the matrices involved in the calculations. As a result, researchers can only verify the results for smaller matrices, limiting their capacity to provide thorough verification. Furthermore, the current process is resource-intensive, primarily because it involves conducting all computations twice - once classically and once quantumly - despite only one set being necessary. Additionally, the process is relatively slow, largely due to the extensive size of the matrices. To address these issues, we have introduced an alternative validation process that is substantially less demanding. The new process is notably less expensive, allowing even larger matrices to be verified. It achieves this by leveraging the unique properties of quantum orthogonality, which enables us to utilize smaller, specially chosen matrices to verify the results of larger ones. The new process is an advancement over the established method in several ways. Firstly, it reduces the necessary size of the matrices used in the verification process. Secondly, it eliminates the need for dual computations. Lastly, it results in faster verification times, largely due to the reduced matrix sizes.

Recent breakthroughs in the implicit neural representations field have generated exciting developments in the fields of computer graphics and vision. Motivated by the complexity of cell shapes, we explore the application of implicit neural representations to model the morphology of stochastic, branching cells. To achieve this, we train a model that learns a distributed and continuous representation of cell shapes, which can then be sampled to generate new, unseen cell instances. Given the scarcity of high-quality cellular data, we incorporate the guidance of biologists through supervised learning and utilize adaptive sampling methods to ensure efficient training. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, showcasing promising generative performance and robustness. Moreover, the trained model achieves remarkable accuracy in predicting morphological features critical for tissue patterning, a complex cellular behavior.

Visualizing three-dimensional space in a two-dimensional format is a common approach, with various geometries and projections being used for different purposes.  Despite its benefits, this type of spatial representation can lead to distortions and misrepresentations, particularly when rendering large datasets or complex structures or when distances need to be accurately conveyed.  Selective training of spatial perception has been achieved using cognitive training programs, with techniques like reinforcement learning also showing potential benefits.  Applying spatial visualization methods that minimize distortions, such as the two-circle method, may also be of value.  Ultimately, the effectiveness of biological depictions of space, whether in science communication or other endeavors, depends on accurately assessing the cognitive capabilities of the audience and tailoring the presentation accordingly.

Vanceby's (1993) theoretical model, which uses reversible dynamics with short-range interactions, is insufficient to explain many observations in hard-disk magnets. These discrepancies involve phenomena like irreversible cooling patterns in temperature-controlled systems and the occurrence of two distinct types of motion in materials with low temperatures. On the other hand, a theoretical framework incorporating non-reversible Markov process has proven capable of accurately predicting numerous behavioral patterns in hard-disk magnets. Specifically, this paradigm has successfully predicted the existence of two different types of motion in low-temperature materials, as well as irreversibly changing temperatures in temperature-controlled systems. Furthermore, this model has provided valuations on key behavioral parameters, such as the relationship between heat and entropy in these materials. Additionally, this theoretical model has predicted the occurrence of "glassy behavior" in systems that experience non-equilibrium transitions, which further highlights its predictive capabilities.

The challenge of identifying the source and nature of multiple overlapping sounds has been a longstanding concern in audio signal processing. The 2020 CHIME Large Vocabulary Recognition Task aimed to tackle this issue by asking participants to pinpoint and categorize sound events from a predefined list of 168 possible sounds. To address this issue, researchers proposed using a complex neural network, referred to as a deep residual network, paired with a data enhancement technique called channel rotation. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated through two distinct experiments. The first revealed that the method could accurately locate sound sources around 30 degrees off the true position, while the second experiment showed significant improvement over baseline models, placing second in the competition with a score of 0.3446.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems, also known as wireless systems based on superposition transmission, are gaining traction in research. Due to their ability to simultaneously transmit data to multiple users with different requirements, these systems are ideal for real-world applications such as 5G and beyond networks. This concept is straightforward to implement, but it presents a range of challenges in areas such as channel estimation, decoding, and optimization. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of superposition transmission based wireless systems, highlighting existing solutions and potential areas for improvement.

In the context of signal evaluation within the context of the spectrogram, a specific geometric interpretation emerges when considering a collection of spectrogram levels in a broader context. Leveraging the principles of random matrix theory, this framework allows for the existence of an associated Hermitian matrix, referred to as a Wigner matrix. As such, the resulting spectral density can be characterized through the Wigner density, ultimately providing insight into various spectrogram-derived statistical properties of signals. Although this approach offers a comprehensive understanding of signal characteristics, it inherently involves mathematical complexities and constraints, ultimately limiting its practical applicability to full-spectrum signal analysis. Nonetheless, this framework does provide actionable insights into the construction of effective signal processing algorithms tailored to various signal types.

In large collections of spike-generating neurons, whether biological or artificial, it's crucial to identify groups of neurons that act in unison as well as individual neurons that deviate from these synchronized groups, by analyzing local and widespread electrical activity patterns. We've developed a universal and adaptable technique for detecting these asynchronous deviations within these collections of neurons. This method's effectiveness is comparable to the best available techniques, and it works seamlessly in the most complex electrical patterns, according to detailed simulations and experimental data. We've tested this approach in three different scenarios: two where synchronized groups and asynchronous behaviors coexist, and one where a single stimulus triggers widespread synchronization. By systematically varying parameters, such as the level of electrical connection between neurons, and observing the associated changes in electrical patterns, we've gained a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics and the timing of these deviations. This new technique enables precise measurement of the time interval between these deviations, in relation to the overall electrical pattern period, and it successfully detects chimeric patterns, even at large scales of electrical interaction and in the presence of electrical patterns that originate and spread.

One approach to advancing astrophysical simulations involves leveraging parallel computing techniques by applying randomized methods to model complex systems consisting of numerous bodies. The intensity of interactions between these bodies is influenced by their positions and velocity velocities, determining whether specialized algorithms like FEGS or FEGS+ are required for accurate calculations. In situations where multiple close encounters are likely, specialized algorithms prove particularly beneficial. This study executes a randomized force method for REBOUND, enabling it to benefit from such specialized algorithms in a variety of astrophysical simulations.

In systems governed by continuous noise, the average behavior is driven forward by deterministic forces, whereas random forces cause exploration, leading to an optimal balance between expansion and uncertainty. The dynamic equilibrium maintained by this balance is characterized by minimal changes in key performance metrics over time. The objective of this work is to develop a quantum Fokker-Planck master equation that describes the collective behavior of populations responding to targeted therapy, with the hope of identifying universal features associated with dynamic equilibrium and effective treatment strategies.

This research explores the two-dimensional flow of a complex fluid consisting of a mixture of Newtonian and fractional Bessel fluid. The goal is to investigate a confined complex fluid under pressure as it flows through a narrow channel with varying obstructions. A novel approach, the direct numerical simulation method, is used for this purpose. The study examines the flow and resistance encountered by a complex fluid as it passes through a narrow channel with obstructions represented by circular discs of alternating sizes. The obstacles are placed at fixed intervals, and their sequences are studied in detail. Key findings relate to the flow patterns and resistance coefficients, which are influenced not only by the sizes and distances between the obstacles but also by the viscoelastic properties of the complex fluid. By manipulating these parameters, it is possible to alter the flow characteristics and resistance experienced by the complex fluid. Therefore, this work presents a comprehensive understanding of the confined flow of a complex fluid with a focus on the obstacles' configurations.

Research on the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation's impact on unique ecosystem conditions is frequently hindered by the absence of long-term data in remote areas. This paper overcomes this challenge by leveraging a large dataset of MODIS images from the early 2000s to the late 2010s, covering various unique ecosystem types. The analysis reveals a noticeable increase in low-seasonal precipitation in areas with limited or no ecosystem changes. In contrast, areas undergoing distinct ecosystem changes are associated with elevated seasonal precipitation. The distinct changes in these areas serve as indicators of ENSO-driven transformation, offering new perspectives on the impact of ENSO on the environment.

We suggest that the formation of supermassive black holes in galaxies occurs through a sequence of events that involve compact objects, which are the remnants of supernovae explosions. This process is thought to occur when a galactic environment's stability is disrupted, leading to a sudden collapse of massive cloud formations. By studying the properties of galaxies that are less massive, like the dwarf galaxy Leo I, we believe that similar physical processes occur that result in the formation of compact objects, which are the ancestors of supermassive black holes. Our research on Leo I reveals an unusual pattern in its compact object distribution at higher densities, suggesting a complex origin story for its compact binary system population. Furthermore, a extensive database of galactic properties is needed to gain a deeper understanding of the formation of supermassive black holes and compact objects, as well as galactic star formation and growth patterns.

In magnetic materials with flat bands, which have an ultra-dense density of states near zero energy, unusual correlation-induced phases can emerge that are sensitive to external magnetic fields.  In a study involving a multi-orbital kagome alloy, flat bands were observed to trigger a significant decrease in electrical resistance as the field increases past a specific threshold, rather than the expected increase.  This unusual response is attributed to a phase transition from a zero-field correlated state to a ferromagnetic state that is stabilized by the field's negative spin-orbit interaction.  This research provides a rare example of flat-band induced magnetism and offers a unique pathway to ferromagnetism through a correlation phase transition.

The extensive variation in human traits can be attributed to an intricate interplay between genetic and environmental influences.
A comprehensive genome-wide association study has elucidated the underlying mechanisms, while efforts to decipher the complex interplay between genetics and environment are ongoing in the fields of epigenomics and systems biology.
We convened a virtual collaboration to integrate functional genomic data and genome-wide association study results for 18 distinct human characteristics.
The examined data encompassed histone modification, messenger RNA expression, DNA methylation, and protein complexity across seven tissue types and two developmental stages.
Through the application of a novel framework, we developed a detailed understanding of the functional genomic markers associated with each trait and uncovered substantial overlap between different types of functional genomic data.
The results further revealed that specific genetic variations are linked to unique epigenetic markers in particular tissue types and that, in contrast, some variations exhibit consistent association with distinct epigenetic markers across multiple tissue types.
The consequent integration of genome-wide association study data and functional genomic information enabled the precise characterization of epigenetic markers regulating the expression of key genes implicated in each trait.
Ultimately, our findings provide a foundational understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing 18 distinct human characteristics and highlight the pivotal role of functional genomic information in interpreting genome-wide association study results.

Resolving an inquiry from Meuyangel, we identify the local structures of two-dimensional residual circuits in two classes of tetravalent partial quadrangles: those classified by Brouse and Tanny, and a new set defined by $r$-vectors. We also characterize the possible block configurations for these two classes given specific localized structures and the condition that $r$ and $\lambda$ are relatively prime.

This research examines the electronic states of confined helium-like ions with consideration of Coulomb interaction. Utilizing the fractional quantum mechanics approach and third-order perturbation theory, we compute various information entropies associated with the energy spectra of these ions. All calculations are performed for the ground state and excited states across a range of confinement potentials. The outcomes indicate that for strong confinement, entropy measures behave in a manner consistent with the standard approach, whereas for weak confinement, Coulomb interaction effects are responsible for the observed trends. Furthermore, by evaluating entropy with respect to the confining potential, we derive expressions that can be utilized to estimate key parameters, such as the fine-structure constant and masses of the nucleus and electrons.

One of the key methods for assessing gravitational theories involves examining systems with a high ratio of mass ($M$) to distance ($d$), typically found in extensive binary star systems. By considering the gravitational influence on such objects, scientists can determine if their motion follows the predictions of a particular gravitational model. For example, in the vast majority of tested binary star systems, the deviation of a certain gravitational theory from others was found to be negligible. However, there remains a small possibility that slightly different gravitational theories could exist, resulting in distinct effects on the motion of objects in these systems. Ultimately, determining the optimal gravitational theory involves identifying the few extreme binary systems that pose the greatest challenge to different theories, as mild cases are deemed insufficient for a thorough comparison.

In the context of multiplicative linear logic, specific connectives serve as reflection and contraction operators. When a subproof is isolated from its broader proof, as in cut-elimination, it's effectively'removed'. We develop two types of removal theories, each corresponding to one of these contraction forms, and demonstrate that cut-elimination can be seen as an application of one of these theories. By leveraging a labeled calculus, we introduce cut-removal strategies that mimic proof normalization, resulting in a deeper understanding of the labeled calculus.

In the past, various methods have been applied to analyze and predict the behavior of time series data, particularly in the financial markets. This research focuses on determining whether the cross-correlation properties of stock time series can be utilized to forecast their future synchronization. Utilizing the cross recurrence plot, our study creates a network that captures the dynamic interactions between different stock prices, enabling the identification of connected components that signify synchronized or disparate stock prices. By acknowledging that higher stock prices are associated with improved market conditions, this project aims to enhance prediction accuracy by incorporating the cross-correlation structure of stock prices into traditional time series models. Through extensive testing using randomly selected stock price datasets from the US market over an eight-year period, our results reveal a significant link between the cross-correlation properties of stock prices and their future synchronization. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of these cross-correlation properties in predicting various stock price outcomes, outperforming models that solely utilize time series characteristics.

The resilience of semiconductors to long-lasting data storage and robust quantum computing is crucial and depends on suppressing noisy vibrations. However, these vibrations interact with electrons in complex ways that must be considered for an accurate picture. By integrating advanced techniques like density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory, our study reveals the dynamic influences of vibrations on electrons in momentum space. We found that electron-vibrational interactions vary significantly depending on the type of momentum, while spin-vibrational interactions become apparent in the presence of defects. These results provide valuable insights for understanding the delicate balance between electron-vibrational interactions in momentum, which could pave the way for the development of more robust quantum systems and data storage techniques.

Enhancing click-through rate forecasting, particularly for new promotions, is essential to boosting ad revenue. Traditional forecasting models rely heavily on historical user behavior and ignore crucial insights from user interactions with visual materials. To close this knowledge gap, we've developed a new forecasting framework that incorporates the effects of visual materials on forecasting accuracy. Our model uses the strength of collaborative filtering and deep learning algorithms to predict clicks for new promotions more effectively, outperforming existing models by 11.3% in experimental evaluations.

Traditional case management tools face limitations in handling complex business cases due to the absence of advanced modeling features for constraints.  As a result, system developers are forced to resort to work-around solutions involving additional entities and relationships.  This technical document highlights the benefits of employing algebraic methods to enrich case models with limitations, thereby facilitating more straightforward and effective implementations.  By utilizing formal techniques, developers can leverage the properties of ordered sets to define business processes and their associated data limitations, ultimately leading to more natural representations of business rules.  This document specifically explores the application of cardinality restrictions to identify relevant limitations in business processes and data models.

Wildfires disrupting air quality have become a pressing issue in major fires.  Understanding the interaction between wildfires and air quality requires detailed information on aerosol physics, which current methods struggle to incorporate effectively.  Bridging this gap, we've developed a framework that utilizes machine learning to incorporate physical aerosol mechanisms into air quality modeling, effectively making use of the vast amounts of satellite data available.  Leveraging the processing power of graphics processing units, we've tested our approach on a large scale, focusing on major fires in the US.  With its exceptional performance, our method has shown considerable promise in addressing the limitation mentioned above.  As such, it's ideally suited for applications such as real-time air quality monitoring and warning systems during significant fires.

Given the widespread use of mobile devices, various techniques for locating users have become commonplace in the sector. As these services grow, they generate substantial amounts of data, which can be sold to third-party companies for analysis and profit. This paper examines the mathematical concept of conditional expectations as a means to measure location tracking users' privacy loss. It presents a general method for computing the conditional entropy of a mixed random variable, which we apply to quantify the privacy breach when tracking users' movements in a two-dimensional space. Additionally, we compare this approach with the traditional Monte Carlo method and propose a new formula for calculating the conditional entropy of a mixed random variable with discrete outcomes.

Accurate prediction precision in fMRI data relies on correlating associated imaging characteristics with underlying brain properties. However, common estimation techniques for functional connectivity might introduce biases when estimating brain properties, potentially distorting relationships between imaging characteristics and brain properties. Furthermore, these estimation techniques often involve making broad assumptions about data, which can result in decreased precision when actual brain properties are considered. To address these issues, researchers studied how different estimation techniques affect precision in predicting brain characteristics, such as target location in the brain, using data from over 500 individuals from different studies. They discovered that estimating brain properties using data from the same location, through techniques like cross-correlation, can be inaccurate and misleading, whereas estimation methods that take into account the unique structure of the brain, like multi-occupancy modeling, might be more suitable for prediction and these techniques could provide new insights into regional specialisation.

The global heat kernel asymptotics and thermal resistance distribution of directed networks are examined, with a novel interpretation of the results utilizing directed Euler-Lagrange equations. A crucial inequality related to the directed Ricci curvature is established, revealing its lower bound's impact on the thermal resistance distribution and global heat kernel function. This lead to the conclusion that a sufficient condition for positive global heat kernel function is a positive directed Ricci curvature. Furthermore, a directed graph's measure density is characterized in terms of the Ricci curvature and thermal resistance.

Recent advances in NLP from English to language models have been extended to code-mixed data, achieving notable results using shared sentence space representations. However, current code-mixed language models primarily focus on the functional aspects, disregarding the significant cultural and social significance of language mixing. Our research addresses this gap by developing a transition-based word embedding model called PESTO, which incorporates transition point-dependent positional information to maintain the distinct identities of individual languages in a mix. A comparative study on four Indian languages, specifically Hindi and Marathi, English, and Malayalam, has been conducted to validate the effectiveness of PESTO. The findings on datasets consisting of social media texts and poetry have shown PESTO to significantly outperform related models in various NLP tasks. The source code for PESTO is publicly available at https://github.com/srikrishnithapaliya/PESTO.

Using a combination of density functional theory and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the Allen-Dynes formula, we have calculated the critical temperature of the H$_{3}$S hydride as a function of pressure, focusing on how it exceeds 250 K. By considering three different molecular orbitals for hybridization with the Fermi surface, we have chosen those near the Van Hove singularities and found that the highest critical temperatures are achieved when these are included. When all three orbitals are involved, high-frequency phonon weights and electron-phonon coupling are maximized, while the isotope effect is heavily dependent on pressure, leading to a significant drop in critical temperature with increasing pressure when only the most singular feature is involved. This critical behavior is shifted towards higher pressures and becomes less dramatic when all three orbitals are included. Our analysis suggests that all critical components must be considered to accurately predict the critical temperature as a function of pressure in this hydride superconductor.

In a 1990 article, Alan Fisher introduced a measure of the average effect of a variable on another variable in a linear model, along with a method for testing its significance. Utilizing the concepts of linear models and directed acyclic graphs, we reevaluate Fisher's approach and demonstrate its equivalence to a combination of existing methods. We further establish that the significance test is equivalent to examining the causal influence of a variable on another, as depicted in a directed acyclic graph, and illustrate this connection through two practical examples.

This research focuses on developing an efficient and robust walking assistance system for individuals with mobility issues. Typically, wearable devices are either powered or passive; powered models rely on electrical power, while passive designs rely on strategically fastened straps. However, we're exploring a novel approach that combines passive and active elements in tandem. Our proposed system consists of an array of terminated springs that store potential energy as the wearer takes a step, which is then converted into kinetic energy as the legs move, eliminating the need for electrical power. Our goal is to analyze the mechanical properties of this spring-based assistance system and evaluate its ability to support gait phases through various parametric studies. It's crucial that the spring's energy storage and release synchronize with the wearer's natural gait to ensure a smooth and even walking motion. To achieve this, we're utilizing a nonlinear least-squares optimization technique to fine-tune key design variables that influence the spring's performance throughout the gait cycle. Our findings show that this spring-based assistance system can facilitate bipedal movement with minimal to no additional energy input from the wearer, while also enhancing the overall efficiency and resilience of the gait assistance technology.

This research introduces a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of reference images is created during the initial mapping process, where each image is linked to a 3D node surfel map. When a query image is encountered, its 2D features are associated with the nearest 2D features from each reference image, and their 3D positions are compared to determine the optimal match. To enhance this alignment, the semantic labels of the query and reference images are utilized to derive new features, which are then utilized in a joint optimization process with the existing image features. By combining geometric and semantic information, our approach achieves reliable relocalization at a 10 cm to 20 cm scale within as little as 10 seconds to 20 seconds.

Mobile devices can learn from labeled and unlabeled data, while reducing data ambiguity, by utilizing the collective knowledge of a server and a local model. This is achieved through a new algorithm that combines the strengths of a localized model and a global model, trained semi-supervised using labeled data from the server and unlabeled data from the edge device. The algorithm allows the server to clarify ambiguous data, which is initially classified differently by the local and global models, by utilizing the collective knowledge. This updated data is then fed back to the local device, which refines its model in turn. The process repeats until data ambiguity ceases to exist.

Simulations of colliding a black hole with a neutron star are conducted under strict laws of general relativity, incorporating the effects of neutrinos, magnetic fields, and rotating neutron stars, using complex equations for how matter and energy behave. The resulting interactions produce massive gamma-ray bursts, distorted gravitational waves, and varied binary-star systems, influenced by initial magnetic field strength, arrangement, and properties of neutron stars. The creation of second-class particles and asymmetric radiation patterns leads to a single, short gamma-ray burst or multiple, shorter bursts depending on the neutron star's equation of state. The arrangement of magnetic fields plays a crucial role in shaping the binary-star system and emission patterns, while different equations of state and field arrangements produce unique second-class particle and radiation patterns, influencing the final binary-star configuration.

We introduce a new topological invariant of a compact Riemannian manifold $M$ of dimension $n \geq 4$, which relates to the variation of its curvature tensor across all smooth metrics. This invariant, denoted by $\Upsilon(M)$, is calculated as the degree of the mapping from the space of 3-forms on $M$ to the space of its top-dimensional cohomology, equipped with a specific connection. Furthermore, $\Upsilon(M)$ can be expressed as the square of a numerical value derived from the curvature tensor's primary characteristic polynomial, specifically its eigenvalue related to the manifold's topological characteristics. This finds analogy in the study of simple connectedness in dimensions up to 3, and we propose $\Upsilon(M)$ as a candidate for identifying the simply connected manifolds in dimensions 4 and higher.

In a situation involving empirical risk minimization, this paper examines convergence of the Q-procedure, a heuristic method for optimizing tasks involving nonconvex data and nonconvex losses. It can be envisioned as a regularization method that incorporates an expressible term derived from the Hessian of the loss function. It has been suggested in previous studies that the Q-procedure may converge to a local minimum when applied to smooth losses. This paper demonstrates that, under specific assumptions, the Q-procedure converges consistently to a minimum of the original objective function, using statistical information to regulate its output. It achieves this by analyzing the properties of the Q-procedure in terms of its asymptotic distribution and then utilizing these results to establish a form of convergence on the probability space. Additionally, this paper investigates the rate of convergence and the range of variability in the Q-procedure's output, ultimately showing that its asymptotic behavior can be represented by a distribution of Gaussian mixtures on the probability space.

This research proposes a novel technique for rescuing nanoparticles using the strong field amplification offered by graphene surface plasmons. The graphical representation highlights how manipulating the dipoles of graphene oscillations enables the convergence of optical and radiowave energy, thereby translating massive nanoparticles into rapidly moving electrons. The underlying physics relies on precise graphene oscillation control and demonstrates a new application of the device for breaking down large particles.

In medical contexts, the typical response patterns for specific illnesses or injuries can greatly improve patient outcomes by enabling early intervention. This study aims to identify the standard treatment courses for acute illnesses in urban emergency settings, which will later be utilized in developing an online learning framework. The authors analyzed real-world data from over 120,000 patients with acute strokes, bleeding strokes, and concussions, and discovered distinct treatment curves for each condition through multiple timescales and variable representations. These patterns show that hospitals following the standard treatment protocols tend to converge toward the typical curves, which were established using a non-parametric technique called Bayesian Hough Ransac. The study demonstrates the efficacy of using the Bayesian Hough Ransac for fitting complex patterns in high-dimensional data and provides a framework for identifying the standard treatment courses.

A multi-agent approach offers a glimpse into designing cooperative robot systems, highlighting the need for basic robot capabilities such as individual action and limited computational powers, and real-time communication abilities. This work examines collaborative tactics for robots operating in a 2D space, focused on executing pre-defined tasks efficiently through local decisions. Each agent uses a simplified calculation method to select the most suitable action, either moving directly, moving with a predicted target, or synchronizing with other robots. We present a novel strategy called Asynchronous Metastable Cyclic (AMC) and compare it to other collaborative tactics, including a metastable cyclic pattern (MCP) and an asynchronous (ASY) approach. Simulation results for 4 to 16 robots in various densities showed that the AMC strategy achieved the fastest completion times, accompanied by the lowest overall distances traveled, outperforming the MCP and ASY approaches.

The relativistic astrophysical phenomena that occur in pulsar wind nebulae can be mirrored in heavy-ion collisions through the chirality magnetism effect, resulting in specific patterns in charged particle distributions. Researchers at the Large Hadron Collider employed the ALICE detector to look for this effect in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. By analyzing particle correlations, they found that certain patterns decrease as reconstructing particles' charges increase, indicating that other non-chirality magnetism influences are dominant. A new method to minimize these influences has been developed and confirms that these patterns exist within a specific range at lower charges.

On online platforms where Crowd Funding (CF) takes place, researchers have identified specific crowd behaviors and metrics that predict the success of campaigns. Despite the vast amounts of data generated on these platforms, there are still many unknowns regarding how crowd interactions influence each other and affect fundraising efforts. To gain insight into these interactions, this study analyzed a large dataset from a popular all-commodities online crowdfunding platform in China, examining the impact of crowd behaviors and metrics on campaign success from multiple perspectives. By applying statistical and machine learning methods to this data, researchers developed and evaluated indicators of effective fundraising, including key crowd behaviors and metrics that can predict success. Our framework has potential applications in other online settings beyond crowdfunding.

Recently, there has been a surge in cyber threats, leading to significant financial losses and reputational damage for businesses. The detection of network breaches is critical, but the varied capabilities of different systems make it a complex task. In this research, a collaborative program for exchanging cyber threat intelligence is proposed, utilizing peer-to-peer training exchanges to address the issue. A decentralized training approach for breach detection models is developed, allowing exchange partners to tailor their training to their unique expertise and resources. Furthermore, a concept for leveraging collaborative training exchanges is introduced, enabling partners to augment each other's capabilities through shared data and model contributions.

In recent years, researchers have become increasingly interested in using robots to improve productivity in everyday life. A key application has been in the area of multi-part assembly, where robots are used to enhance productivity by reducing the time and complexity involved in assembling items that were previously done by hand. This has led to a notable exception in the field of robot planning, with a notable challenge being the efficient ordering of tasks by robots to facilitate easy assembly. While some methods simplify the problem by applying predefined patterns to task interdependencies, this approach can result in suboptimal outcomes if the initial assumptions are incorrect. In response to this limitation, a notable study presented a technique for automatically determining task order based on visual analysis of parts during the assembly process. However, this method's reliance on visual information makes it prone to errors and limitations, particularly in environments with poor lighting or when multiple parts appear similar. As a result, the study's performance was underwhelming, achieving only 47% of the tasks in a given assembly. In response to these limitations, our research presents a clustering-based algorithm that utilizes an avaricious bias to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of robot task ordering. This is achieved by leveraging the underlying structure of robot interactions, which tends to cluster tasks with strong dependencies together. Our approach achieves remarkable results, outperforming the existing benchmark by 85% using the same evaluation metrics.

The focus of this research is on moving SiMOOSFETs (a type of MOSFET that uses a quantum well at the interface) further along in their development. We have conducted a comprehensive 300mm CMOS process and discovered a straightforward and effective method to increase the speed of these transistors while maintaining good electric properties. Our measurements show that the current performance of SiMOOSFETs compares favorably to state-of-the-art data, with a record-breaking maximum current density of 1.1 MA/cm² and a relatively low voltage of 0.2 V. We also achieved an exceptionally high current density of 10 A/cm² at low voltage in n-SiMOOSFETs, along with a reliable threshold voltage of around -2 V, demonstrating the potential for these transistors to be used in high-performance digital circuits.

In a collection of identical oscillators coupled with each other, their collective behavior remains straightforward to analyze, resulting in synchronized patterns. However, when coupled oscillators have distinct properties, complexities arise, both theoretically and empirically, leading to a deeper understanding of how individual differences impact group dynamics. This study examines the impact of diverse parameters within a team of oscillators on their overall synchronization, highlighting the role of intra-group connections within these collections of identical oscillators. Through our findings, we have discovered that teams with numerous internal interactions exhibit more resilient synchronization, whereas teams with limited interactions between their members demonstrate lower resilience to parameter discrepancies. Furthermore, we have observed that these collections of identical oscillators can display both localized and extensive synchronization.

In online video platforms, source variability bias refers to a phenomenon where different categories of videos are preferred by distinct groups of viewers. For instance, families might prefer kid-friendly content over adult material. Most research focuses on understanding bias within a single user group. This paper delves into a more complex challenge - measuring bias across multiple user groups and eliminates existing obstacles by using publicly available data, crafting a search engine that's both effective and unbiased, and assessing bias in a comprehensive manner. Our research reveals a notable connection between video content and viewer preferences, with our proposed framework dubbed VideoSearch. For our experiments, we created a virtual environment simulating YouTube, comprising 40 broad categories with sufficient quantities of videos and user agents. Our results demonstrate a notable improvement in search accuracy and a straightforward method to assess bias across diverse user groups and content categories. This research contributes to the knowledge of video source variability bias and offers practical recommendations for search engine design to ensure bias minimization in the future.

In a superconformal field theory with a $\mathcal{N}=2$ setup, we're analyzing the monodromy of three-point functions around a special point in the coupling space. These three-point functions are constructed using primary operators of specified dimensions and a specific operator $\Delta_F$, which has a set role in the theory. By examining the monodromy of these functions, we can determine if new constraints exist beyond existing ones as the coupling reaches its critical value. Additionally, we explore the impact of introducing additional operators and examine the monodromy under these variations. These analyses rely on a detailed understanding of the operator product expansion, particularly how $\Delta_F$ interacts with other operators, and on the properties of the resulting operators.

We have found 26 elliptic surfaces, each with 13 points of order 3 on a cubic curve defined over a cyclic cubic field, and from these, we have derived 26 Shafer cycles in 13 different settings. These cubic curves are defined over different cyclic fields and have a associated rank 13 point. Additionally, each cycle corresponds to a unique elliptic surface with 13 points of order 3 on it, as well as an independent rational point on it, as per the hypothesis of the Furstenberg-Park-Conrad theorem's partial case. These unique elliptic surfaces, as specified, are defined over specific number fields that are subfields of a cubic extension of the rationals.

In wireless networks, interference relationships among devices complicate data transmission. Current medium access control (MAC) protocols either disregard interference relationships or treat them as constant, which is not the case in practical scenarios. Our proposed stochastic MAC approach designs a control mechanism to manage wireless data collection networks with complex interference relationships. Utilizing stochastic control theory, we developed a simple and efficient MAC protocol that maximizes throughput while ensuring packet arrival rate is bounded. Our approach involves devices adjusting their transmission probabilities independently, which reduces complexity, and uses a single vector of controls instead of intricate scheduling. Our analytical and simulation results demonstrate the asymptotic optimality of our MAC protocol, along with superior performance compared to existing MAC protocols.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown remarkable performance in node classification, but their reliance on extensive node labeling can be impractical in real-world scenarios. Pseudo-labeling, a popular semi-supervised learning technique, generates labels for unlabeled nodes during training, effectively expanding the labeled node set. However, the accuracy of these pseudo-labels is error-prone, particularly in unlabelled nodes connected to faulty labelled nodes in the initial expansion. The problem is further compounded by current Pseudo-Tagging approaches, leading to a chain reaction of errors in the expanded labels. Our proposed model, Pseudo-Node Expansion (PNE), tackles these issues by introducing a double-iteration pseudo-labeling strategy, incorporating Label Correlation to ensure trustworthy pseudo-labels for nodes in the initial expansion, and a novel node relocation technique to mitigate label contamination. The PNE approach outperforms state-of-the-art deep pseudo-labeling methods in various graph datasets.

In the realm of computer vision, particularly in applications like video-based semantic segmentation and object detection, pinpointing objects within frames is a crucial task. Most existing models treat frames individually, neglecting the sequential nature of video data. Furthermore, they often fail to account for the temporal continuity of objects in a scene, which is vital for generating precise segmentations. To address this limitation, we've developed PatchNet, a cutting-edge deep learning model that leverages patch-level alignment to effectively exploit both intra-frame and inter-frame relationships in a video. By applying PatchNet, we've achieved state-of-the-art results on leading benchmarks like KinDensen, JFT-300K, and COCO, thereby illustrating its efficacy in real-world, high-resolution video analysis.

We examine a system of one-dimensional weighted, multi-species particles that move according to a specific rule: particles whose weights sum to a factor of the system size are sorted in ascending order and distributed evenly throughout the system. When these particles are placed randomly within the system, we show that their final configurations approach a stationary state characterized by a sequence of particle groups of varying weights. These particle groups move en masse and maintain their shapes due to repeated application of a specified rule, inducing a wave-like motion. A detailed description of the system's equilibrium state is provided, along with an algorithm for calculating the frequencies of all possible particle group configurations. Furthermore, we simulate a version of this system where particles can change their weights in response to certain events, and we demonstrate that the resulting system is comparable to a system of non-interacting particles whose spectra are determined by a specific mathematical concept called Wigner matrices.

A future wireless system known as SWIPT-based multi-service wireless systems, which combines energy harvesting and data communication techniques, aims to efficiently utilize resources by minimizing overlap between a power controller's coverage range and the distance over which data signals travel. To overcome this goal, we initially analyze energy harvesting capabilities in a system using a power splitting approach, before developing an iterative method for optimizing data communication and energy harvesting performance, and finally propose a high efficiency protocol that achieves optimal performance in certain scenarios.

In a repulsive SU(N) Fermi mixture with both spin polarized and polarized components, specifically in the repulsive SU(6) mixture with two components and repulsive SU(5) mixtures with both one and two components, our analysis shows that the energy per particle exhibits a similar, component-independent, strong-coupling behavior. The component independence of the strong-coupling expansion is demonstrated for the repulsive SU(6) mixture with two components using both exact numerical calculations and an analytical approach. The exact numerical calculations employ the Cluster-DMRG method and are compared to an analytical approach that involves expanding the energy in both the particle density and the coupling strength, resulting in a series expansion. The latter is then compared to the known strong-coupling expansion, which is itself based on a series expansion in the particle density and the coupling strength but is instead evaluated at a specific finite coupling strength and then extrapolated to the infinite limit. The repulsive SU(5) mixture with either one or two components, however, requires an even more complex analysis, specifically in the construction of the many-body wave function, particularly the Gaudin matrix, which is necessary to evaluate the energy per particle at both moderate and strong couplings, and also shows component independence.

We present a simple electrical circuit model that mimics the behavior of standard microwave optomechanics, featuring a cavity coupled to a lumped mechanical oscillator represented by a parallel RLC circuit. By equating microwave cavity field predictions in both the optical and electrical frameworks, we derive a fundamental identification principle for mapping the optical measurement results to the electrical circuit components. Furthermore, we extend the circuit model to account for various optical laser driving configurations, including the linear and nonlinear geometries, and demonstrate the mapping in this case by comparing the electrical and optical responses experimentally. Our circuit model offers a versatile tool for analyzing and optimizing optomechanical systems, providing valuable insight into their behavior.

Witten's quantum field theory formula generates a series of correlation functions in a specific framework and these correlation functions exhibit remarkable, intricate patterns despite their seemingly random origins. Previous research has identified particular correlation functions with specific properties, such as the presence of minimal models and coset models, and the creation of multiple universal airiness through nonlinear transformations. Building on this previous work, new correlations have been found, and existing connections to Lie algebras have been extended to include B-type affine Kac-Moody algebras. Additionally, the development of multiple universal airiness has been linked to key concepts within representation theory, particularly the multiplicity of a certain operator's eigenvalues and the presence of a secondary, less understood duality principle.

During exploration, robots operating in unfamiliar environments can encounter sudden obstacles, necessitating swift adjustments in their movement plans. The emergence of these obstacles poses a challenge for robots, as their built-in plans frequently fall short due to the inevitable discrepancies between predicted and actual paths. In this research, we examine the potential of utilizing uncomplicated, robust movement strategies suitable for navigating through complex environments, focusing particularly on the case when objects adhere to the robots' surface. We consider two scenarios: (i) when the adherence is predictable, (ii) when it is not, causing unexpected changes in the robots' movement plans. The movement strategies were tested on a diverse set of objects in both scenarios; the results show their simplicity and robustness despite their limited efficiency compared to their optimized counterparts. The study offers an alternative approach for facilitating obstacle-free movements in scenarios featuring unpredictable obstacles and situations with limited visibility, thereby enhancing the robustness of movement strategies.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Smoke exposure during laparoscopic surgery has well-documented negative effects on surgeons' visibility. To counter this, smoke clearance has long been the primary focus. However, improving visibility can be a more effective approach. To explore this, we investigated the impact of smoke reduction on identifying smoke in surgical videos. Smoke detection proved easier in smoke-reduced images, suggesting that clearance could facilitate better video processing. Building on this finding, we explored smoke-reducing algorithms' potential benefits for video processing. One such algorithm, Wavelet Thresholding, not only reduced smoke intensity but also enhanced image quality, making smoke detection simpler. Similarly, the Fast Wavelet Transform derived model performed well. Notably, the Temporal Smoke Detection model, which incorporates Wavelet Thresholding, outperformed other derivatives by 11.52%. This outstanding performance could be attributed to the algorithm's smoke suppression, which corrected low-frequency spatial smoke components, thereby mimicking smoke removal. We believe our findings will serve as a starting point for a new area of research, 'Smoke Clearance via Visually Helpful Smoke Clearance', which aims to establish a connection between smoke clearance and smoke detection.

This research proposes a new type of M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate that is designed to be resilient to frequency changes. To achieve this, the gate uses a complex entanglement process involving multiple atomic and crystal waveguide modes. By carefully preparing a specific quantum state, the gate becomes highly resistant to frequency errors, requiring only slightly longer execution time to remain accurate. This improved gate design is an essential component for creating more durable quantum gates and is particularly useful when working with complex quantum systems.

Research into the theoretical aspects of ferroelectric materials is a popular area of study due to their unique properties, but the high cost and scarcity of single crystal samples for analysis hinder practical research opportunities. To overcome these limitations, researchers often rely on computer simulations to gain insight into the materials' behavior. Specifically, they study the materials in their paraelectric state, as this allows them to compare simulated results with experimental findings of the material's polar properties in its ferroelectric state. The main goal of these simulations is to develop a comprehensive understanding of the materials' phase Curves and switchability characteristics based on the electronic structure of the materials. 

We present our new approach to modelling the paraelectric structure of ferroelectric materials, focusing on the bismuth-based materials BiT and BZT. We show that the external pressure applied to these materials results in increased internal pressure, which triggers a symmetric distortion of the lattice grid and creates a pathway for dynamic switchability. We also explore the impact of chemical modifications to these materials on their Curves and switchability characteristics, revealing that certain substitutions can make the materials paraelectric at room temperature, while other substitutions can improve switchability by reducing the energy barrier, even if the switch occurs through a centrosymmetric phase. We demonstrate that such substitutions can increase the dynamic ferroelectric response by one order of magnitude. 

These findings highlight the potential of our structure-based approach to design ferroelectric materials that can easily be switched even at room temperature, paving

Multivariate data analyzed in various fields often exhibit intricate dependencies among variables that can be modeled using covariance or correlation matrices. The Gaussian process is a fundamental model extending beyond individual data points to collections of variables, yet its graphical representations are limited, making it difficult to capture data relationships. We introduce the functional Gaussian graphical framework, a novel approach that enables modeling complex relationships among variables within Gaussian processes through a covariance or correlation matrix defined by a functional matrix. This introduction is rooted in the existing concept of graphically generated Gaussian processes. We derive distinct characteristics of our model, including the requirements for functional matrices to ensure the validity of their underlying Gaussian processes. We also provide a method for estimating the parameters of our model using existing estimators, along with a simulation-based evaluation of our approach and its potential applications to modeling the relationships within Gaussian processes.

In constructing a quantum circuit with recurring unit patterns as inputs/outputs, determining the circuit's overall period becomes a crucial challenge. This paper presents two straightforward, combinatorial approaches to achieve this goal. Firstly, we propose a direct method to calculate the circuit's period. Alternatively, we can utilize a simpler method that divides the circuit into fundamental building blocks, then analyze the pattern's behavior within these components. Furthermore, we develop a practical framework for assembling quantum circuits featuring overlapping patterns as inputs/outputs, enabled by our period-determining techniques. This framework allows us to precisely define the circuit's output pattern through a straightforward, finite process.

We examine the average-case complexity of optimizing convex functions over symmetric boolean functions and explore its relationship with differential privacy and other relaxation notions. Our research reveals that a specific concept of average-case strength is more relevant in this context, and we establish that it satisfies certain desirable properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that average-case complexity does not provide the desired improvement over traditional worst-case analysis for certain problems, but also shows that average-case complexity is indeed more versatile than worst-case complexity in various scenarios. Moreover, we extend our concept of average-case strength to other functional properties like Lipschitz continuity and infinity convergence. Our research explores the relationships between these properties of average-case strength and other relaxation notions like propagation rules and approximation ratios.

In a bilayer semiconductor system with weakly coupled excitons, the collective excitonic field has a significant influence on the kinetic behavior of the carriers. By drawing on polaron theory, our study examines the effect of excitonic field on carrier mobility in such a bilayer semiconductor. We find that the excitonic field interacts with the carrier's kinetic energy via a complementary manner during the carrier's motion, which in turn determines the carrier's effective mass. Additionally, our investigation of the carrier's motion in the presence of an external electric field reveals that the effective mass of the carrier increases with reduced distance between the layers in a bilayer semiconductor.

High-determinacy, high-dependency systems like autonomous vehicles risk catastrophic failure if their reliability heavily depends on a single source. In this paper, multiple independent methods for pinpointing a vehicle's location are evaluated and an adaptive algorithm is developed to select the most trustworthy estimation. A specialized tracking mechanism is also designed to utilize consistent data streams from various sources and an innovative method is introduced to validate the integrity of each method's output. Furthermore, an adaptive algorithm detects and adjusts to changing conditions such as signal strength, motion pattern, and a combination of both. Working in tandem, these components ensure the highest reliability of the system's operation.

Investigations of $W^{\pm}Z$ production in $pp$ collisions at 13 TeV are conducted with the ATLAS detector, utilizing 2015-2018 data totaling 139 inverse femtobarns of collected data. $W^{\pm}Z$ events resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons are analyzed to examine their production properties and compare to theoretical predictions from the Standard Model and beyond.

In the framework of gravity theory, the Cotton tensor serves as a means to extend the gravitational field description beyond what is offered by the Einstein tensor. This report aims to illustrate the significance of the Cotton tensor within the context of 3-dimensional gravity models. Specifically, we will examine its relation to the equations of motion, the conserved currents stemming from Einstein's equations, and its role in defining new conserved charges.

This research explores both Boolean geometric duality and Stone geometric duality in the context of orthocomplemented lattices. A specific algebraic structure known as a weakly distributive lattice has been identified, possessing unique properties that enable the replication of both duality theories. Furthermore, a generalized form of the Stone theorem has been established, allowing a compact Hausdorff topology to be constructed from any orthocomplemented lattice in a topologically consistent manner.

We introduce a visualization tool, coq-psv, that renders proofs from the Coq theorem prover as interactive flowcharts, allowing users to explore and traverse these proofs. coq-psv supports visualization of a broad range of tactics, including multiple induction schemes, cut, and inversion. It is particularly useful for enhancing understanding of individual steps and the overall proof development process. coq-psv is fully compatible with newer versions of Coq and can import files from multiple locations, including local folders, GitHub, and GitLab repositories. While designed primarily for educational purposes, it is also suitable for any user seeking to gain insight into their proofs, improve teaching and learning activities, or simply gain a deeper understanding of their work. coq-psv is free, open-source, and available on GitHub, alongside comprehensive documentation and a pre-configured Docker image for easy installation and use.

We show that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is the most advanced result in this field since the work of Iwaniec, Sarnak, and Borain at the Sunbelt Conference in 1988.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence is a primary concern.  By accelerating the convergence of the iterative solution, IPMs can reach their optimal limits more quickly.  One effective means to enhance the interior point method is to utilize an efficient solver for the linear equation system that can take advantage of its special properties.  In this article, various methods for accelerating the convergence of the iterative solution are presented.  Additionally, several popular methods for speeding up the interior point method are reviewed.  It is also demonstrated how an efficient solver can contribute to achieving optimal Lanzos and Conjugate Gradient-like solutions even in the presence of a preconditioner.  This can result in further improvements in convergence.

Determining large Q values for the polarized $N$-th flavor parton number is essential but difficult to achieve. Researchers propose an innovative approach, the Variable Flavor Number Scheme (VFNS), which enables them to calculate $N$-dependent parton densities at a specific scale mu^2 as Q approaches this value. However, this method requires intricate theoretical calculations and is heavily dependent on mathematical intricacies. In this study, we simplify these complexities by deriving exact expressions for crucial matrix elements and simplify the calculation of the crucial soft function, ultimately leading to the derivation of the crucial scale-dependent part $A_{gq}(N)$ at the third order of $\alpha_s$ and is similar to previously published results but is calculated through a different, more complex method. Researchers also analyze how this derivation is influenced by different mathematical methods and find that these results are consistent with a pre-existing matrix element but with modified behavior at large Q values. Researchers also examine and discuss all assumptions and analyze various scenarios, including the behavior of matrix elements as Q approaches infinity and when $\alpha_s$ approaches zero. Researchers further investigate and derive associated expressions for the crucial gluon and light quarks. Researchers also derive associated expressions for the crucial gluon and light quarks when certain conditions are not met.
