In the assessment of students' performance, commonly employed methods involve
scale-based evaluation, ranking, and percentage assignments.  This paper
investigates how these measures are propagated during the calculation of
standard deviations and means.  We have discovered that using these evaluation
methods can lead to distorted averages and increased variability, ultimately
affecting further statistical analyses.  In most cases, the distortions can give
rise to erroneous conclusions.  We have also identified instances where the
distortions may not result in significant outcomes but have still presented
alternative solutions to mitigate their impact.  In addition, this paper also
examines the distortions caused by rounding students' test scores to the nearest
whole number and how this practice can result in distorted statistics.

When moving randomly within a two-dimensional space, the possible locations of a path of a fixed length can be counted by considering all the possible sequences of steps that comprise this length. For instances where the geometric structure of the space needs to be taken into account, such as in a hexagonal lattice, the number of possible locations can be determined using a quadratic equation. However, when the lattice structure becomes more complex, as in the case of a lattice with a structure that can be formed by connecting the points of a cube with the diagonals, the number of possible locations can be described using a formula involving the factorial function. For instances where the geometric structure of the space is not taken into account, such as when moving randomly within a two-dimensional space with a length of 2N, the possible locations can be counted by considering all the possible sequences of steps that comprise this length. For instances of such movement, the possible locations can be described using a formula involving the factorial function and the base of the logarithm used to express the size of a certain set that comprises the grid of numbers from -N to N in the dimension of d.

Building upon previous work by Bodendorfer, et al., we have expanded the
Gambini-Olmedo-Pullin model of spherically symmetric black holes into a more
detailed polymerized phase space. We employed the Hamiltonian formulation to
generate symplectic structure components, which ultimately enabled the
calculation of sharp quantum corral boundaries and initial data constraints.
Furthermore, our research involved analyzing the impact of quantum gravity effects
on the black hole's quasinormal frequencies, as modeled by the eikonal method.
Our specific findings include the derivation of first-order quantum corrections to
these frequencies. Additionally, we discovered that these corrections are
universally applicable, extending beyond the initially considered $l=0,1,2$ cases.

Thanks to the unique thermal properties of the electrons in graphene, the thermal conductivity of the material is extremely high. However, the thermal conductivity of graphene is significantly affected when the material is in contact with other substances, particularly if those substances have significantly higher or lower electrical resistances. The interface between graphene and the other material causes a significant increase in the thermal resistance when the temperature differs substantially from its ideal value, indicating a significant increase in the thermal conductivity of the combined system. The total thermal conductivity of the combined system can be effectively described as a sum of the thermal conductivity of the two individual materials and the thermal conductivity resulting from the effective heat transfer at their interface, which must be below a certain critical temperature. The total thermal conductivity of the combined system can also be effectively described as a sum of the thermal conductivity of the two individual materials and the thermal conductivity resulting from the effective heat transfer at their interface, which significantly varies with the electrical resistance of the other material, particularly at low electrical resistances. The total thermal conductivity of the combined system can be effectively described as a sum of the thermal conductivity of the two individual materials and the thermal conductivity resulting from the effective heat transfer at their interface, which significantly varies with the electrical resistance per layer, particularly at high electrical resistances. Automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech technologies have advanced significantly, enabling high-quality speech synthesis from written text. Nonetheless, speech generation directly from text remains an intricate challenge, primarily due to the disparities between spoken language and standard written rules. To bridge this gap, a novel non-parallel dataset was developed, containing spoken words with explicit word focus, which are subsequently combined to form sentence-focused speech. A model was proposed to tackle the new dataset, leveraging masking and prioritization techniques for context-sensitive word generation. Experimental results on the FocusedSpeech dataset revealed that our approach surpasses the performance of baseline systems, achieving noticeable enhancements in word-level accuracy.

This research introduces an advanced method for mapping inference, leveraging hidden data to improve predictive predictions. By utilizing a comprehensive model that incorporates hidden information and is based on Gaussian Processes, we can generate accurate predictions and assess the reliability of these predictions. Furthermore, we analyze the computational expenses associated with incorporating hidden data, demonstrating that its impact can be significant, especially when dealing with large datasets. To mitigate these expenses, we propose an iterative approach, removing the least influential hidden data points iteratively until a predetermined threshold is reached. This method allows for the mapping inference to be applicable on datasets that were previously too large to process.

Advances in deep learning have enabled the creation of sophisticated artificial intelligence systems, prompting a growing need for robust security measures. While existing security protocols primarily focus on controlling data access, there is an emerging need for techniques that can safeguard against malicious attacks on machine learning models themselves. This paper explores the threat posed by intercessors launching attacks on machine learning models, and sheds light on the particular challenge posed by data manipulators who exploit vulnerabilities in the training process. A novel intercessor-assisted attack on the generative adversarial network (GAN) is presented, along with two practical applications that compromise both supervised and semi-supervised machine learning models. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this intercessory GAN attack, and highlight potential avenues for future research into the robustness of machine learning models.

In recent years, social media platforms have become a primary source of information for a broad audience, allowing a vast range of voices to be heard. As a result, social media platforms have become ideal settings for spreading conspiracy theories, including those that deny the urgent need to address climate change. Our study examines the most prevalent forms of climate change denial conspiracy theories found online, and their dissemination through social media posts by influential social media personalities. It also delves into the impact of these conspiracy theories on social media platforms during significant climate events, and the strategies used by these platforms to address them. This research provides an overview of the current landscape of climate change denial conspiracy theories on social media, highlighting their implications for discourse and content moderation.

We have conducted a comprehensive investigation into dark matter production coupled with a single top quark or a pair of top quarks in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level.  The study was undertaken utilizing a dataset totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data that was recorded by the CMS experiment.  Top quark-associated dark matter is categorized into two primary scenarios, namely a dark-boson, derived from a top quark, or a dark quark, derived from a top quark pair.  To establish the optimal model parameters for our search, we utilized two distinct theoretical models.  The results of our experiment fell short of the predicted signals from the simplified models, thereby resulting in limits that are more stringent at 12.8 TeV and 6.6 TeV, respectively, for the dark-boson and dark quark models, both of which are based on the ideal scenario in which the mass of the dark particles equals half the mass of the top quark.  The limits that we have established are the most stringent to date as they relate to this particular process and offer substantial enhancements over previous limits, thereby expanding our understanding of the theoretical models, thereby resulting in substantial enhancements.

Given an n-exangulated framework (C, F, W) that adheres to specific criteria and a functor T that meets certain conditions with respect to C and Ang(C), this study demonstrates the existence of a unique functor T' such that T' is isomorphic to T when restricted to thin kernels of morphisms in C and that both functors T and T' maintain the Ang(C)-duality property. Consequently, for n-exangulated categories that satisfy specific criteria, the study establishes the equivalence of the Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality for subcategories comprised of thin kernels and the Ang(C)-duality property. Additionally, the study provides explanations and examples that support these findings.

Economists' understanding of instrument validity relies heavily on the concept of 'disciplines of study' being suitable instruments for returns on investment in various fields of study. Although the model appears to offer extensive applications of instrument validation, we reveal in this paper that the premise is faulty. Investment returns are unbounded and often negative in many fields of study. As a result, the model's conclusion does not apply when the outcome is binary, and the assumed discourses may not be applicable in certain cases. We present an empirical example related to higher education in the UK, demonstrating that using the model's argumentation to justify returns on investment in different subjects of study may lead to erroneous results.

The collective behavior of numerous antinucleons and antibaryons is essential 
for understanding hadron dynamics but due to limitations in existing experimental 
research, many features of these particles remain unknown. A high-energy electron 
beam facility has the potential to produce a substantial quantity of these antiparticles 
and we propose that a next-generation nuclear and particle physics experiment utilizing 
this beam could provide precise measurements of their properties. This could in turn 
enable new insights into the behaviors of their positive counterparts. Furthermore, 
by studying these negative particles, we can gain insight into their positive counterparts 
and enhance our understanding of quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the discovery 
of new baryons is possible with these experiments.

In systems consisting of three stars orbiting a shared center, the general theoretical framework suggests that the widening rate outpaces the overall orbital expansion. This acceleration is attributed to various factors, including the transfer of energy from inner to outer orbits, which occurs as smaller celestial bodies like planets or asteroids move within the system. The widening rate is expected to be influenced by key factors such as the mass of these smaller bodies and the area within the inner orbits where they reside. This paper establishes precise mathematical relationships for these factors in a comprehensive theoretical framework. Additionally, the study includes detailed analyses of the predicted timeframes over the course of 200 billion years, considering various possible scenarios and comparing the outcomes to observed data from relevant astronomical studies.

In four-dimensional lattice quantum gravity, the state space is composed of locally flat spacetime configurations with varying geometries represented by quantum operators. The predictive ability of the theory depends on how these different spacetime configurations interrelate, particularly in cosmological settings where the spacetime geometry can shift significantly. Researchers examined the properties of the quantum Hamiltonian in the cosmological framework to assess how different spacetime geometries interact. Their analysis focused on a specific type of spacetime, three-dimensionally topologically complex, where the global structure can vary substantially. The results showed that, even in this case, the Hamiltonian's properties remained largely unchanged, adhering to established principles. To further investigate the behavior of the Hamiltonian, researchers explored an explicitly two-dimensional model of quantum gravity, where the phase space encompasses a wide range of geometric configurations. In this setting as well, the phase space's diverse geometry did not affect the Hamiltonian's characteristics. Ultimately, the study concluded that, regardless of the geometric diversity of the state space, certain properties of quantum gravity remain unchanged.

This study proposes a novel variational image model that integrates the successes of image recovery techniques with image partitioning methods. Our approach divides an image into distinct regions, where each retains significantly more image detail, and thereby eliminates the challenges associated with processing incomplete or low-quality images. Our model incorporates a data-driven term to preserve texture information, and a seamless image transition criterion to enhance region classification. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our approach in producing meaningful image segments, and its effectiveness in overcoming obstacles typically encountered in image partitioning methods.

Our research focuses on the relationship between ultralight bios and the spin properties of supermassive black holes. We used the theory of black hole superradiance, establishing that as a result of superradiance, the spin of the black hole should decrease over time. We calculated the rate of spin decline, determined the maximum amplitude of the process, and identified the specific frequency range in which it occurs, all of which are influenced by the initially rotating black hole. By applying our findings to a dataset of 86 quasars, we used statistical analysis to investigate the diversity of black hole spins in the local universe. Ultimately, our research revealed that the majority of these black holes have low to moderate spins, with a few exceptions of highly spinning black holes.

Creating intelligent, bioinspired systems poses significant challenges due to diverse underlying computing architectures. For successful deployment in real-world settings, it's crucial to address fundamental hurdles such as cross-platform compatibility and predictable error behavior. We've developed an emulator to bridge the gap between software and hardware, allowing bioinspired systems to function across different platforms. Our approach leverages the popular Brian simulator to provide a clear path for transitioning hardware-inspired solutions to software-based solutions. We've detailed the technical aspects of our emulator, focusing on how Brian's dynamic language components can be expanded to include hardware-specific timing aspects. Our work has paved the way for systematic assessments of the accuracy and reliability of bioinspired computing systems, enabling the development of robust cross-platform intelligent systems.

A significant finding has been made about the dynamic properties of coronal arcs, which have been linked to minor solar flares, providing new insights into their non-thermal behavior. Observations of a solar active region on June 6, 2021, revealed a brief solar flare of less than one hour, associated with tiny X-ray brightening, originating from a fine-scale coronal arc. Studies of the arc's structure over time showed how it changed in response to the flare. Just before the flare the arc appeared as two separate entities, but moments later they had merged into a single entity with two distinct peaks. Data suggested that the peaks represent the arc's components which are linked by a shorter magnetic field. The discovery of this brief solar flare and related events offer a unique opportunity for studying the brief solar flare's impact on coronal dynamics in detail. The findings also shed new light on how magnetic field instability, for the first time, is thought to have triggered a brief solar flare, which in turn has a significant impact on coronal dynamics.

A novel, planar, and compact optical trap has been developed using a magnetic core at the center of a ferromagnetic core transformer. This innovative design leverages the magnetic field's spatial variation to trap particles, eliminating the need for an external magnetic coil. The magnetic field's gentle gradient provides a soft trap for particles, while its simplicity and compactness enable integration of the trap within a planar microfluidic system. The device effectively captures 2-μm diameter polystyrene beads and demonstrates a high degree of magnetic field sensitivity, as well as resistance to external magnetic fields. The design's planar architecture facilitates integration with a microfluidic system that has undergone the PDMS process, and it can be easily integrated with various microfluidic systems using a PDMS substrate.

The accretion of rotating gas near a supermassive black hole is investigated using advanced computational methods, where the gas is modeled as a dynamic, collisionless entity governed by the Vlasov equation. Coupled with a hydrodynamic approach, this study accounts for the importance of angular momentum in shaping the accretion process. Initially, we focus on the accretion rates derived from analytical and numerical models for non-rotating gas within an infinite, homogeneous distribution. Next, we explore computer-simulated scenarios for rotating gas within a finite, bounded area near the black hole. Our simulations consider a black hole of 1.4 x 10^9 solar masses and a gas component with a fixed angular momentum distribution. As such, these scenarios represent a reasonable approximation of the environment surrounding a supermassive black hole at its formation. Within a limited radius (approximately 3.2 parsec) surrounding the black hole, our simulations reveal that the accretion rates for rotating and non-rotating gas differ by a factor of at least 10, indicating the significant impact of angular momentum on the accretion process. Furthermore, by comparing non-rotating gas models for a finite versus infinite radius, we find reduced accretion rates by a factor of 1.5 to 3, implying the global influence of a surrounding sphere of matter on the accretion process.

The rate at which radiation is emitted from an atom, powered by slow movement along a slim mirror, is examined in detail. This rate is influenced by several factors including the non-relativistic velocity of the atom, the angle at which it approaches the mirror, and the thickness of the mirror. A rigorous approach based on the principles of quantum electrodynamics is employed to analyze this phenomenon, utilizing a sophisticated mathematical framework known as the in-out formalism. This method involves representing the atom and the mirror as components of a larger system with well-defined properties, and then expanding its Hamiltonian and Lagrangian to identify key interaction terms. Following this, the system's time-evolution is studied under the influence of strong interactions between the atom and the mirror, and finally, the probability distribution of radiated photons is calculated in different scenarios. Notably, our findings show that not only is the rate of radiation ramped up by this method, but also that the emission occurs in both directional and diffuse patterns, depending on specific conditions. This research presents a new understanding of the relationship between atomic movement and electromagnetic phenomena, and it could potentially be applied in the development of advanced technologies, as well as in fundamental research on the properties of atoms.

The extraordinary young cluster Westerlund 2, hosting a spectacular HII region and rich stellar population, boasts an impressive array of luminous stars including multiple red supergiants and a historic O star supernova precursor. A recent study by Bonanos et al. (2022) focuses on classifying the cluster's outer members, and our analysis digs deeper into their constituent stellar types. Unlike other clusters, Westerlund 2's distribution exhibits an uneven spread towards its periphery, particularly in the region surrounding the HII region, where a distinct cluster member population emerges, notably rich in red supergiant and O-type stars. Notably, these cluster members display an extended radius when compared to the HII region's core, signifying a historic displacement of these stars from the core, hinting at past mass ejection episodes and potential future supernovae explosions that could reshape the cluster forever.

This paper investigates the ground ap proximations to a biharmonic Choquard equation that incorporates exponential growth terms, under Hardy-type inequalities present within the same mathematical space. Utilizing a fixed point argument and truncated potential functions, we demonstrate the existence of a standardized ground solution to the given equation. Additionally, we establish the non-degeneracy of this solution and its unique characteristics within the context of its associated energy functional, which possesses a definite sign in its H\"older space equivalent.

In the field of Optical Character Recognition (OCR), it's widely acknowledged that successfully processing degraded handwritten text leads to better results, as it allows for more accurate error detection and correction. Motivated by this understanding, a novel two-stage adversarial network is proposed, which aims to enhance handwritten document images while promoting their readability. Initially, a network focused on data augmentation and image improvement is trained, utilizing a deep learning strategy to convert low-resolution, degraded images into higher-quality, more legible forms. Subsequently, these improved images are fed into an OCR system, where a specially designed task is implemented to identify and mark areas of the image that contain recognition errors. These error markers are then incorporated into an error correction module, enabling the ERNIE-OCR framework to provide precise error correction. Thorough experiments conducted on multiple large datasets conclusively demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, as the integration of this method yields a significant 60% increase in ERNIE-OCR's accuracy and a 12.57% reduction in errors.

Indonesia's rapid population growth poses significant challenges in identity document management. To address these issues, the government implemented an electronic identity document (E-KTP) system; however, the process was hindered by widespread corruption. To combat document forgery and counterfeiting, the government introduced a new generation of E-KTP cards featuring a microcontroller and radio communications capabilities. Despite these efforts, numerous fake ID cards continue to persist in the system. To combat document forgery, this research proposes an Indonesian ID card extraction tool, which leverages a combination of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to efficiently retrieve ID card information from both scanned and real images.

In Intelligent Transportation Systems, the reliability of wireless connections is crucial. Research has shown that IEEE 802.11p's performance can be enhanced through Clear Channel Assessment (CCA). Recent analyses highlighted an issue with instantaneous CCA CIR Cancellation CCA (IC4) in real-world scenarios, where vehicle movement affects IEEE 802.11p's CCA accuracy. This led to the development of an IC4-based strategy that utilizes deep learning to improve IEEE 802.11p's CCA reliability. However, rapid changes in wireless channel conditions pose a challenge to IC4's effectiveness. This can be mitigated through incorporating a temporal averaging approach. Early testing indicated a superior performance of the modified strategy in adapting to dynamic wireless environments. This paper presents an enhanced temporal averaging approach, temporal averaging of IC4 (T-IC4), that incorporates deep learning with temporal analysis. Comprehensive simulations validate superior performance of T-IC4 in diverse channel conditions, surpassing IC4 and instantaneous IC4 in reliability, false negative rates, and packet loss ratios.

This research presents an innovative color correction and image enlargement technique inspired by the Celestial Gradient Hint, and incorporates it into a Generative Adversarial Network to accelerate training. We evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness across various color correction scenarios and compare its performance to existing image enlargement techniques.

We've developed a novel neural network architecture that bypasses traditional gradient-based optimization challenges. By incorporating the Universal Approximation Principle, our method enables neural networks to effectively learn complex non-linear relationships without becoming overfit. The Universal Approximation Principle states that any continuous function can be approximated to a high degree of accuracy using a weighted sum of the outputs from non-linear units, typically polynomial or sigmoidal in nature. Building upon this principle, our approach focuses on constructing neural networks capable of approximating complex functions more efficiently.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCA) serves a crucial purpose in connecting young researchers from various European countries working in experimental particle physics. In this role, the committee organizes bi-annual online meetings that bring together ECRs from 32 ECFA member countries, focusing on relevant topics to their careers and interests. This is achieved through invited talks from renowned speakers and engaging discussions led by experienced individuals. Additionally, the committee conducts regular surveys to gauge ECRs' concerns and preferences, using the feedback to shape its activities and goals. This document outlines the committee's structure, goals, accomplishments from 2021-2022, and future objectives.

The behavior of waves propagating through periodic structures is fundamentally impacted by their underlying geometry. By incorporating elements with optical properties into traditional wave theory, researchers can manipulate wave dispersion and roton characteristics to achieve directional propagation. To exploit this phenomenon in optical applications, there is a need for structures exhibiting dual periodicities, where theory currently lacks comprehensive analysis. This work presents a dual metastructure capable of guiding waves in multiple directions, and provides optical modifications to this design, facilitating directional wave control.

As human-robot cooperative learning advances, the scale of its applications is expanding beyond manufacturing and into service industries. However, current cooperative learning platforms have several limitations. They require pre-defined models and inputs from experts, assuming the availability of ample expertise and time. In real-world cooperative learning, 'teaching the expert' often proves to be a costly and impractical approach. To address these issues, there is a need for more intelligent and adaptive learning systems that can leverage available data and learn from experience, especially in complex and dynamic environments where human input may be scarce. This paper introduces a new concept, known as Cognitive AI Frameworks, which provide a versatile solution for cooperative learning applications. We demonstrate their effectiveness in a complex drone-aided search and rescue scenario, characterized by high uncertainty, dynamic environments, and limited availability of labeled data, thereby highlighting their potential to revolutionize the balance between cognitive load and adaptive capabilities in cooperative learning systems.

A new bias-corrected estimator is developed for the average absolute deviation around the median. The proposed estimator is specifically designed for the median absolute deviation and is constructed by applying the influence function of the median. Properties of the estimator, such as consistency and asymptotic normality, are established under certain conditions. The theoretical results demonstrate that the new estimator shares many of the desirable properties with the standard maximum likelihood estimator. The performance of the estimator is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations and comparative studies on real-world data.

Unsupervised relation discovery focuses on identifying correlations between high-level semantic concepts and specific word meanings.  Recent approaches involve constructing a knowledge graph from datasets and then predicting how words in a dataset's vocabulary are connected.  Our method uses connection prediction between word embeddings and concept embeddings to boost relation discovery performance.  Additionally, we've developed a new metric for evaluating connection prediction that takes into consideration the dataset's annotation cooccurrences.  Our results show that using this new metric leads to improved performance on the SemBert dataset using just 10 concept annotations.

In a N-dimensional QCD environment with momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential, we investigate the characteristics of quarkonium disintegration in a heated QCD matter. Employing an approach based on quasi-particle Debye mass, we derive an expression for the dissociation temperature of quarkonium states in terms of anisotropy, number of spatial dimensions, and baryonic chemical potential. Furthermore, utilizing this approach, we calculate the disintegration characteristics of quarkonium states such as J/ψ, ψ', χc and charmonium states in a N-dimensional and 3-dimensional QCD environment for varying values of anisotropy, number of spatial dimensions and baryonic chemical potential.

The arrangement of magnetic bonds in Tb3RuO7, featuring chains of spin-3/2 ruthenium, has been determined to be a non-uniform state. Located in a crystallographic axis offset by approximately 3.5 degrees, these bonds are subjected to varying internal magnetic fields. As a result of the uneven field, the bonds within the ruthenium chains experience distinct states of magnetic ordering - some are synchronized, while others are randomly aligned. Resonance spectra, measured using neutron-diffraction experiments, further confirm the presence of magnetic ordering within the ruthenium chains. Typically exhibiting long-range magnetic ordering, substances with spin-3/2 chains often exhibit unique properties that arise from the competition between internal fields and magnetic coupling.

While the primary focus of deep learning is image processing, the technique has not been equally effective in replicating the physiological responses of early stage visual areas, particularly V1. To bridge this gap, researchers have employed various methods, but most are limited in their ability to generalize representations across different scales. Our approach tackles this challenge by developing a modulated cylinder coordinates learning framework, which enables the creation of a comprehensive, scale-agnostic representation of local functions. Our key contribution is the introduction of modulated cyclic activation units (MCAs) that serve as the fundamental building blocks for learning the coordinates of features. By utilizing a combination of symmetric and anti-symmetric element-wise activations, MCAs are capable of expressing scale-related as well as phase-specific information, resulting in a comprehensive representation of positions in multiple scales. Our proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on various numerical cognition tasks such as generation, denoising, and completion, and our results show that it outperforms existing methods and generates representations that resemble those found in the biological responses of V1.

Traditional instance learning and semi-supervised learning techniques may not be effective in real-world scenarios where data is often annotated, but class labels do not exist or shift when the distribution of instances changes. We introduce semi-generative modeling, which uses a generative model to predict probabilities and data instances, and can handle such complex scenarios. Specifically, we propose a new method that utilizes cause and influence attributes to adjust its predictions and account for covariate shift. When incorporating labeled data, it learns to integrate instance and attribute probability distributions. When only unlabeled data is available, it learns to synchronize instance and attribute distributions. Our approach successfully applies to real-world datasets, outperforming existing methods in both direct and indirect comparisons. The developed code is freely accessible on our laboratory's website.

Despite its impressive practical results, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain poorly understood. This lack of clarity poses significant obstacles, hindering efforts to develop more robust models, reduce reliance on costly grid searches, and inform the creation of new neural network architectures. This study seeks to shed light on these mysteries by comparing the mathematical principles underlying deep learning models to established concepts in physics and engineering. By translating the training process into a force-based analogy, researchers can leverage centuries of experience from physics, clarifying concepts such as generalization, overfitting, and the role of geometry in feature learning. This line of inquiry may also provide novel insights into the behavior of complex systems and the potential for deep learning models to capture essential properties of the world.

This research aims to extend previous findings regarding a unique generator, the chief, within a local commutative polynomial ring containing a single variable over a local Noetherian ring (especially in the case of $k[[x]]$ where $k$ is a local Noetherian ring). It demonstrates that any proper prime ideal generated within this ring, when considered over its residue field, contains a chief. Furthermore, it establishes the equivalence of two depths (the lattice depth and Cohen-Macaulay depth) for ideals within this ring, and also their relationship with another depth measurement.

Machine learning's broad utilization spans numerous scientific and engineering disciplines, yet its reliance on a data-driven approach frequently hinders understanding. To address this, machine learning systems are increasingly being supplemented with explainability tools. Conversely, these explainability measures can introduce new challenges, not the least being the creation of trustworthy systems. This study seeks to develop a novel approach to guarantee the reliability of machine learning-based jet classification systems. It proposes a framework that identifies and prioritizes key features using multivariate statistical analysis and uncertainty measures. Utilizing this framework, we create an interpretative AI system that systematically disseates relevance to the various layers of a deep neural network, maintaining a focus on the most crucial features for each task. Additionally, the framework's use of specialist variables enhances the understanding of the learning process. An in-depth look at the development and implementation of this framework, along with its technical details and results, can be found in the companion article.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into r distinct subsets whose members have the same number of items. In this research, we identify a pattern within these numbers known as degenerate r-connected Stirling numbers, which occur when a set with k distinct elements is divided into r distinct subsets where the size of each subset can vary. A mathematical formula determining these numbers is provided, along with an explanation of their name origin due to the extreme cases where the numbers describe combinations and various generalized Stirling number variations.

A comprehensive analysis of the irreducible symmetric Properties and local symmetry-induced Symmetry in one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional systems is presented. The study covers all types of Symmetry, including elementary, advanced, double, and B-type Symmetry. The paper provides a detailed classification of the Symmetry groups and their associated properties, followed by a calculation of the fixed-point sets and character tables for each group. Additionally, the study offers an analysis of the local Symmetry-induced Symmetry and the construction of the complete Symmetry group from the one-dimensional elementary Symmetry group. The findings outline the complete Symmetry strategy for various Symmetry groups and suggest possible applications and future research directions.

Momentum operators associated with a metric are examined in this research. We show that one type of momentum operator, derived from Killing vectors along geodesic lines, has a key property - it's conserved along those geodesic paths. This leads us to a broader statement: such an operator can't distinguish between events occurring at the same spatial point in time. This result holds universally, without dependence on specific physical systems. Additionally, we look into a particular example of how these findings relate to de Sitter space.

In the field of neural networks designed to mimic complex quantum systems, a significant hurdle must be overcome - the sign problem. This challenge is particularly evident in studies of light nuclei and arises when exact numerical solutions are computed using Monte Carlo methods. A novel approach, the Complex Neural Network, has been developed to circumvent the sign problem. This model, inspired by the Gibbs-Bargmann variational method, utilizes complex-valued weights to approximate the exact ground state of neutron-rich systems. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated in preliminary calculations of the deuteron and triton, and further tests in systems such as the alpha particle and hydrogen isotopes are planned.

In this framework, a composite model of flavor, featuring a set of flavon fields, is used to tackle the challenges of neutrino masses, quark and lepton mixing, and the stability of the electroweak vacuum. By incorporating a Z2 symmetric model of composite right-handed scalars, a natural outcome is the lightness of the flavon mass eigenstates, whereas the heavy flavon states decay into standard model Higgs bosons or gauge bosons. A four-loop diagram enforces the natural value of the strong CP phase. A pairing of flavon fields with Standard Model Higgs bosons generates absolutely stable flavon vortices and leads to indirect signatures of flavor-changing neutral current interactions in jet and lepton signatures. A numerical analysis of the parameter space, based on neutrino oscillation data and various experimental constraints, is also presented.

User-immersive virtual reality experiences are characterized by perceptual alterations, 
temporally aligned with user behavior, and are therefore susceptible to manipulation in VR applications.
However, these modifications also introduce a significant challenge for creating more engaging and realistic VR stories.
The necessity of maintaining user engagement in stories is compounded by the absence of clear guidelines on leveraging the shadow aspect of perceptual alterations.
Therefore, this research aims to provide a theoretical framework for incorporating the shadow aspect, which refers to the subtle nuances of these modifications.
By developing the SAPE (Shadow Aspect Perceptual Extraction) framework, this study demonstrates its practical utility through the design and testing of a VR game prototype that successfully incorporates the shadow aspect, thereby enhancing player engagement and providing new possibilities for storytelling in VR.

Currently, major pre-trained multilingual models, like mT5 and mBART, prioritize popular languages such as Spanish, Hindi, and Arabic, but often overlook others with limited linguistic research, threatening to leave them underserved. To address this disparity, our research develops an adaptable system for extending modern multilingual models to lesser-studied languages, specifically in the Balkans and Central Asia. By combining tiny transforms and utilizing reduced, high-quality datasets, our approach efficiently brings these models up to speed. As proof of concept, our results show notable improvements in performance in languages such as Bosnian, Serbian, Albanian, and Uzbek, matching or surpassing the results of more highly-resourced languages like English and Spanish in all evaluated tasks.

Using advanced simulations, the formation of a dual planetary system is studied when a parent core undergoes fragmentation following spinning instability, causing its orbit to rise due to the conservative effect of angular momentum. As a fragmented core's distance from the parent core increases, it enters the protoplanetary disk's outer regions and may capture surrounding material, leading to the development of a dual planetary system. The mass of each planet is determined by factors such as the initial mass of the fragmented core, the time of fragmentation, and the amount of material captured. It's discovered that planets formed through this process typically have masses similar to those of our solar system's planets, with errors marginally greater than those produced by a standard core accretion model. The variability of resulting planetary masses is attributed to changes in the proportion of light material (rocks vs ices) in the core, as well as the impact of surrounding material's accretion on the planet's mass. The research suggests that a core accretion and dual planet formation process involving spinning parental cores could provide a plausible explanation for the origins of small to medium-sized planets in our solar system.

This research introduces the M-ar-K-Fast Autonomous Component Analysis (MAF-ACA) 
method, an efficient and innovative approach to solving the ACA problem.
The ACA problem is a nonconvex optimization challenge with unique constraints 
and positive semidefinite matrix elements, and existing solutions either fail to 
guarantee convergence or are computationally impractical due to their complex 
algorithms and high storage requirements.
In contrast, the proposed MAF-ACA approach offers several significant advantages: 
it ensures global optimality, requires minimal computational efforts, and needs 
minimal storage space for a large number of data samples.
Furthermore, our theoretical findings and experimental results demonstrate the 
rapid convergence of the MAF-ACA approach for both small and large datasets.

This paper revisits earlier research by Bull, Bulatov, Hofmann, and Tsuboikin, focusing on acyclic labelled tuples that can be distinguished through first-order logic, particularly when using a specific type of logic that doesn't involve choice. We make a significant contribution by providing a new upper bound for the computational complexity of acyclic labelled tuples that can be distinguished in this specific type of logic. We achieve this by establishing a connection between this logic and two other decision procedures: the Polynomial Calculus and the Extended Polynomial Calculus. We derive our results from an in-depth analysis of a specific type of algebraic circuits known as choiceless polynomial duration circuits. We also propose a new notion called "reversible" and demonstrate its importance by showcasing its utility in distinguishing certain types of logic. Additionally, we revisit open problems from the original paper and provide solutions by establishing new upper and lower bounds for the computational complexity of decision procedures. We achieve a level of closure for infinite structures, providing new upper and lower bounds for their complexity. We also provide solutions to problems that were considered beyond reach, such as determining the level of closure for 3-colourable graphs.

The collection of $\sigma$-elementary rings comprises a specialized subset of uncountable rings. A particular subcollection within this group consists of rings whose additive groups exhibit unique properties when divided into subsets based on $\sigma$. Specifically, for any infinite cardinal $\kappa$, the additive group of ring $R$ can be divided into $\kappa$-many subsets that each contain elements additive-idempotent of index $2$. It has been demonstrated that for any such division, a unique unary operation exists that enables the satisfaction of a particular polynomial equation, thereby allowing the characterization of rings within this subcollection based on their compliance with this operation and equation.

The framework approach to modal logic asserts that a specific set of modal symbols can be interpreted in various ways to form different modal logic systems. In this study, we analyze the modal logic system known as S5U, which is part of the broader family of modal logic systems, and confirm that it can be represented through the use of modal formulas within an intuitionistic arithmetic framework, as demonstrated by Prior and Kincannon in earlier research. Additionally, we establish in this work that S5U can be expressed within the framework of classical arithmetic, as shown by Bostad and other researchers. We also investigate the relationship between the modal logic system and arithmetic relationships known as the 'Double Negation Shift' and 'Negation Elimination Theorem'. We demonstrate how these arithmetic relationships known as 'Double Negation Shift' and 'Negation Elimination Theorem' are necessary and sufficient to verify the removal of double negations from modal formulas, as well as the validity of the box-diamond equivalence in the presence of negation elimination. We also show how these relationships are interconvertible with the system S5U.

The proliferation of social media platforms has rendered individuals incapable of surviving a day without them. These platforms have evolved into an essential aspect of modern daily life, encompassing various forms such as online forums, blogs, and photo-sharing networks. As a direct result of their widespread adoption, social media datasets have become a treasure trove for researchers in numerous fields, including geographic information processing and analytics. In this research paper, a novel technique is employed to extract spatial and temporal event patterns from large volumes of social media data in real-time. We have developed an event-detection framework that utilizes an enhanced Inverted Index approach, thereby facilitating real-time analysis of vast datasets. Our experimental outcomes, derived from real-world testing on Twitter and Instagram, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over existing techniques in terms of performance and accuracy.

To gain deeper insights into the Universe's complex phenomena, we are developing a new and efficient method to analyze the distorted patterns of noise in the cosmic microwave background. By applying Legendre functions up to a specified order $L_{max}$, we effectively use the CMB's spatial coefficients to compare with those of large-scale structure through a rapid computation of the trispectrum. Although our approach guarantees complete accuracy within the CMB framework, it does come with a theoretical risk of miscalculating noise when comparing with theoretical predictions from scenarios such as modified gravity theories. To mitigate this, we are creating a set of simulated datasets that mimic real data noise, which we are using to test our method's ability to accurately quantify noise distortions in up to four dimensions. To achieve this, we are employing a particle simulation method that allows us generate simulated datasets at a rate comparable to our capability for producing real data, while also providing a high degree of precision through the use of random phase selection.

To enhance the reliability of electronic voting systems and protect sensitive information from manipulation, we need robust estimation procedures that can withstand sophisticated attacks. We develop novel Bayesian estimation methods for critical parameters, such as the proportion of fake votes cast, and demonstrate how they can be implemented using sparse signal processing techniques. The proposed estimators not only provide accurate results but also guarantee their reliability in the face of potential deception. We accomplish this by leveraging the inherent properties of the data generation process and the adversarial interference. Furthermore, we illustrate the computational feasibility of these estimators by presenting a practical implementation based on the iterative hard thresholding algorithm. The consquences of underestimating fake votes and the effects of overestimating them are also explored, along with a discussion of how they can be mitigated.

Digital rumors spreading through social media platforms like Weibo and WhatsApp are significantly threatening national stability and public health in China, as seen during the COVID-19 outbreak. This paper examines the process of digital rumor dissemination in China and assesses its impact on public health, revealing key factors that contribute to spread. Notably, our study finds that rumors promoting traditional Chinese medicine as an effective COVID-19 treatment were particularly prevalent. To counter this issue, we recommend that authorities leverage machine learning-based algorithms to identify and eliminate digital rumors in real-time, accompanied by swift law enforcement action. Furthermore, our research suggests enhancing public fact-checking skills through educational initiatives and promotes the development of a citizen-led rumor-debunking network to foster community responsibility.

Reducing the number of spectral bands in a hyperspectral image leads to diminished computational costs in machine learning tasks, but this reduction can also hinder performance. Understanding the effects of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral image classification is crucial, as it involves balancing computational costs with accurate results. This study investigates how various methods of dimensionality reduction affect the local structure and global connectivity of data, using local spectral features and geometric analysis. A new framework is introduced to evaluate and compare different dimensionality reduction methods, using multiple criteria such as global connectivity, local spatial consistency, and clustering coefficients. Applying this framework to real-world hyperspectral images, our results show that certain methods of dimensionality reduction outperform others in preserving the original image's structural features.

We start with an assumption that numerous symbolic AI frameworks share a shared foundation in natural language. The underlying principles of these frameworks, although expressed in different languages, inherently rely on natural language. The key challenge lies in the vast number of possible word combinations, making it essential to identify the essential features needed to construct these frameworks. In this context, we conduct a cross-disciplinary analysis of existing AI frameworks within the context of natural language, uncovering key concepts and their interconnections. We utilize a unified conceptual graph to demonstrate the relatedness of these concepts and establish a hierarchy of natural language-based AI frameworks. By defining a family of these frameworks, we open up new avenues for natural language-based AI research, enabling comparisons between different approaches and identifying promising areas for further exploration. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of the diverse AI frameworks and their inherent complexities.

A newly developed tool called "ProVal" evaluates and assesses the integrity of protein structures by analyzing the behavior of amide protons, leveraging quantitative physics. Based on the behavior of these protons, ProVal assigns a score to evaluate protein quality, specifically for assessing the accuracy of NMR-derived structures. By comparing different quantum physics approaches, ProVal determines the average positions of amide protons in high-quality proteins, serving as a reference standard. This reference is then utilized to evaluate the accuracy of NMR-derived structures, making it possible to distinguish true structures from inaccurately determined ones. Furthermore, ProVal can suggest corrections to improve poorly accurate structures, implementing these changes through quantum physics-based calculations, facilitating the refinement of protein structures.

The choice of loss function plays a vital role in the training of neural networks, yet it remains an understated factor in many machine learning applications. Typically, the cross-entropy loss is the go-to choice for classification tasks, being both effective and straightforward to implement. However, recent research suggests that alternative loss functions can yield superior performance in certain scenarios, though it often requires substantial adjustments to the model architecture. In this paper, we delve into the impact of loss function alteration, presenting a framework that enables systematic exploration with minimal computational overhead. Our findings reveal that, across multiple datasets and network architectures, gradual loss function transitions uncover previously unnoticed performance enhancements, while our analysis also sheds light on the underlying challenges of error resistance and feature generalizability in deep learning classification.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise mathematical representations. One approach towards this end involves breaking down a system's collective motion into a set of distinct, localized patterns, or "blocks," with the assumption that these patterns remain relatively independent of one another. Four distinct block-schedules have been developed in the study of strongly interacting elements. One such schedule, known as the parquet series, is specifically designed for systems in contact with a heat bath, utilizing a notation that resembles a musical score. In this study, the parquet schedule is reinterpreted through the lens of classical mechanics, utilizing a Hamiltonian framework that treats all elements equally. As a result, the theory becomes inherently "particle-orientated," rendering it more suitable for applications in quantum chemistry. Our findings also reveal that the parquet schedule is, in fact, an iterative convergence of two distinct Hamiltonian dynamics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the parquet schedule is resilient to disruptions, preserving key properties even in the presence of perturbations. Lastly, the study applies this new understanding to develop a method for accurately predicting the movement of systems comprised of a few strongly interacting elements, demonstrating the theoretical possibility of achieving precise mathematical descriptions for such systems.

Achieving static static dipole polarization in matter remains an unresolved issue in ab initio theory. Researchers have recently tackled this challenge by developing a new approach based on conditional deexcitation, which builds upon existing ab initio methods for electron and hole deexcitation. Notably, this new approach has shown significant potential in simulating exciton condensation, a fundamental phenomenon observed in superconducting transition metal dichalcogenides. We have taken this new approach and applied it to the study of static dipole polarization in $TiSe_2$, a promising superconducting $1T$-polytype with an unique mechanism. Our results from both the initial developments and the detailed analysis accurately match experimental data and demonstrate the static dielectric response of $TiSe_2$. Furthermore, our findings also indicate that the intraband transitions play a crucial role in driving the observed static dipole polarization.

In the context of community safety, dispatchers serve as a link between emergency services and users, facilitating effective communication. Although dispatchers play a vital role, there is a pressing need to comprehend their workings, primary responsibilities, and interactions with users. This research aims to reveal new perspectives on dispatcher-user engagements through analysis of a text-based reporting system called CrisisConnect. By examining the system's text-based data, our analysis focuses on understanding underlying patterns in dispatcher workflows, the language and tone employed, and the types of emergencies handled. Furthermore, we develop two new features in our model to address the inherent biases often affecting machine learning outcomes and derive actionable insights capable of informing the development of more intelligent, people-centered interactive systems.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic field on superconducting properties in a particular class of superconductors known as nematic superconductors, we employed a 3D model having two coupled Cooper pairs that interacted with a strongly coupled spin system. By applying an external magnetic field along a particular direction, we observed the distinct appearance of a paramagnetic contribution to the magnetic moment in nematic superconductors, resulting in an observable shift in the upper critical field beyond its initial London value. Furthermore, the coefficient of this paramagnetic contribution is significantly influenced by the pairing parameters of the superconductor. Additionally, for very low values of coupling between the Cooper pairs and in the extremely low temperature limit, we found that the paramagnetic contribution is dominated by one of the Cooper pairs acting as a normal reservoir, thereby producing a notable magnetic moment in nematic superconductors.

In education, "engaged time" refers to the minutes a student is actively learning, as opposed to being distracted or uninvolved. Research by Kanade et al. (2020) demonstrated that engagements in their online course conformed to a universal pattern, as did scores, as both followed a predictable minimax trajectory. Building on this discovery, this paper develops an engaged learning model, as well as a scoring model, both of which are based on minimizing maximum values. The stack monotonic nondecreasing (SMND) algorithm is introduced to calculate these optimal scores and engagements, taking into consideration that they are both nonnegative and follow a stack monotonic nondecreasing pattern. The paper also derives various scoring and engagement scores that result from using different scoring rules, as well as provides numerical examples to illustrate the effectiveness of these new scoring and engagement rules.

Between 1750 and 1922, a significant shift occurred in the data complexity of European music, which stabilized by the mid-20th century.  Investigating more contemporary music from Europe and the US between 1950-2002 reveals a contrasting trend: the data complexity is once again rising.  Our analysis suggests this growth may be linked to influences of African and Latin American music traditions.  To clarify these findings, the new study used a more sophisticated method for measuring data complexity than its predecessor.

We're examining a complex situation where multiple events are sequentially reported as they occur, and the sequence is analyzed for notable patterns using a statistical tool called a confidence sequence. Our focus is on identifying the patterns that will certainly be detected as the amount of data collected becomes infinitely large, the rate at which data is collected becomes infinitely large, and when the distance between these events also becomes infinitely large. By understanding these asymptotic findings, we can better comprehend the statistical method's limitations and potential biases, even in situations where the data may not yet be sufficient.

This article explores the concept of computational playfulness, examining its various facets and how they're illuminated through different analysis methods. By harmonizing three distinct approaches to understanding playfulness, we refine the concept and suggest a unified perspective. Furthermore, we investigate how computational playfulness can be inferred from data, considering the impact of noise and model uncertainty. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this perspective in processing and interpreting data through a practical case study.

The problem of reward learning is pivotal in reinforcement learning, however, a substantial amount of time is required to accomplish this task using conventional approaches. To tackle this challenge, we have devised an innovative method where an agent's learning is guided by a human's simplified ranking of its agent teammates' performance. Building upon this concept, we have created an agent that can learn from basic group rankings without needing to map states to rewards. We have tested our approach and found it compares favorably to other time-efficient reward learning methods, requiring just ten minutes of human input to achieve similar results as an agent trained for 80 hours using a traditional reinforcement learning approach.

We show that core-conciseness does not apply to Smyth powerspaces, which includes the Smyth powerspace of a poset, contrary to the case for the Neumann and Wallman consoles. Moreover, we construct a poset with a finite Neumann console that is not core-concise.

When two moving objects stir the surface of an extremely calm water-like environment, the resulting vortex loops can either stay localized or move quickly away due to the high water viscosity, causing the stimuli's effect to fade rapidly. However, in ultra-stable two-dimensional fluids,aimed vortex loops can persist and make their impact felt for an indefinitely long time, thus requiring significantly higher forces from the stirring objects to disappear. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of these long-lasting aimed vortex loops and their rapid, extended movements within the context of ultra-stable 2D fluids, also exploring their local and widespread forms. Additionally, this research is supplemented by an experimental investigation aiming to identify the occurrence of these long-lasting aimed vortex loops in an ultra-stable 2D fluid that is artificially created.

One common prediction method, exponential smoothing state space, is straightforward to interpret but often outperformed by deep predictive models. The goal of $\tau$ physics is to precisely determine the weak mixing angle at various energy scales. Accurate $\tau$-charm form factor measurements near the $\tau$ mass are crucial for a theory prediction with a high degree of uncertainty, as they are heavily influenced by short-distance interactions and quark masses. Nevertheless, the current understanding falls short of explaining the observed data. While theory incorporates different approaches to describe the strong and electroweak interactions, discrepancies persist due to differing treatment of quark masses, form factors, and correction terms. Furthermore, the estimation of uncertainties in these calculations is a pressing issue, particularly in relation to off-shell vector boson effects and grid-based computations.

A fundamental study of a spinning, hollow water mass ($\beta$-plane configuration) has been conducted through both laboratory and numerical simulations to assess how its shape influences the formation and movement of circular baroclinic waves. These waves appear in both the laboratory and the model due to disturbances in the water mass's borders, and in the laboratory, they lead to the formation of distinctive jet and anticyclonic ring patterns on the water's surface. By altering the water mass's distance from equilibrium in the simulation, similar changes to the wave's shape occur in the $\beta$-plane quasi-geostrophic model, including increased amplitude and energy spread. Although the distance from equilibrium does not affect the wave's frequency, it does influence the wave's characteristics in both studies. Furthermore, the distance between the water mass's inner edge and its critical point location affects both the wave's shape and its frequency. Notably, the distance between these points in the laboratory experiment, called $L$, can be calculated through a previously established theoretical equation, and when used to create a 'benchmark length', the equation correctly predicts the wave's frequency.

To analyze extreme events, statistical models are often used that account for the heavy tails in probability distributions. The parameterization of these models as a Poisson process reoccurring at regular intervals is useful in Bayesian estimation because it enables the transformation of extreme values into interval lengths. This representation makes it possible to conduct posterior calculations in a more streamlined manner. A suitable choice of prior distribution for the model parameters needs to be made and suitable estimation methods are required to achieve this. A method of estimating the parameters is suggested which is based on a statistical model for spatial data and gives rise to a manageable posterior distribution, allowing for both computational simplicity and statistical clarity. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through applications to real-world data sets.

This research focuses on the theoretical foundation of offline reinforcement learning when data is imperfect due to corruption. It aims to establish robust policies that remain effective even in the presence of corrupted data. The study starts with an initial assumption that the corruption is random and limited to specific actions. It is found that at least $\Omega(d^2 p^{-1})$ samples are necessary to create an $\epsilon$-optimal policy when the corruption rate is $p$ and the number of possible actions is $d$. This requirement is comparable to the number of actions, and it is shown that this bound is achievable. The approach for developing this result involves transforming the offline reinforcement learning problem into a more manageable Markov decision process with a finite action space. The achievable density of samples is then used in an online reinforcement learning framework based on upper confidence bound (UCB). The technique is inspired by the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the multi-armed bandits problem. The initial assumption is relaxed to account for specific types of corruption, and a corresponding modification is made to the initial approach. The study also examines the effectiveness of the corrupted samples in offline reinforcement learning by introducing two metrics: the probability that the induced model is closer to the target reward model and the expected distance between the induced model and the target reward model. The expected distance metric is found to be a convergent quantity and can be optimized with the amount of corrupted data. The research establishes a trade-off between optimizing the reward and reducing the error caused

This research investigates the obtainability of solutions to the 1-D heat equation subject to spatially variable boundary conditions, via the introduction of new obtainability indicators derived from combined harmonic analysis and the Lopatinskii method. To establish efficient algorithms for calculating obtainability indicators, we present them in an expanded form at each boundary. Furthermore, we introduce new notions of obtainability indicators derived from the indicators at each boundary and their average, which allow us to determine sufficient conditions for obtainability using these constructs. To illustrate the utility of these constructs in simulating non-admissible data, we examine a specific example involving non-stationary heat conduction problems with non-constant boundary conditions.

When evaluating the performance of models in out-of-distribution (OoD) testing, it's common to analyze datasets that have never been seen during training. However, these datasets are fragmented into multiple categories that cannot be learned from context or labeled easily. As a result, current methods struggle to consistently detect data patterns in these scenarios. In an effort to improve this limitation, we've developed a new framework for classifying textual OoD data into distinct categories, as well as proposed three specific categories that offer notable challenges in different domains. Furthermore, we've introduced two new simplified benchmarks alongside existing benchmarks for out-of-distribution data, providing a comprehensive set of 12 benchmark datasets in total.

This research outlines a theoretical model describing propulsion mechanisms of molecular motors powered by tunneling currents. The model accounts for the detailed dynamics of tunneling and assumes that the tunneling process is hindered by the molecular engine's motion. The model also considers the thermal fluctuations of the tunneling rates and the molecular engine, which is modeled as a Brownian ratchet. The outcome is a force-velocity relationship that is dependent on the molecular engine's geometry and material composition. Additionally, the theoretical model predicts that molecular motors powered by tunneling can achieve high propulsion speeds while remaining in equilibrium.

It is demonstrated that a dual framework exists for term transducers, which includes a linear programming dual based on multifunctions and a second one founded on the concept of unidirectional resynchronizability. Furthermore, it was found that the latter framework possesses a strong property - its closure under composition. This duality, in addition to providing insight into the computational complexity of long enough word decision problems for term transducers, also offers a new perspective on verifying preservation of unidirectional resynchronizability under various module constructions in static analysis.

In this research, we explore the speed and efficiency of processing sums of arbitrary powers of elements within a finite field. These power sums can be computed quickly, at a rate of O(n), when the exponent is a fixed value. We demonstrate that generalized convolutions, which involve more complex expressions like exponential terms or polynomials of powers, can also be efficiently calculated, at a rate of O(n^3), for polynomials of fixed degree. This is a longer computation than power sums, but still faster than a basic check of every possible combination, which would take O(n^4).

The discovery of T-Dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 proved pivotal in understanding Brown Dwarfs and Jupiter-mass planets. Recent findings from ALMA data revealed a protoplanetary disk surrounding the low-mass star GJ 229A, suggesting the presence of a planet or additional disk components. Our study re-examines GJ 229B's origins, utilizing data from ALMA and spectroscopic analysis. Our calculations using the APOLLO code consider the accuracy of observed data and possible variations in the model parameters. Based on these calculations, the most likely model indicates that the system may be in a dynamic equilibrium, with the possibility of an unstable regime. Our analysis also reveals a discrepancy between the observed and simulated spectra, particularly at 0.3-0.5 $\mu$m, and identifies potential factors contributing to this difference. Our model further highlights the difficulties and uncertainties associated with the creation of T-Dwarfs through planetary engineering, due to the considerable mass required.

The possibility of creating a $J^{PC}=0^{--}$ state that deviates from the conventional model is being considered. Most studies attribute the phenomenon of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, known as negative probability or probability amplitude, in the context of $J^{PC}=0^{--}$. However, this concept is deemed unacceptable from a relativistic perspective. Despite the disagreement, researchers have explored the potential for exotic hadrons with the $J^{PC}=0^{--}$ designation. Recent studies using an effective model confirmed the existence of a narrow scalar state and a state with negative parity that could be explored through the $\Lambda \vec{p} \pi^{-}$ system in internal momentum regions. Additionally, researchers discovered that the reaction $p+d\to \pi^{-}+\Lambda+\vec{p}$ could serve as a suitable detection method for these exotic hadrons through the use of spectroscopic factors.

We obtain predictions for $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ based on the parameters of the Standard Model and the theoretical uncertainties associated with these quantities. These predictions are then compared with experimental findings. By correlating $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$, we prepare for future results that may help clarify whether observed $\phi_s$ values conform to the predictions made by the Standard Model or point towards new physics.

Understanding and predicting the spread of infectious diseases requires considering various factors such as population movement and contact tracing. Unlike previous studies, our research takes a novel approach – assuming a perfect knowledge of population mixing patterns, we investigate the predictive capabilities of this framework in forecasting infectious disease outcomes on an urban bus network. Utilizing a detailed model of the Atlanta bus system and accounting for passenger flow and mixing patterns, we develop a mathematical model that incorporates the characteristics of urban mobility. Additionally, we adapt and apply established methods from epidemiology and transportation forecasting to derive key performance indicators of infectious disease transmission. Our findings reveal a surprisingly strong correlation between passenger travel and disease transmission, along with insights into the relative importance of different transmission routes. Ultimately, while our assumption of a perfect understanding of population mixing patterns may be unrealistic in real-world applications, our results demonstrate the significant predictive value of this framework in forecasting infectious disease outcomes, along with potential practical implications and avenues for future research.

Utilizing the shell-model, the $\beta$-decay characteristics of $^{135,137}$Te isotopes have been analyzed. The study leverages the INDO1 and INDO2 interaction frameworks, which effectively describe the nuclei within the Te block. The calculated values of the corrected $\beta$-decay strengths and the resulting fine-structure components are compared to previous experimental findings. The goal is to reconcile the discrepancies between the theoretical and experimental results, particularly concerning the $\log ft$ values.

A secure double-faced auction mechanism, inspected under a scenario of semi-honest assumptions, showcases its capability to safeguard the privacy of bidders and seller in each transaction. By incorporating a novel approach combining homomorphic encryption and Oblivious Transfer, the mechanism achieves this while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that each party requires performing a constant number of operations. We compare our mechanism against the currently existing solutions and demonstrate its superior advantages in terms of security, general applicability, and computational complexity.

Utilizing heavy quark effective theory at the lowest order of perturbation theory, the mass spectrum of bottom baryons known as $\Lambda_b$ mesons are examined under an assumption of no electromagnetic interactions. By incorporating the effects of orbital angular momentum and color spin, a mass splitting is identified and expressed in terms of physical parameters. Additionally, a scale independent measure of color spin effects is accounted for. Based on currently available data, the impact of color spin effects on the mass splitting is estimated and found to be relatively small. A theoretical prediction of the mass splitting is made and compared to experimental results, showing reasonable agreement. This approach may provide a means to determine the QCD string tension in the study of heavy hadrons.

Given a curve $\gamma$ in the complex plane, we define its composition with $z \mapsto z^k$ as $\gamma^k$. The authors study mappings that are composed with curves, specifically those that are non-expansive, meaning they adhere to the inequality $|\gamma(z)^k - \gamma(z_0)^k| \leq |z - z_0|$. The papers examine periodic compositions of these mappings with semigroups consisting of fractional linear transformations, further investigating non-expansive curves defined by specific polynomial functions and discussing certain inequalities related to these mappings.

Future aerospace systems will significantly benefit from dynamic data analysis techniques, particularly Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD), which facilitates deeper understanding and insight into complex systems. However, the standard DMD algorithm has notable drawbacks, including a lack of robustness to noise and limitations in capturing non-linear behaviors. To address these shortcomings, researchers have developed various iterative and optimization-based methods, such as the Iterative DMD (iDMD) and Low-Rank DMD (LoRanD) algorithms. Another alternative is the Kernel DMD (KD) algorithm, which utilizes a non-parametric approach to model non-linear systems by transforming the original problem into a higher-dimensional space. Despite these advancements, the kernel version of iDMD (K-iDMD) and LoRanD (K-LoRanD) algorithms has not been thoroughly tested. This study aims to provide a detailed analysis and validation of these algorithms, which are collectively referred to as Kernel Education for Resilient Dynamic Data Analysis.

The objective of this study is to examine the complex nature of chess openings by leveraging data from the extensive online chess community, specifically focusing on chess strategy forums and the database of recorded chess games. Firstly, the research quantifies the intricacy of each chess opening by calculating the standard deviation of game outcomes and overall chess-related discussion on online forums. Subsequently, the paper employs a clustering algorithm and cluster validation techniques to group chess openings based on their similarity to simply elected chess strategies, as inferred from the online discussions.
