Current advancements in automatic speech translation and speech understanding from transcripts significantly benefit from additional data, yet gathering relevant transcripts is labor-intensive. To overcome this limitation, we suggest enhancing existing data with automatically created transcripts, thereby leveraging a cheap and effective solution to data augmentation. Our approach enables the joint training of transcription, translation, and understanding models on data with varying transcript quality, utilizing a straightforward objective function to minimize errors in all three tasks. As demonstrated by our experiments on multiple datasets, our proposed method efficiently improves transcription, translation, and understanding performance, especially when handling lower-quality transcripts. Notably, on the LSOD dataset, our method achieves nearly par with high-quality transcripts baselines obtained through extensive manual effort. Our findings and source code are available at https://github.com/ku-kovai-opendata/TransEnhancement.

A generalized approach to maximum likelihood estimation is developed for the basic parameters of mixtures. The method is demonstrated to effectively handle issues with sullied samples, yielding reliable results in such cases. The proposed method is exemplified through two real-world applications.

Achieving balance between maintaining private data and ensuring data utility is a pressing issue in today's world. To address this, various studies have been made on Differential Privacy, resulting in the development of one-sided differential privacy. It's essential to note, however, that the current models relying on independent data characteristics for protection are insufficient when data dependencies are considered. This research introduces a new model capable of handling data interdependence in the context of one-sided differential privacy. Furthermore, a customized framework is presented for evaluating the trade-off between data utility and privacy when data dependencies are present. Additionally, the research includes methods for analyzing the trade-off between data utility and privacy in specific statistical problems, such as statistical estimation, as well as exploring the trade-off in the context of privacy breach under dependent data characteristics.

In systems with multiple planets, it's common to see a significant decrease in specific organic molecules surrounding the star, suggesting up-to-date models still fall short of explaining this phenomenon. By examining the submillimeter continuum and CO emission from the disk of AS 209 with the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we found a notable CO-free zone at 13 astronomical units (AU). However, a decrease in CO abundance within this void is not observed, instead implying that CO is being converted into other compounds. This result poses a challenge to the theory that radial mass diffusion governs the disk's chemistry. Alternatively, it suggests that reactions at the gas-grain interface or more intricate organic molecule formation could be responsible for the void's distinctive appearance.

This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation toolkit called 'ChronoEval', which enables seamless analysis of time-sensitive data. The toolkit boasts an versatile metric calculation feature, allowing users to define both traditional mathematical expressions and more complex functionalities like support vectors. Furthermore, the toolkit is adaptable to various programming frameworks and can be utilized as a standalone application or integrated within Java-based pipelines. The toolkit's functionality is detailed in this research and accompanied by an illustrative case study as well as an easily accessible open-source software package.

We establish the existence of solutions to average field games of controls with state limitations and define 'gentle solutions,' which meet specific average cost minimization and control limit constraints.

Stellar threads appear to be long, thin objects extending from the Galactic plane in the Milky Way, measuring over 1000 parsecs in length. Recent studies suggest these threads are composed of multiple stars, molecular clouds, and other celestial objects, clustered together in the Galaxy's dense regions. This research presents an alternative explanation for the threads as distinct stellar entities connected by dark matter, thereby justifying the continued concept of these objects in the study of the Milky Way's structure.

Inconsistency identification in e-commerce has become a crucial issue that retailers need to address to ensure a smooth shopping experience for their customers and build a strong reputation. Most existing studies on visual inconsistency detection are confined to general object classes and rely on comprehensive object segmentation labels to characterize the image content. However, this can be impractical and expensive, especially when dealing with fine-grained content. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel task called visual inconsistency detection and propose a new model called VICTOR, which leverages a transformer encoder to extract feature representations from input pairs and a encoder-decoder structure for inconsistency prediction. To facilitate general visual inconsistency detection, we introduce additional pre-training objectives based on product categorization and visual consistency. Our approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance on the Fashionista dataset and achieved practice-inspired improvements in practice.

Asset theories provide a unified framework for understanding different forms of light, including classical, quantum, and nonclassical light. Classical light is represented by coherent states, quantum light by thermal states, and nonclassical light by a broader category of excitations. The various types of nonclassical light can be defined by specific properties, such as anti-bunching, number nonconservation, and quantum degradation. This overview explores the underlying principles of nonclassical light, highlighting key differences and similarities between its various forms.

As the need for performing machine learning tasks on private and distributed data grows, federated learning has become a crucial tool. Current aggregation methods in federated learning involve securely combining client submissions, but they typically do so under the assumption that data is labeled and that the training occurs on fixed-natured datasets. A new aggregation method has been developed to handle a broader range of data types (unconstrained sensor data). The proposed solution utilizes encrypted gradient sharing and buffered aggregation to efficiently combine client contributions. The experiment results demonstrate the performance gains achievable when applying this aggregation method to common deep learning models. The developed technique has been formally evaluated through both analysis and testing.

The purpose of this research paper is to explore derivatives and integrals of distributions within a finite dimensional space, and to establish the principles of the direct and inverse Fourier transform in relation to distribution theory. We draw on polynomial tempered functions as the foundational space for our investigations into distribution theory. We then derive the principles of the Fourier transform within this space, and utilize these results to construct differentiation and integration operators. To this end, we adopt an approach rooted in the principles of Gelfand and Paicu.

A new theoretical framework attempts to resolve three separate mysteries from the 2020 Rhic Collaboration paper. Firstly, it explains the origin of the obscure dimension, a concept that may hold secrets of the universe's high-energy beginnings. Secondly, it grasps the nature of the Marshland region, a transitional area between the dark matter halos and intergalactic space. Lastly, it proposes a possible composition of dark matter, specifically suggesting that it could be made up of black holes formed early in the universe.

A floating raft is considered, consisting of square elements that are linked by springs with a specific failure point. The liquid's viscosity is directly proportional to the distance between the nearest pair of points on the perimeter of the hole forming due to fracture. The hole's shape is initially prescribed as close to circular as possible, but its geometry changes over time based on the liquid's viscosity. The liquid's surface tension plays a significant role in the evolving hole shape. The hole's growth rate is determined by the rate at which energy is absorbed by the surrounding liquid. When the hole's size reaches a certain threshold, the fractures spread rapidly across the raft, leading to the breakage of multiple cracks at roughly the same time. The rate of energy absorption per unit length of crack is constant, which implies that the fracture velocity remains steady throughout the process.

The quest for high-mobility p-type gallium nitride has been ongoing due to its vast potential in integrated electronics and optoelectronics. In an effort to enhance hole conductivity in GaN, we explored the strain impact on hole mobility when aligning GaN epilayers to specific lattice structures. By matching the strain conditions to those caused by ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, the hole mobility improved significantly. Following comprehensive simulations and experimental analysis, our results demonstrate that the optimal hole mobility can be further increased to near-ideal levels with the aid of compressive strain along the c-axis, opening doors to higher-performance GaN electronic devices.

Our novel TGPT variation model allows Gaussian Process regression models to effectively capture their evolving dynamics while navigating underwater. By leveraging GP's inherent ability to model non-linear relationships, along with its ability to provide predictions and their associated uncertainties, our approach empowers applications such as navigation and motion planning by factoring in future predictions. In the context of marine navigation, our contribution lays the groundwork for robots to automatically learn, recognize, and adapt to various underwater currents and their patterns. Our findings demonstrate our model's capability to effectively learn and accommodate shifting dynamics, which would otherwise cause traditional GP models to diverge from reality. Our approach achieves this using a sparse learning technique based on Relevance Vector Machine, which successfully mitigates the scalability limitations associated with maintaining full covariance matrices, thereby enabling our model to seamlessly integrate new data points without compromising its precision. Our results are showcased using actual data collected from an autonomous underwater vehicle, which successfully verifies our model's accuracy and efficiency.

This study expands upon two transformation theories - Darboux and Calapso - within the context of isothermal surfaces with meromorphic functions. Darboux transformation is applied to specific families of minimal surfaces with particular functions, resulting in new minimal surfaces. Additionally, Calapso transformation theory is applied to minimal surfaces with embedded lines. Our findings incorporate previously published results from T. Banos to showcase the variety of derived surfaces.

This review summarizes the current knowledge on estimating conditional expectation functions, focusing on a broad class of functions that can be represented as polynomials. The discussion is grounded in long-standing, non-parametric estimation methods that pre-date the popular Bayesian Dolce analysis technique.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on modified Stirling numbers and their associated identities. We define three distinct types of $\lambda$-versioned r-Stirling numbers of the second kind and establish various related identities, including a comprehensive formula for the $\lambda$-versioned r-Stirling numbers of the second kind that generalizes existing research by Kim-Kim and Kim.

Considering the fast-growing knowledge graph database, static model approaches, such as connection prediction in temporal knowledge graphs, pose significant challenges due to extensive static model learning requirements and potential model obsolescence. 

We propose using fixed models for connection prediction, where previous knowledge is not used and only existing data is leveraged to minimize the impact of knowledge graph age on model effectiveness and downtime between model updates.

Empirical results demonstrate the substantial efficiency and effectiveness of fixed models in connection prediction, reaching a connection subjection mean absolute error of 0.6233 and a mean ranking loss of 0.6184 when compared to other popular methods.

This note enhances and reinforces the findings of Brown and Guay's paper, which characterized robust shift equivalence for row-finite directed graphs. Additionally, it offers an equivalent characterization for the C*-algebras associated with these graphs.

In this research, we have developed a novel approach to creating precise images of heavy quark scattering patterns in a strong magnetic field, building on previous work by Strickland and Greiner. We have expanded their image construction protocol to account for anisotropic effects by using a correlated Gaussian model for the heavy quark movement. This improved framework enables the precise measurement of separate heavy quarks in a magnetically polarized quark matter under extreme conditions.

Several recent studies have demonstrated the potential benefits of knowledge graph-based language models in question-answering tasks. These models, engineered to generate plausible sentences based on knowledge graph entities and relations, can significantly enhance the language model's ability to output accurate and grammatically correct responses to inquiry prompts. Notably, previous research advocated for the use of knowledge graph paths rather than discrete knowledge graph edges, due to concerns about path injection and knowledge overload. However, our findings indicate that incorporating actual graph edges can prove beneficial when combined with appropriate training objectives. We propose an innovative approach that involves fine-tuning both language and knowledge graph models simultaneously, leveraging local and global graph inference techniques to mitigate the challenges associated with knowledge injection. Ultimately, our model outperformed existing benchmarks in inquiry answering, showcasing the potential benefits of integrated knowledge graph reasoning for natural language generation.

We introduce an efficient method for creating detailed descriptions of complex events in high-dimensional spaces by utilizing existing models and incorporating random elements. This approach builds upon previous work and offers a more versatile alternative to current frameworks, which are often based on specific models or require substantial computational calculations. Our method allows for precise descriptions of complex events and provides a range of adaptable options for simplifying calculations, including approximate analyses and intuitive assessments of likelihood. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in identifying novel associations between factors, using the example of analyzing price movements in S&P stock prices.

Recent advancements in language models have highlighted the importance of pre-training data and prompt engineering in determining system performance, particularly in task-oriented scenarios. Researchers have made significant gains by examining how natural language prompts interact with language models in zero-shot settings, often achieving impressive results with minimal data input. Nevertheless, a key challenge persists in ensuring prompt models are resilient to prompt manipulation and data disruptions. To address these concerns, this study investigates the cross-task applicability of pre-trained prompt models, evaluating their effectiveness when applied to diverse classification tasks and assessing their ability to generalize across different data distributions. By leveraging a new dataset of natural language classification tasks called QuestionVisualClassification, this research compares the performance of various prompt models when adapted to task-oriented scenarios, aiming to provide insights into the conditions required for prompt models to achieve high levels of system performance in zero-shot settings.

We introduce and investigate the concept of $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of Artin algebras.
Our computations for hereditary Artin algebras reveal that the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant
mirrors the cokernel of a pivotal map derived from the first Hochschild class of the
category of projective modules, whereas for general Artin algebras, the relationship
remains an open query. Additionally, we identify key criteria for the $\mathscr{L}$-
 invariant to be defined and derive both upper and lower bounds for its value.

We have developed an innovative deep learning-based method to detect complex microwave patterns using Rydberg atoms. This approach leverages the unique properties of Rydberg atoms to sense electromagnetic fields, and our algorithm generates microwave fingerprints via hidden neural networks. By utilizing two elementary Rydberg atoms, we have demonstrated the simultaneous detection of multiple frequencies within a microwave pattern and evaluated our method's accuracy for various frequency spacings and powers. This technique holds tremendous potential for high-precision measurements of electromagnetic fields.

UGC 8839 is an spiral galaxy with an exceptionally stable and low-mass fraction of cold gas, a rare feature among spiral galaxies. Despite being near the center of the Ursa Major cluster, UGC 8839's stable disk suggests it hasn't experienced significant interactions with the cluster. Observations reveal a nearly perfect ring structure composed of cold gas, lacking in the galaxy's center and characterized by a sudden and sharp transition at a specific radius. This feature may indicate past interactions with smaller galaxies that stripped away gas from the center of UGC 8839. A comparative study with similar galaxies in the cluster reveals that UGC 8839 stands out due to its strong bar structure and the unique ring formation, suggesting these characteristics contribute to the galaxy's stable and ultra-stable disk environment.

For a homeomorphism φ on the boundary of the complex plane and a measure μ that is compatible with the Hausdorff metric, we investigate the large-scale behavior of μ(φ^k(B)) as k approaches infinity, where B is a bounded subset of the boundary. The general result applied to quasiregular mappings in the sense of Marshall-Riebman shows that if a mapping φ is sufficiently non-normal, then the growth rate of μ(φ^k(B)) is directly proportional to the Hausdorff dimension of the set attracting repetition under iterations of φ. The proportionality constant depends on the boundary distortion of φ. In the case of a typical iteration, when the hypothesis of non-normality is relaxed to certain averaging conditions, the above proportionality remains valid. The above findings are further extended to the scenario of distinct homeomorphisms on the boundary of the polydisk and on the Julia set of a hyperbolic rational function.

Using the Neutral Gas Imager on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory, an extensive study was conducted to better understand gravity waves in Mars' upper atmosphere. Researchers analyzed over 2700 density profiles from 140 to 300 km in altitude, focusing on waves triggered by specific geologic features and their comparison with similar phenomena on Earth. It was discovered that certain types of waves are only observable during specific times of the day and year on Mars, while others exhibit persistent patterns over the entire Martian year. Notably, waves triggered by the most repetitive Martian feature are observable twice daily and show little seasonal variation. When comparing these features to similar occurrences on Earth, it becomes clear that some sources of gravity waves on Mars are comparable to those on Earth, but others are uniquely Martian. Furthermore, it was determined that certain types of waves are only capable of traveling up to 100 km in altitude in Mars' atmosphere, while stronger waves can affect even the very upper atmosphere of the planet. An in-depth analysis of the observed amplitude and phase speed of these gravity waves revealed that they are consistent with previous models of the phenomenon. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the significant role that source characteristics, like size, shape, and movement, play in the transmission of gravity waves through the atmosphere.

The LHC holding steady at its original energy of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair for Pb-Pb collisions has provided an opportunity to examine photoproduction of the J/psi vector meson mediated by virtual photons. The measurements were taken using the ALICE detector at both forward and backward angles, with statistical significance exceeding that of previous experiments. The findings consist of differential cross-section measurements for J/psi production at forward angles, cross-section measurements for J/psi production in Pb-Pb collisions at both mid-rapidity and forward angles, and a comparison of these cross-section measurements with theoretical predictions from the NLO EPS09 FM FRK PDF set, revealing agreement between experimental and theoretical results for both lead-central and lead-peripheral collisions.

Three methods for generating sound in response to vision are explored, 
all of which use deep learning. One approach relies on connection between the 
visual and auditory systems, while the other two rely on language processing 
and translation. When participants are able to freely sample sound, the 
model produces sound with roughly the same characteristics as ordinary audio 
recording. However, when sound is triggered by specific images, the model's 
performance improves significantly. In tests of how effectively the model 
responds to visual input, it outperforms a baseline model by a substantial margin.

Recurrent neural networks have excelled in semantic graph applications due to their ability to sequence inputs, although temporal knowledge acquisition remains underexploited. By incorporating a temporal knowledge module in recurrent neural networks, it becomes feasible to adapt these models for sequential data learning and temporal knowledge acquisition in one unified framework. Our proposed approach lies in the recurrent temporal knowledge module which leverages the inherent capabilities of recurrent architectures for temporal knowledge acquisition. In essence, the proposed RTKM acquires sequential temporal knowledge alongside learning sequential patterns, thereby circumventing the need for explicit indexing or temporal feature engineering. Our experimental findings using Deep Graph Convolutional Networks on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that incorporating RTKM into recurrent neural networks leads to superior performance compared to conventional recurrent neural networks and rival state-of-the-art models.

Epidemics pose a threat to both human health and the global economy, and understanding the interplay between these factors is crucial for making informed decisions.  The model utilized in this research utilizes a multiplicative epidemic model, incorporating both health and economic factors. It reveals that timely countermeasures can mitigate both medical hardships and financial losses, and that optimal timing results in maximum utilization of available measures. The model indicates that the ideal time for measures is proportional to the product of transmissibility and infection risk and the availability of measures divided by the severity of infections. The model holds universal applicability due to its broad assumptions, including the absence of specific epidemic characteristics. The analysis accounts for various countermeasure applications, including non-pharmaceutical and pharmaceutical measures. The findings obtained can provide broad guidance for decision-making purposes during epidemics.

This work tackles a key problem in data analytics - identifying and fixing data quality issues. These issues not only slow down a data scientist's workflow but also negatively impact machine learning model training. While data quality issues have been studied in the past, there's no universal approach to detect them yet. To address this, we propose a new framework called DataTroubleShooter, which uses the Shapley Value framework to pinpoint problematic data and quantify the impact of various data quality issues during machine learning model training. This framework is composed of three main modules: (1) a module that extracts insights from machine learning model performance using metrics such as accuracy and loss, (2) a module that aggregates insights from different model phases, and (3) a module that leverages optimization techniques and user-defined thresholds to determine data quality issues and recommend fixes. To evaluate our approach, we conducted two case studies using real-world datasets and showed that our framework successfully detects data quality issues and provides data quality assessment scores. This leads to improved machine learning model accuracy and enhanced data quality for automated decision-making purposes.

This review focuses on various mathematical concepts that relate to the statistical calculations made during the early stages of a quantum field's development. It incorporates concepts from combinatorial mathematics, in particular the theory of hypergraphs, enumerative geometry, and discrete topology. Specific mathematical ideas explored include the application of Fulton's intersection theory to study hypergraph combinations, calculating the statistical probability distributions of quantum fields using enumerative methods, identifying discrete topological properties through the analysis of simplicial complexes, and composing quantum fields by combining enumerative geometry formulas.

This study presents an investigation of how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. At normal pressure, this material exhibits a significant anomalous Hall effect, primarily attributed to its internal spin structures. However, our research reveals that exposing Mn$_3$Sn to high pressure results in a significant decline in its anomalous Hall effect, ultimately reversing its direction. Through the use of synchrotron x-ray diffraction, we observed that the spin structure in Mn$_3$Sn transforms from a $6m$ symmetry at normal pressure to a primitive lattice under high pressure, as supported by comprehensive modeling. Notably, our findings also include the identification of an unusual by-product and an aberration in the material's lattice pattern, both of which were not anticipated.

Research into relation extraction using deep neural networks has undergone significant advancement in recent years, resulting in outstanding performance compared to traditional approaches. To provide insight into this progress, we have developed a comprehensive overview of deep neural network-based relation extraction techniques. Starting with an examination of the underlying principles of deep neural networks, we delve into the design of state-of-the-art models and the datasets employed for evaluation. The paper also presents an analysis of the advantages and shortcomings of current methods, subsequently discussing promising avenues for further investigation in the future.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a domain $\Omega$ formed by removing the smaller ball from the larger set. Under these conditions, we let $\partial\Omega\setminus\{0\}$ denote the exterior boundary, and $\gamma$ represents a boundary condition parameter. We aim to analyze the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenfunctions of the given Steklov-Robin problem as they relate to this setup, and in doing so, we derive essential spectrum, a countable set of eigenvalues, and the properties of eigenfunctions. Additionally, we use a semigroup approach and spectral shift functions to study the Steklov-Robin problem and its relationship to the classical Dirichlet Laplacian on the same domain, and in particular, we observe the influence of the boundary condition parameter on the spectrum and eigenvalue counting functions.

In the guided hypergraph restoration problem, we aim to enhance an incomplete or degraded hypergraph by incorporating limited global information. This task has practical significance in various fields such as social network analysis and data mining. The guided hypergraph restoration model can be viewed as an extension of the guided graph restoration problem. We have developed a mathematical framework to express the optimal solution of the guided hypergraph restoration problem. Furthermore, we have proposed an iterative algorithm that converges to the optimal solution. The computational results from synthetic data suggest that this algorithm is capable of accurately restoring the original hypergraph structure even in the presence of significant noise. The performance of this algorithm is evaluated in terms of its convergence speed and efficiency. The applied studies indicate that the proposed method outperforms general hypergraph completion techniques.

To advance computer vision research in understanding X-ray images, this work provides a detailed annotation of 14,069 chest X-ray images, including lung conditions, fractures, and other abnormalities. Our system uses 3D convolutional neural networks to generate 2D labels for images by projecting them from previously annotated 3D full-body scans. Our dataset and annotation are accessible online.

Using the techniques developed in recent research on cohomology in contact geometry, 
the Euler characteristic of tight contact frameworks can be calculated by multiplying the maximum Thurston norm by 2. This result generalizes the previous findings of Michael Stoffel and the second author of this paper. Additionally, the Euler characteristic can also be determined through a different method by subtracting the Euler characteristics of the link complement and the contact manifold in tight contact frameworks. This discovery also generalizes the previous findings of the second author.

Research into quantum dynamics of small cavity systems is proliferating due to their potential for understanding quantum phenomena on a small scale and in isolated systems. The entropic characteristics of the electromagnetic field in these systems can provide insight into their directional discharge behavior. This study investigates the entropic properties of a passive microcavity laser, specifically exploring the link between its entropy and directional discharge features. By applying the generalized entropy formula derived by Cabral and Garrido, our results show that this link exists and can provide insight into the system's dynamics.

Due to their inherent volatility, cryptocurrencies aren't widely used as a medium of exchange despite their potential. We're examining the feasibility of maintaining a stable price in the long run, known as price consistency, in a general framework of the exchange process. We've found that, under certain assumptions, an equilibrium exists where the price of a cryptocurrency remains stable over time. This happens when the transaction costs imposed by both public and private parties are non-negligible and are met by users, who are motivated by utility maximization. We're also exploring the impact of malicious activities, including 51% attacks, which can occur when a single entity controls the majority of a blockchain's network.

Linking the inverse scattering of the Zakharov-Shabat system to the linear fractional heat equation allows us to explain the persistent, weak fluctuations observed in destinations of one-dimensional KPZ equation, specifically in cases where initial conditions have sub-domains with significantly differing heights. This connection also reveals how weak noise, arising from the non-uniform nature of initial conditions, influences the KPZ equation's flip parity-based, local time constant properties. Furthermore, our study clarifies the significance of 'heights' in KPZ models, particularly in determining their local time constants, and thus their waveforms. This theoretical framework is confirmed through numerical simulations.

Recent findings from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission have yielded first-of-their-kind observations of solar wind turbulence extremely close to the Sun, specifically near the height of the Parker spiral. Data collected over multiple solar flares have provided scientists with comprehensive insights into this type of rare and intense phenomenon. Analysis of the data has led to the discovery of unusual properties within the solar wind, including high-frequency waves and intense heating patterns that defy conventional expectations. One common thread among these observations is the prevalence of small-scale turbulence, regardless of the solar wind's direction of propagation. Additionally, measurements have detected numerous electric fields at frequencies higher than those typically associated with the solar wind. These high-frequency electric fields are particularly prevalent in regions of intense heating and coincide with periods of high density in the solar wind. Most remarkably, the total electric power measured during these intense periods is equivalent to three times that of normal conditions, and is directed in the same direction as the magnetic power. The data suggests that a significant amount of this power is a result of the interaction between charged particles and magnetic fields, and that this process may be the primary driver of solar wind turbulence.

In SASE FEL facilities, generating attosecond pulses poses significant challenges, primarily due to long electron pulses and unwanted beam chirp. This research focuses on harnessing the capabilities of the saturated FEL gain to produce attosecond pulses through an innovative charge-exchange scheme. This method utilizes an undulator with a specific design to achieve the required seed pulses and exploit the inherent gain to produce XUV and soft X-ray attosecond pulses. Recent simulations conducted using the CODES and MAGIC codes have demonstrated the feasibility of producing such bursts with high peak powers, exceeding tens of GWs. Notably, the proposed scheme offers the advantage of providing a high average power output, potentially exceeding several kW, making it highly suitable for applications in natural sciences and medical research.

Field observations from desert environments over nearly four decades have 
yielded extensive data on dust storm dynamics, yet the intricate processes 
governing such storms remain complex and poorly understood. In this study, we 
introduce a novel approach to modeling internal storm dynamics through 
nonlinear array waveguide optics. A tangible opto-mechanical system is used 
to simulate viscous Bingham fluid layers, revealing the inherent link between 
reynolds number and wave number in the shear stress spectrum. Our results 
validate the use of tangible optics estimation as a powerful method for 
interpreting and clarifying the intricacies of arid dust storm dynamics.

Quantifying the uneven distribution of votes in favor of a particular party across electoral districts is the primary purpose of measuring gerrymandering. Past attempts to achieve this goal have led to conflicting results and an overall lack of clear, consensus-driven definition. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach that leverages the principles of statistical mechanics and utilizes advanced machine learning techniques to evaluate the fairness of electoral boundaries. By incorporating expert knowledge into a neural network, we are able to formulate gerrymandering as an optimization problem and employ simulated annealing to explore its mathematical underpinnings. Ultimately, our method allows us to establish a clear, objective measure of gerrymandering based on the political balance of each district.

Textile authentication is of significant importance in various industries such as fashion and textile production. When examining textured document images, experts often rely on visual patterns or marks that require identification. However, existing methods may fail to accurately locate or distinguish subtle marks, particularly those with intricate patterns or adverse lighting conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce an advanced technique for detecting and differentiating marks in textured documents, even those with multiple pages. This approach employs Global Haar-like Orientation Code (GHOG) to effectively analyze texture patterns and accurately pinpoint marks within images, followed by low-rank decomposition to remove background noise and enhance mark identification. Experimental results demonstrate our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in flaw detection and can efficiently handle both Breton cross cross-sectional and Herringbone pattern. This technique yields promising results and could potentially be applied to various real-world textile authentication challenges.

To enhance the robustness of vision-based reinforcement learning methods for navigation, our study centers on regularization techniques in relation to the inherent structure of visual data. By integrating the principles of information theory and deep learning into conventional regularization methods, our framework aims to develop more effective strategies for visual navigation. Through theoretical analysis and experimental validation, we examine the coherence between different regularization methods and the robustness of the learned agent. The outcome of our research indicates that, despite numerous existing approaches, few regularization methods have a clear theoretical foundation. The empirical results demonstrate that our proposed information-theoretic regularization method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Investigating active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their relation to supermassive black holes (SMBHs) is of great interest to researchers.  In the theory that SMBHs drive the evolution of galaxies through their growth, it is proposed that AGN activity peaks at a certain black hole mass.  At higher masses, the black holes slow down their accretion, and this is seen as a critical point in the AGN phase in the broader galaxy evolution picture.  In past studies using various methods, the predicted mass at which this peak occurs has been different, and this discrepancy is now the focus of research.  A recent study by Reines et al. placed the mass at which this peak occurs around 10^7-10^8 solar masses using radio and X-ray observations.  A different recent study by Fu et al. suggested the mass at which this peak occurs is significantly lower, by a few solar masses using infrared data and took into account the uncertainty associated with the Fu et al. study's findings.  A further recent study by Ruffaytser et al. placed the mass at which this peak occurs around 10^4 solar masses using a different statistical approach.

The initial stars in dense galaxy centers might have created massive black holes and neutron stars that reside there today. In a study published in the research journal, [Authors' Names] investigated the remnants of these primeval stars, focusing on the potential emission of gravitational waves from the remaining black holes over the past 13 billion years. By utilizing a detailed computer simulation of the early universe's chemistry, the researchers found that the rate of merging black holes is relatively low but not insignificant. In a typical nearby galaxy like the Milky Way, the predicted merger events would likely number in the low thousands. These merging events would primarily involve equal mass black holes in short-period orbits, leading to a distinct spectral pattern and lower frequency range in the resulting gravitational waves. In contrast, events involving black holes of vastly different masses would have a lower volume density, reducing their overall contribution. Additionally, the model takes into account the effects of gravitational waves' propagation through the crowded galaxy center, which could significantly lower the detected signal rate, especially at higher frequency ranges. Ultimately, the analysis suggests that the predicted gravitational wave spectrum might be within range of detection by upcoming instruments like the Square Kilometre Array, offering a potential test of the theory of black hole retention in dense galaxy centers.

In modern power distribution networks, smart meter data can be analyzed in real-time to monitor energy consumption and detect significant events, such as sudden energy demands or disturbances. This research aims to develop an event detection algorithm using smart meter data, enabling continuous monitoring of distribution networks and enhancing operational efficiency. The proposed method involves identifying typical consumption patterns at different time intervals and detecting irregularities through comparison with these patterns. Experimental results from a case study of a real power distribution network confirm the effectiveness of this method.

Our study focuses on examining the radiative and resonant electromagnetic decay channels of the $X(3872)$, specifically its transitions to $J/\psi \pi \gamma$, $J/\psi \pi\pi\delta$, and $J/\psi \pi^{0}\pi^{+}\delta$. The $X(3872)$ is assumed to consist of an $s$-wave $J/\psi 0^{+}$ component and possible $J^{L}/\psi$ wave contributions with $L \neq 0$. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ decay is analyzed through two distinct processes: direct radiation and intermediate $\rho$ or $\omega$ states. The latter scenario is further explored by considering the influence of loop effects and off-shell corrections to the $\rho$ or $\omega$ meson. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\delta$ decay is solely attributed to intermediate $\rho$ or $\omega$ mesons. The branching ratios of these decay channels are calculated as functions of the $X(3872)$ width and its coupling to the $\rho$ or $\omega$ meson. The obtained branching ratios are compared with existing experimental data and theoretical model predictions, aiming to provide additional insights into the $X(3872)$ composition and its quark content.

We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics within the context of bounded symmetric domains, offering insights into their structure and properties. Additionally, we establish a categorical representation of quadrics that facilitates the description of their scalar quadrics, bilinear quadrics, and affine quadrics through a systematic and unified approach.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a cutting-edge text-based game engine designed for fair exploration and learning, boasting unparalleled speed at one million moves per second. Unlike traditional gaming frameworks, it deliberately foregoes sophisticated AI optimizations in favor of a level playing field, making it an ideal tool for research and development. At its core is a high-performance search algorithm that achieves remarkable speeds through strategic use of data structures and multiple processing threads. To further boost efficiency, it leverages a cutting-edge indexing technique and compromises on AI optimizations that would otherwise limit the size and complexity of games. Additionally, TextWorldExpress includes an user-friendly interface and comprehensive tools for creating new games, as well as a benchmark suite consisting of 65 complex challenges spanning 10 diverse game types, which serve as a solid foundation for future research and can be used to evaluate the performance of various game-based learning agents.

Our ageometric method for studying gapped topological insulators with defects breaks down at the boundary, where it struggles to capture the surface states' discrete spectrum and localized characteristics. However, we've developed an amended strategy applying Floquet theory, revealing that surface states are dynamically generated through periodic driving forces on the defects. We illustrate our findings using a notable Z2 topological insulator with a diverse collection of boundary flaws.

This research delves into a classification of p-harmonic functions within two-dimensional sectors. Our investigation establishes both local and global bounds for these functions, similar to those found in earlier studies by Lehtelä and Marjala. Our analysis also identifies key factors influencing the results, including a critical value of p = 2.

Understanding the environmental factors influencing marine species' distributions
requires analyzing the local environmental characteristics alongside species' presence and behavior.
This study develops a spatial analysis model for extreme marine environments, which identifies habitat-specific extreme conditions and their impact on marine species' distributions.
The multivariate spatial peaks model can analyze multiple environmental variables and species' responses together, taking into account the interdependencies among these variables.
Applied to field data from the South African rock lobster, the model reveals the relationship between species' presence and the interaction between two key environmental variables, and identifies the extreme conditions preferred by the species.
The results show that the species prefers specific combinations of temperature and depth conditions and avoid others, and the model's to be preferred conditions were accurately predicted.
The proposed model can be utilized for studying the environmental influences on other marine species and in conservation and ecological assessments.

We consider certain symmetric functions of $n$ elements and establish an upper limit on their number over a number field, given specific conditions. This limit holds provided the functions in question are non-constant in each variable. Furthermore, our finding takes into account the potential equivalency of the functions, accounting for their field of definition and possible differences in irreducibility. To derive this upper bound, we utilize estimates based on the height of the functions, effectively generalizing an earlier result by Dubois and Pechini into the context of multiple variables. To tackle the complexity of working with multiple variables, our approach involves employing a method similar to that of Pechini's recent work with Vetillard, which involved leveraging fundamental inequalities related to the height of functions over a finite field.

Our manipulability realm adjustment method ensures a smooth transition between human and robot joint spaces, accounting for obstacles, to optimize interaction between the two. To resolve the paradox of parallel convergence, we employed a series of local filters and sequence comparisons on manipulability distributions to establish corresponding parallels, relying on kernel density estimates to accurately represent these distributions. To efficiently compute and align correspondences between the two spaces, we developed a novel, obstacle-aware version of the Iterative Closest Point algorithm, where we utilize a beam search strategy to efficiently prevent the collapse of parallels and preserve obstructions, using a entropy-based metric to optimize the alignment of parallel distributions and facilitate robust real-time operation. Experimental results using our ICRCKE-SLAM tool, applied to simulated and real human-robot collaboration scenarios, demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods.

Investigating Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC provides essential insights into high-energy collision processes and the nature of the Higgs mechanism. This study examines the potential of the matrix element method in separating signal from background contributions. To achieve this, events from proton-proton collisions are simulated using the Feynman diagrammatization of the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\texm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process, along with relevant background processes, and then analyzed through a systematic evaluation of kinematic configurations. This thorough analysis incorporates accurate matrix elements, parton distribution functions, and next-to-leading order terms. The separation of signal and background is achieved by contrasting exact and approximate matrix elements, ultimately demonstrating the matrix element method's efficacy in the given scenario.

When an object rotates in 3D, its turntable's position isn't necessarily known and must be inferred from the observed rotation. However, when viewing 2D images, it's impossible to determine all possible 3D orientations without some prior knowledge. In this research, we show that when multiple objects rotate in 3D, it's possible to calculate their turntable positions using only 2D image observations. We test this theory by creating a novel task, where an agent learns the 3D position of an observed object without seeing it rotate in 3D first. Our experiments involve both simulated and real scenes and demonstrate that the proposed approach is successful in determining the 3D position of an object's turntable from just two 2D images.

In recent years, social media has served as a primary source of information for the general public, and recent developments in the field have highlighted its significance due to the global health crisis caused by COVID-19. This study focuses on reversing the underlying processes used by misinformation spreaders, and in doing so, we identify key factors that contribute to the acceptance or rejection of false information regarding COVID-19 vaccines disseminated through Twitter dialogues. Our proposed framework consists of two primary components: (a) a novel retweeting framework and (b) a context-aware learning approach utilizing bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully identifies the acceptance or rejection of false information regarding COVID-19 vaccines on Twitter and outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a remarkable overall accuracy of 92.69%.

Controlling high-energy, ultra-short electromagnetic pulses in the soft X-ray and soft extreme ultraviolet range is crucial for enhancing their energy and manipulating their energy spectra. Achieving this requires precise laser field control over ionization and recombination processes that produce and shape extreme ultraviolet pulses, known as attosecond bursts. We have developed a comprehensive model to analyze the ion and electron dynamics modulated by robust-field coherent laser pulses in noble gases. Our approach considers the impact of electrons released during the initial ionization process and utilizes the generalized perturbation series to evaluate ionization and recombination probabilities. Applications of our methodology include the manipulation of isolated attosecond surges and the modification of their spectral patterns, offering promising prospects for enhancing attosecond pulse measurement and applications in areas like quantum electrodynamics and materials science.

In a 1970 study, Franklin F. Graham identified 877 objects within the Algol domain.  Recent research led by Shude Mao rediscovered 51 new Algol systems, bringing the total count to 928, significantly expanding the known catalog.  To achieve this, the team analyzed photometric and spectroscopic data from multiple surveys, employing both machine learning algorithms and automated software to facilitate the analysis.  A notable approach involved using the $WISE$ data to accurately predict the orbital periods of these new systems, matching the expectations from the theoretical framework of mass conservation.  Additionally, the study highlighted 106 wide binary candidates and 29 new Algol system candidates following the 'touching binary' pattern.  Further examination of these new contacts is set to provide valuable insights into the structure and composition of the primary stars.

We demonstrate a permanent solution of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation in the area beyond a convex obstacle, which resembles an explosion in physics. To derive this solution, we start with a modified version of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation within a narrow well near the obstacle and use a specific mathematical technique to establish a bound on the wave function's magnitude. Subsequently, we expand the obstacle using a limiting process and show that as the original well becomes extremely narrow, its modified version leads to a confined and permanent wave function, essentially resembling an explosion in physics.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in Physics-Informed Neural Networks, which incorporate engineering knowledge into neural networks to solve partial differential equations. While Physics-Informed Neural Networks have shown promising results, they face challenges representing discontinuities and adapting to changing solution characteristics. To address these issues, there is a growing need for flexible neural network architectures. In this research, a new node creation approach called RANG is presented for adapting the Physics-Informed Neural Networks to solve a wide range of partial differential equations efficiently. RANG uses a residual-based adaptive technique to create new nodes based on the local properties of the solution, without requiring expert knowledge. By comparing RANG with existing methods on multiple test cases, it has been demonstrated that it outperforms other methods in terms of approximation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, RANG is particularly efficient when solving partial differential equations with significant changes in the solution, as well as those with inherent discontinuities.

In this study, we have examined the behavior and simulation of FeFETs with multiple domains, where the interface between these domains acts as a variable capacitor. Our research involved both theoretical and experimental analysis, using both ferroelectric material properties and device simulations to predict outcomes. Our findings show that, like nano-scale FeFETs, the domain walls in FeFETs also exhibit unstable behavior when stimulated by an external electric field, causing a sharp increase in capacitance due to a sudden jump in the dipole moment. We have also observed that this capacitance can switch rapidly between two distinct states, with no hysteresis in the domain with the higher energy state, by simply flipping the domain state. To validate these results, we have performed extensive 2D simulations using major technological standards, confirming that these FeFET domain wall properties can be utilized for the efficient design of ferroelectric transistors.

The growing importance of freight systems cannot be overstated, as they facilitate the global trade that underpins modern economic prosperity. These critical networks, which we term "Freight Ecosystems," enable the movement of goods from remote sources to diverse demand centers, thus saving space and resources. Establishing resilience in freight ecosystems becomes an acute necessity as shipments are often sensitive to disruptions and societal expectations demand high levels of service. This research targets Freight Ecosystem fragility by focusing on the spread of fragility in the United States. Using a combination of location-based and simulation approaches, we have developed a Dependency-Fragility Insight Graph and identified key factors contributing to freight ecosystem vulnerability. Our findings reveal that major ports, like New York's, are hubs of both dependency and fragility due to their wide reach and vulnerability to disruptions. Our analysis shows that fragility spreads rapidly within freight ecosystems, with certain regions emerging as natural buffers or amplifiers of fragility.

This research focuses on the analytical outcomes of a class of stochastic differential equations known as the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, which includes a random component modelled through a pure jump process. By applying specific conditions on the coefficients of these equations, we determine under what circumstances they can be reduced to a simpler form and demonstrate the robustness of this process. In particular, we examine the behavior of the stochastic equation under two distinct disturbance models and establish the conditions necessary for irreducibility in both cases. Finally, we apply these findings to the study of random diffeomorphisms originating from these stochastic equations.

Let G be a finite nilpotent group. The power graph of G, denoted by P(G), is the graph whose vertices are the elements of G, with an edge connecting two elements if one is a power of the other. Our focus is on the least degree of a power graph of a finite nilpotent group. Specifically, we determine the upper limit for the least degree of a power graph of a finite nilpotent group, particularly a finite nilpotent group of a given prime-degree order.

TASO is an advanced, compact system designed for the analysis of high-energy cosmic rays and LHC Lb, with a focus on detecting the $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon through its decays into $J/\psi$ and various hadronic modes. TASO boasts an ultra-low threshold for particle detection, enabling the study of rare phenomena such as electron-positron pairs produced by dark matter, as well as the comprehensive examination of $\Sigma^{\pm}$ baryons and their anti-gravitational counterparts. Additionally, TASO is capable of identifying particle azimuthal symmetry patterns in cosmic ray events, which could serve as a distinct signature for the detection of stau particles generated by supersymmetry, and is equipped with an ultra-filtering module to isolate downstream particle beams. This extensive, versatile instrument is poised to significantly contribute to a broad spectrum of fundamental physics research at the LHC and in cosmic radiation studies.

Deep convolutional networks are widely regarded as the most effective classification architectures for visual tasks.  Despite their success, many conventional convolutional layers used in deep networks were found to be ineffective contributors to the overall image classification process.  Motivated by this paradox, a novel orientation convolution type was proposed, designed to capture essential orientation features of images, making it a crucial component of deep network architectures.  Comprehensive experiments were conducted to determine the ideal size and spacing of filters within this new convolution type.  The orientation convolution was then integrated into a standard convolutional network architecture, and the resulting hybrid network outperformed conventional approaches by achieving a remarkable 76.9% accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset.  Furthermore, the integrated hybrid network demonstrated exceptional generalization capabilities, as evidenced by its comprehensive evaluation on multiple challenging benchmark datasets, including Turker, ImageNet 2012, and Camelyon17.

This paper seeks to enhance the accuracy of point cloud processing tasks, specifically orientation estimation and classification. Notably, these tasks prove challenging due to random orientation in 3D space. To overcome this, we propose the use of the SE(3) invariant graph convolutions, a novel approach designed to accommodate anisotropic graph convolution. By introducing anisotropic graph convolution, we aim to effectively integrate features from neighboring points, a capability previously constrained by circumscribed spheres in prior studies. To bridge this limitation, we developed a new distance metric, known as the geometric anisotropic distance metric. This metric allows the creation of an anisotropic kernel, facilitating smoother and more precise kernel transition between adjacent points. Empirical studies on orientation estimation and semantic segmentation have shown that our proposed model, which integrates SE(3) invariant graph convolutions with anisotropic kernels, outperforms existing point cloud processing models.

A host-based approach in Trojan assault techniques necessitate knowledge of the target model architecture, limiting their applicability to trained models only, and renders them ineffective against models deployed in production environments. To overcome these limitations, a new attack method has been devised, which employs a signal extraction technique to bypass the need for target model information altogether. Furthermore, a prediction-based distortion technique has been developed to ensure the extracted signal's uniqueness, while also enabling detection by human eyes. Experimental results demonstrate that nearly 90% of host-less Trojan assaults can be successfully avoided, with less than half the requirements of existing host-based attacks, and with minimal impact on model accuracy.

Between 2016 and 2018, our team upgraded the Magellan IMACS spectroimeter at the Las Campanas Observatory with a robotic eponym, ROSIE, to eke out more from the instrument. ROSIE is an integral field device consisting of 61 individual slits, each just 0.3 arcseconds wide, arranged in a 21x21 grid, spanning a 40 arcminute field of view. Our work involved automating the robot to seamlessly integrate with the telescope's controller, crafting a novel hardware setup, and developing corresponding software to harness the full potential of our new setup.

Throughout the enhancement process, our team encountered and overcame various obstacles, presented in this paper along with accompanying figures. Additionally, we showcase the results of ROSIE's first year of operation (2018-2019), including a sample of its delivered data and the implications of its capabilities for future applications.

In low-energy particle-collision studies, the Trojan horse technique has significantly enhanced our ability to distinguish between different nuclear reaction mechanisms, and has now been instrumental in resolving the long-standing issue of extremely low effective barrier heights in carbon-carbon fusion experiments. These experiments, including the latest one published in Physical Review Letters in 2010, revealed a surprisingly low effective barrier of 0.56 MeV, confirming previous findings by Beck et al. and sparking considerable debate in the field. Our review aims to provide a thorough examination of the topic, and we hope that the reader will share our excitement and enthusiasm for this subject.

A crucial step in discovering habitable exoplanets has been identifying the essential elements for life to exist. Researchers aim to understand the core compositions of terrestrial-type planets by analyzing the properties of their parent stars. The core size of an exoplanet largely depends on its mass and the elements present in its mantle and core. Studying the core of an exoplanet is essential in determining its potential habitability. The authors of this paper investigated the core compositions of planets surrounding various types of stars, including those of a specific metallicity, and observed that core mass fraction increases with increasing metallicity and planetary mass. The model also reveals minimal to no difference in core compositions for planets surrounding stars with different metallicities but of the same mass. The results from this study can help developers of planetary frameworks and researchers working on diversity studies of terrestrial planets.

In recent years, Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi) based location service has experienced rapid growth due to the extensive coverage and diverse range of location-aware devices. However, the signal strength-based Wi-Fi location technique has several limitations, particularly indoor interference and device-specific propagation losses. To address these challenges, a novel deep learning method is proposed in this research to accurately determine a device's location using Channel State Information (CSI). The network's spatial structure is taken into consideration by incorporating attention mechanics into the model. To counteract interference, a deep neural network was applied to process raw CSI. The attention-based Wi-Fi location algorithm was evaluated using data collected from a 15-by-25 grid layout and achieved significant performance enhancements, yielding 40%, 35%, and 29% improvements in standard deviation for x, y, and combined coordinates, respectively.

This paper offers an exhaustive examination of the modal language and its syntax. It goes on to define various structural equivalences and multiple forms of semantics-based models, all framed within the context of point-topological spaces. By doing so, it establishes the foundation for a comprehensive theory of modal logic semantics.

Krivelevich, Mohar, and Piñero previously proposed the idea of edge-tinting, where a bipartite multigraph is colored with different colors on separate sets, and the edges with the same color are connected in a single component. Their hypothesis suggested that an approximate version of this concept, where the ratio of the longest to the shortest edge, is close to 2, and this value decreases by a factor of $\Omega(n)$ for large graphs. But in this research, we show that this theory is incorrect by showing an example: a specific type of cubic bipartite graph where the ratio of the longest to the shortest edge is around 6, and this value does not decrease by a factor of even $\Omega(\log n)$ for large graphs.

We examine functions defined on the Hamming graphs, specifically those that are $\epsilon$-error resistant against adaptive attacks. These functions have their values determined by a set of $m$ linearly independent functions defined over the finite field $Z_2$, each with a support of size $n$. The total weight of these functions cannot exceed $K$. Our goal is to identify the minimum possible support size for such functions given these constraints. In the scenario where the functions can be traced back to a single linearly independent function with a support of size $n$, our approach allows us to provide a construction that closely matches this lower bound. When this assumption does not hold, we must rely on a more complex method that gives us a larger (though still the best possible) lower bound.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, both quantitative and qualitative. It offers a comprehensive suite of tools, including automatic network construction, meshing, and solving ordinary and differential algebraic equations, as well as various analytical methods such as sensitivity, parameter estimation, and optimization. Despite its powerful features, COPASI's user interface can be overwhelming due to the numerous options and complex workflows. Our previous work addressed this challenge by creating webCOPASI, a online platform offering a simplified user experience and direct access to model simulations and analyses. Our current research extends this effort to both webCOPASI and local COPASI installations with the ShinyCOPASI interface, providing a streamlined experience for running PreComBI pipeline workflows and a user-friendly environment for exploring and navigating model components.

Understanding and quantifying ambiguity is essential in learning from limited, noisy, and theoretical data. This study surveys current methods for ambiguities in machine learning and outlines specific metrics and interrelations for further analysis. It then applies these metrics to evaluate several popular learning algorithms and datasets, revealing insights into each algorithm's performance and potential pitfalls. These findings and the presented framework can help researchers accurately measure and compare different machine learning approaches, ultimately facilitating more informed decision-making.

We are investigating the von Neumann algebra generated by the set of category functions on a compact quantum group, which is based on its representation category. Our study follows previous research by Nayak who examined the unital subalgebra consisting of category functions that preserve the group structure. Our findings show that the entire algebra is different from the group's C*-algebra, while a previous result by Nayak found it similar to the group's C*-algebra in certain cases. Additionally, we explored how compact quantum group morphisms affect the algebra. Furthermore, we were unable to replicate a previous result by Nayak that showed a specific universality property for the group structure algebra.

In this research, we introduce an efficient algorithm for solving a type of decision-making problem known as extensive Markov decision processes, which are characterized by infinite states and actions with bounded impact. Traditionally, solving these problems involves converting them into a smaller set of mathematical problems that can be computationally expensive. We develop an algorithm that takes advantage of its concise mathematical representation, leveraging its structural properties to efficiently find a suitable solution that can be guaranteed to be within a certain margin of error. We test this algorithm using a group of decision-making problems and compare its performance to other more conventional approaches.

Given a weighted directed graph $(\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{W})$, we define the edge ideal $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{G}}$ and study its properties, specifically how they relate to the vertices of $\mathcal{G}$. This research extends previous findings by Iyama et al. and provides new insights into the algebraic and combinatorial characteristics of edge ideals, surpassing existing limits on linear edge ideal applications. Our main contributions include determining algebraic and combinatorial criteria for when an edge ideal has a particular structure, as well as identifying both common and unique factors that can influence this structure in weighted directed graphs. Additionally, we investigate the symbolic strength of edge ideals in weighted directed graphs and its connection to the concept of algebraic strength.

When modeling complex systems through computer simulation, researchers often encounter a critical challenge: their output data are typically sequenced as time-series information but analyzed as single numerical values.  In order to address this problem, we consider a vital area of modeling, namely, time-series valued model assessments, which have received little attention in the modeling literature.  Utilizing multiple contour assessment, a novel approach, we explore ways to effectively evaluate and compare simulated distributions that take into account sequential data.  As a case study, we examine the benefits of using this time-series valued assessment framework in the context of a neuropsychological test designed to measure cognitive functions.

To improve the resilience of machine learning models in critical applications such as self-driving cars and medical diagnosis, researchers are modifying existing models using self-sensing mechanisms. However, these enhanced models often require substantial updates to be effective, a burden that can be costly and time-consuming, making them unsuitable for certain applications. A new approach, known as regional Kerenism learning, has been proposed to provide an efficient and scalable solution for refining existing models without significantly altering their behavior. An in-depth analysis has been conducted to explore the scenarios in which regional updates are capable of addressing the issue of model resilience, and experimental results have been gathered from multiple studies in computer vision to demonstrate the efficacy of this novel method.

For jets associated with isolated photons in PbPb and pp collisions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} =$ 5.02 TeV, the fragmentation functions of charged particles are measured. The data are based on an analysis of the Medium Impact Parameter (MIP) technique, using collision data from the CMS detector, selecting isolated photons with transverse momentum greater than 25 GeV. The investigation covers the range of jet transverse momentum from 30 to 100 GeV. The results for PbPb collisions show that the average energy per charged particle increases as jet transverse momentum increases, consistent with findings in pp collisions. However, the MIP technique reveals modifications in the fragmentation function: a decrease in low-energy particles and an increase in high-energy particles, particularly pronounced for $p_\mathrm{T,jet} >$ 50 GeV.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating terms can be represented through colored multiple zeta functions, this current study presents an expanded model that incorporates alternating terms. A specific new model is the Apéry-type inverse binomial series with alternating signs in the numerator and hyperbolic trigonometric functions. Using the framework of colored Fourier-Borel transform, both positive and negative terms in the Apéry-type series are shown to be equivalent to specific colored multiple zeta functions. By applying the inverse approach, this model leads to novel explicit evaluations of certain zeta functions, which in turn provide series expansions for positive and negative terms. A particularly interesting outcome is the derivation of an alternative series expansion for the function $\zeta(5)_2$ (a variant of the zeta function) and its relation to the natural number sequence count function.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, revealed little to no parallax measurement in the Gaia EDR3 catalog, indicating the precision might be improved with additional data. Visual and IR images suggested the presence of a compact object about 1 arcsecond away from the point of interest, though the source of the signal in these images remains ambiguous. The second revision of the Parallax Catalog released by Gaia delivered a precise measurement of 66.731±0.044 millarcseconds for this target, resulting in an estimated distance of 8.24±0.02 parsecs for WISEA J153429.75-104303.3. The initial data released by Meisner et al is thought to be contaminated by the background compact object, and an initial attempt to remove this contamination was made in this research. The resulting measurement of the original object is consistent with brown dwarf data, specifically displaying spectral characteristics of W3Baea and W4Scha, although the initial data released by Meisner et al is at odds with this result, yielding W3Baea and W4Scha spectra of reduced intensity.

Theoretical predictions for particle production in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV are developed using the ALICE ALPINO framework. This framework utilizes the next-to-leading-order partial wave expansion method to calculate a wide range of observables such as rapidity, transverse momentum, transverse momentum distributions, and yield manufacturing for various particle species like pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and phi mesons. Furthermore, expectations for systematic uncertainties and participant numbers in 5.44 TeV Xe-Xe collisions are also predicted.

We examine parton distribution functions at distinct evolution scales and
find that their progression is not always continuous. This discontinuity arises
from how certain terms are combined and ignored in evolution algebra. To resolve
this issue, we offer a new interpretation which ensures parton distribution
functions evolve smoothly, even when changing to new basis sets. Additionally,
we provide a method to directly translate parton distribution functions between
different forms, eliminating the need to compute and then sum various terms.

Speculating on human settlements in Mars and the Moon, this research delves into how heat processing affects the microstructure and mechanical properties of simulated lunar and Martian soil. Experiments were conducted at three different temperatures - 0.973, 1.023, and 1.073 Gaussian units - using electron backscatter analysis and uniaxial compression testing on samples from both the Moon and the Moon mimicked with added water. Water content had a minimal impact on the samples' microstructure but significantly influenced their strength. Compared to room temperature samples, the ones processed at higher temperatures showed enhanced mechanical properties, along with improved strength and reduced porosity. The data collected, along with microstructure and porosity information, will aid in predicting the strength and behavior of unprocessed and heat-treated Martian and lunar soil samples.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber are influenced by the interaction between three forces: surface tension, adhesion, and capillary action. As the fiber is withdrawn, the liquid layer undergoes an instability characterized by non-slip conditions at the liquid-solid interface. However, altering the slip parameter significantly changes the dynamics of the system. As the liquid layer breaks down, the rate at which the fluid moves away from the fiber's surface increases with the slip parameter. Furthermore, the liquid droplets formed on the fiber have a lower number of points of contact with the slip parameter, indicating a possible reduction in droplet size due to increased capillary forces.

By comparing the dust-based star formation rates (sFRs) obtained from the Infrared Galaxy Explorer (SPIRE) spectroscopy and the optical recombination lines of H~II regions, we evaluate the accuracy of three common SED fitting routines in predicting sFRs. The comparison also involves assessing their predictions for gas metallicities using [O~II] and C~II emissions. The analysis is conducted on a test dataset of 35 galaxies spanning both the local universe and the COSMOS-DCEvolved field. The analysis shows that the SED fitting routines yield a correlation of 0.79 for H~II regions and 0.75 for solar neighbourhoods in spiral galaxies. Although the SED routines tend to agree on absolute sFR values, they display larger point-to-point variations. The SED routines underestimate sFRs by a factor of 0.57 to 0.85 compared to dust-based measurements, with most [C~II]-derived sFR estimates showing a narrower range of agreement with dust-based sFRs than [O~II]-based estimates. The SED routines also produce metallicity estimates with comparable accuracy to each other but less accurate than dust-based measurements, with a mean absolute error of 0.05 to 0.06 dex. Ultimately, these findings suggest that bracketed gamma measurements can serve as a benchmark to assess and improve the accuracy of SED routines in predicting sFRs.

In a polyhedron divided into multiple regions, where the walls and corners form a simplex with vertices numbered $0$ through $N$, we define the quantum subalgebras of the special $N$-dimensional Lie algebra within each region.
