These structures, driven by a central element representing the region's area, exhibit a two-fold nature similar to the $\mathfr{gl}_{2}|k$ algebra. They possess a $\mathfr{gl}_{2}|q$ embedding, revealing a connection to the q-deformed special unitary group. Furthermore, these subalgebras serve as second symmetric powers of the algebra obtained from the q-deformed projective line, $\mathfr{qP}_{1}$. This work lays the groundwork for a broader exploration of these quantum structures in relation to the quantum affine Weyl group of type $A$.

Utilizing the Adomian decomposition method to solve nonlinear differential equations, we analyze in detail the solution to the universal diffusion equation, especially its fractal dimension, and find that it can be expressed as a sum of unique, interconnected solutions that correspond to various diffusion rates. Calculating the associated Lyapunov exponents reveals that these dimensions possess multiple, distinct values. By comparing these exponents with the calculated fractal dimensions, we establish a criterion to determine their equivalence. Furthermore, our investigation into the universal diffusion equation's solution reveals a diverse range of behaviors, including the emergence of chaotic patterns, particularly in cases where the differential equation's nonlinear term exhibits countably many local maxima and minima.

Recent advancements in gesture recognition technology from various sensor platforms have made it possible to capture online handwritten mathematical expressions with high precision. A new dataset, referred to as MMathExpressions, has been developed to advance research in this area by incorporating diverse online mathematical expressions captured through a built-in camera, accelerometer, gyroscope, and touchscreen. A groundbreaking approach has been introduced to automatically recognize complex mathematical expressions captured via multi-modal sensor data. Unlike conventional offline mathematical expression recognition, which leverages rich contextual information, our method focuses on processing raw signal data from various sensor sources. By applying a signal feature extraction technique and utilizing a dedicated feature set, including time-frequency, geometric, and touch-based characteristics, along with a carefully designed classification architecture, we have achieved exceptional performance results. Specifically, our proposed method has attained class-level accuracy rates of up to 93% for simple and 83% for complex mathematical expressions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the reliability of our approach by achieving online recognition rates faster than real-time on a touchscreen device.

This research presents an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech at various lengths using a non-statistical method. Typically, speech synthesis lengths are defined as either whole or fractional values, but this work explores the possibility of specifying lengths with greater precision. We propose a two-step median-driven protocol for adjusting the number of speech frames in a synthetic utterance. Initially, we modify the target speech length to an equivalent whole number via a finite mathematical transformation, and then employ this value to select intermediate frames from multiple nearby utterances via a median-based averaging process. To test our approach, we conducted detailed analyses and evaluations of speech synthesis at lengths of 4.79 and 7.18 frames per utterance.

Species distribution models have expanded considerably in recent decades, with various software programs and methodologies now available to analyze and predict species presence. However, certain techniques remain underrepresented in distribution modeling, such as presence-only data analysis. A new R software, spHabitat, has been developed to address this limitation by incorporating logistic regression, machine learning algorithms, and energy-based models to analyze species presence-only data in a spatial context. Furthermore, spHabitat also enables the joint modeling of species abundance and habitat quality using general additive models, along with variable selection methods. The software comes with a range of demonstration examples and is freely available on CRAN and GitHub.

The Skincare system utilizes a deep learning framework to help dermatologists overcome common challenges in diagnosing skin cancer more accurately. By gathering extensive data from various sources, such as patient histories and biopsy results, Skincare can provide valuable insights to inform clinical decisions. Additionally, the system leverages an interactive module that enables physicians to incorporate patients' personal characteristics and establish a baseline for comparison, ultimately facilitating more precise differential diagnosis of skin lesions. This technical report outlines the details of Skincare's development and showcases its capabilities.

To enhance the accuracy of cosmological measurements derived from type Ia supernovae, researchers are developing techniques to mitigate the impact of uncertainties associated with these explosions. One approach involves using artificial neural networks to model the complex phenomena affecting supernovae in a more effective manner. This is achieved by treating unknown factors, such as inhomogeneous environments and internal explosion mechanisms, as random variables that can be learned from observational data. This article describes the development of a type Ia supernova time sequence model focusing on spectrum features, which incorporates the inherent uncertainties associated with these events. This is done by treating the unknown factors as noise in the input data, which is addressed using a stochastic version of the autoencoder. The efficacy of this model is demonstrated through the application of it to a dataset of 550 supernovae, which is the foundation of the "Open SN 2021gy" dataset. This approach enables the incorporation of epistemic uncertainty into models based on deep learning, which in turn facilitates the transfer of this uncertainty to cosmological distances measurements and subsequent analysis using Bayesian methods.

A massive galaxy at a distance of approximately 1.8 billion light-years is the closest example of a massive star formation event observed so far. The study utilized ALMA to map a neutral hydrogen gas outbreak within this galaxy and found evidence supporting a theory that such outbreaks are primary sources of gas re-injection into the galaxy's center. The outbreaks were seen leaving the galaxy at speeds ranging between 500 to 700 km per second. It's possible that these outbreaks could be what supplies the gas for the galaxy's ongoing and intense star formation. The outbreaks were seen using an ALMA dataset with a high angular resolution, despite being partially obscured by a massive dust cloud at the galaxy's center. The observed neutral hydrogen outbreaks were seen spreading out of the galaxy in a symmetric pattern, supporting the idea that such outbreaks are a byproduct of supermassive black hole driven winds that have picked up material. The study's findings support the idea that these outbreaks play a crucial role in regulating the flow of gas within the galaxy. The study's data was compared to simulated data from the MACS1159B galaxy, which is one of the furthest away objects observed, and a galaxy thought to be in an advanced stage of star formation. The comparison showed that these outbreaks can be seen at distances as far as approximately 1.8 billion light-years away, using highly sensitive observations, provided that the gas is targeted directly.

The process of a fluid flowing into a region filled with particles under conditions of turbulence is investigated through both theoretical and experimental means. Through a developed analysis, the rate at which the fluid enters the region can be determined based on the characteristics of the surrounding turbulence and the properties of the particles under certain conditions. This prediction is further validated by comparing it with the results obtained from both past studies and a novel experiment conducted in a controlled environment.

Understanding the spread of epidemics on complex networks, especially hypergraphs, requires analyzing how infectious diseases transmit from infected to uninfected individuals at neighboring nodes within the same cluster. A crucial model for this phenomenon involves the "inclusion-exclusion" model, where the probability of infection depends on the ratio of infected and uninfected individuals in each cluster. However, calculating these probabilities is extremely challenging when the underlying network takes the form of a complex hypergraph. In response to this difficulty, researchers have developed theoretical models that make predictable predictions about the likelihood of disease spread under specific conditions. In the present study, researchers developed new theoretical frameworks for both the "inclusion-exclusion" and "infection-only" models related to this phenomenon. These frameworks rely on limiting the spectral properties of specific matrices derived from the hypergraph's cluster structure. The resulting theoretical models, presented in detail, make accurate predictions about the critical threshold for the emergence and spread of epidemics within the specified type of network. In the case of the "inclusion-exclusion" model, these predictions take the form of an exponential relationship between this critical threshold and key parameters of the disease and the network. The research also investigates how these theoretical models are affected by specific patterns present in the underlying hypergraph, particularly those resulting from random generation techniques. The study's primary focus is on understanding the abrupt changes, or "phase transitions," that occur as the critical threshold is approached or crossed. The behavior of magnetic properties in two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic materials is of considerable interest, and our investigation focuses on the spin structure in the 2D ferromagnetic compound CrI3. Specifically, we analyzed a bilayer version of this material, which exhibits optical symmetry. Initially, we used the effective field theory to examine the magnetic properties of this bilayer within a external magnetic field applied in the plane, and found that it exhibits a comprehensive range of spin arrangements. Then, we used the density functional theory with the Hartree-Fock exchange-correlation component to calculate the spin-resolved density matrix, and our results are in agreement with those obtained from the effective field theory. Moreover, we explored the influences of Rashba and spin-orbit coupling on the magnetic properties of this bilayer, and our analysis highlights the pivotal role of these factors in shaping the spin structure in materials with these characteristics. Finally, we examined the electrical resistance of this bilayer under various conditions and its response to an in-plane magnetic field, and our results are in agreement with those of other researchers, indicating that the spin structure in this bilayer is 2D isotropic and shows no directional dependence.

Past studies of mean-field dynamos in stars have demonstrated that sun-like rotation patterns can lead to magnetic activity cycles, while other types of rotation patterns cannot explain the long-term magnetic variations observed in the sun and a few other stars.  Researchers now speculate that certain non-constant rotation patterns in a star's middle latitudes could be necessary for generating long-term magnetic variations, and that these patterns might be connected to a star's external influences, such as its distance from the star's center of mass and its surface rotation rate.  To understand how these external factors affect a star's internal rotation, scientists create theoretical models of stars like the sun, assuming various rotation rates and distant factors.  They then use these models to study how a star's internal rotation affects its magnetic behavior, and find that when a star's rotation patterns in the mid-latitudes are similar to those at the poles, it cannot generate long-term magnetic variations, regardless of its distance from the star's center of mass.  However, when a star's rotation patterns in the mid-latitudes are slower than those at the poles, it can generate long-term magnetic variations, and this phenomenon is more pronounced in stars that are far from the star's center of mass.  These results suggest that early rotational patterns in a star's middle latitudes could be necessary for generating long-term magnetic variations, and that external factors can influence the development of magnetic cycles in sun-like stars. Recent breakthroughs in deep multimodal learning have successfully addressed various challenges involving multiple data types. Nevertheless, proposals have often been confined to specific problems or datasets, typically using complex architectures that are difficult to adapt for other tasks. In contrast, fan-based multimodal models offering considerable flexibility have fallen short of delivering impressive performance. In this paper, we upgrade traditional K-fan models, incorporating innovations such as shared hypersectors, and successfully apply our enhanced model to tackle three distinct classification tasks involving image-text and video-text data. Notably, our model achieves remarkable success in 8 out of 9 evaluation metrics, surpassing current state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets.

McMini, a static model verifier for multithreaded systems based on McMillan's SPIN model checker, was developed to identify potential race hazards and deadlocks in program execution. Although McMini is adaptable and efficient, its original version had a crucial flaw: it failed to effectively handle programs with nested locks, causing the model verifier to generate an endless sequence of new reachable states for every lock, essentially making it unusable for complex multithreaded programs due to its rapid state explosion. In this research, we address this issue by incorporating improvements into McMini: (i) partition-based, Dulbois-Reichman, and Chakraborti-Kar early termination techniques; (ii) a new McMini model with nested lock capabilities; and (iii) an optimized McMini variant, mlmc, featuring a localized memory model. These modifications render mcmini versatile, efficient, and efficient enough for use in evaluating multithreaded program correctness.

The widespread misuse of social media platforms in disseminating false information has been a longstanding issue in modern society. Our investigation centers around the role of social media platforms in encouraging misinformation dissemination and the consequent societal repercussions. Specifically, we examine the effect of limitations on social media posting and the subsequent alteration in the spread of coercion-related misinformation during the 2019 Brazilian elections. Working with WhatsApp, the most popular messaging app in Brazil, we devise a metric that quantifies its potential impact on the misinformation landscape. Our results suggest that coercion-related misinformation proliferation in Brazil declined substantially in the four months following a national regulation limiting WhatsApp usage in the country.

The prevalence of a particular allele within a population is estimated to be roughly equally distributed between two categories: present or absent.  This assumption holds approximately when the allele's prevalence follows a binomial distribution, approximately equivalent to the sum of two independent gamma random variables with small values.  Approximately half of the possible values within the range of nonnegative integers will be the allele's prevalence.  This approximation holds when the probability of the allele's absence or presence exceeds a certain low threshold, which is dependent on the allele's mean prevalence.  This approximation also holds when the allele's prevalence follows a continuous distribution, approximately equal to the combination of two general branching processes.

The primary goal of anti-spoofing systems is to identify and counter potentially fabricated audio inputs. These mechanisms typically function as activation functions within a deep neural network, amplifying relevant features that indicate the likelihood of a voice being fake. Existing anti-spoofing functions, however, struggle to target artificial features specifically, as they often become over-sensitive to background noises in real inputs. This problem highlights a critical challenge for these functions: they fail to accurately distinguish between artificial characteristics and legitimate background noises. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new mechanism that mimics the attention mechanism often employed in machine translation systems. This new activation function utilizes the weights of the preceding network to emphasize features that provide the most insight into whether an input voice is genuine or fake. During training, it leverages the weights of the preceding network as an adjustable factor, thereby facilitating backpropagation. Additionally, we prevent over-sensitivity by limiting excessive activations. This novel activation function successfully boosts the performance of end-to-end spoofing counteraction systems, as experimental results verify its superiority.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, is used to develop a theoretical framework for an inflationary cosmological model. The study focuses on a specific supergravity model featuring a chiral superfield with a potential controlled by an $\alpha$ parameter and an $\epsilon$ parameter. Based on the slow-roll conditions, the paper determines the range of the $\epsilon$ parameter and develops solutions for the scale factor of the universe and the primordial scalar fluctuations. The resulting universe models have scale potentials resembling the chaotic inflation scenario or a natural inflation scenario, with the inclusion of scalar particles contributing to inflationary dynamics. The choice of the $\epsilon$ parameter value allows for a natural alignment of the scalar fluctuations with observations from Planck, while a discussion on future fluctuations from the moduli fields is included in the model.

We investigate the associated photon production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The study focuses on the central region of the collisions, specifically on isolated photon pairs with transverse momenta greater than 10 GeV and rapidity within -1.45 to 1.45. The findings are based on a large dataset of 137 fb^-1 collected by the ATLAS detector. The probability distribution of the transverse momentum of one photon in pairs is examined, showing an asymmetry when photons have similar momenta. The results match theoretical predictions of next-to-leading-order parton-level processes.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as a leading platform for quantum computing and information technology. To accelerate their development, it is crucial to gain a thorough understanding of how they function. This involves scrutinizing the behavior of individual Josephson junctions within superconducting resonators using terahertz microscopy, focusing particularly on the local disruption of the electromagnetic field. By near-field imaging of these resonators, researchers can obtain precise measurements of device parameters, ultimately leading to enhanced device performance. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of terahertz microscopy in analyzing cpw resonators and highlights its advantages in comparison to far-field characterization methods.

We explore a general problem that encompasses a specific question posed by J.INDUSTRY in a MathOverflow query. The broader problem involves determining the validity of two distinct assertions regarding collections of subsets of the real line. These assertions can be applied to create a valid division of the real line into Borel sets. One assertion states that if a countable collection of closed sets does not cover the real line, it is possible to divide the real line into two non-empty sets such that each set contains only elements not contained in the other. The second assertion is a complement to a well-known Borel partition theorem, stating that if a countable collection of open sets does not cover the real line, it is possible to divide the real line into two non-overlapping, Borel sets.

This research investigates novel investment methods' potential impact on established strategies in an ever-changing economic environment. We employ an agent-based model that simulates an open economy with two types of investors: those who adhere to traditional approaches and those who exploit new investment opportunities. Our findings suggest that novel approaches tend to coexist with established strategies rather than replacing them. However, when agent-based models are modified to include external shocks, novel approaches prove more resilient than traditional ones. Ultimately, our study advocates for the integration of novel and established investment methods.

Identifying network protocols is a crucial process that involves determining and categorizing protocol data to extract relevant information, and this process has been simplified by improved identification methods. However, over time, various techniques have been developed to evade identification, and some of these are particularly effective against common network defense tools. Although these tools rely on rapid and efficient protocol identification to function properly, they are susceptible to evasion methods that exploit specific characteristics of each. In this research, common network defense tools were tested for their responsiveness to various assaults on protocol identification, and the results revealed not only the effectiveness of certain evasion methods but also the varying resilience of each tool to these attacks. The study provides an overview of each successful assault and suggests potential areas of improvement for future development.

We propose and simulate an experimental setup that involves superconductors and magnetic materials in a quantum system. The unique interaction between the superconductors and the magnetic materials creates a robust and controllable magnon blockade by generating a significant amount of energy between the superconductors. The 4K technology that we are utilizing is an important advancement in the field, as it may enable the development of quantum devices using readily available materials. Additionally, this energy scale could potentially facilitate the transfer of information between materials through magnons, which could offer an alternative to existing technology for data processing and communication.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, this methodology poses a challenge in training models due to significant data distribution disparities across users and the consequent difficulty in achieving model convergence. Furthermore, the emergence of novel categories during federated learning complicates the classification process. In this research, we address these challenges by exploring the use of zero-shot federated learning. Initially, we establish data relationships for each user, incorporating unknown novel categories. Subsequently, we develop a novel classification rule and a convergence assessment technique tailored to this new data environment. Our proposed framework is validated by applying it to three distinct datasets, thereby showcasing its effectiveness in a real-world audio classification context.

Achieving high scalability in quantum computing and communication relies heavily on the successful implementation of high-dimensional quantum systems. The development of versatile and robust quantum tools is crucial for advancing multi-dimensional quantum technologies. Specifically, advanced multi-dimensional entangled states serve as essential references for assessing the performance and capabilities of quantum systems. This research presents a detailed proposal for determining high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, along with the associated measurement analysis. Furthermore, we examine the efficiency of standard optical components in three and four-dimensional configurations, highlighting the advantages and limitations of both fiber and free-space implementations. Our study outlines a comprehensive plan for evaluating multi-dimensional entangled states, which will be instrumental in assessing the performance of multi-dimensional quantum tools.

This research paper delves into the development of efficient channel estimation techniques for large-scale networks involving a single base station and multiple users, aided by a reflective surface. Due to the scalability issue posed by conventional approach, a novel approach utilizing the base station's high transmission power is proposed. It splits the channel estimation process into two stages, using the base station's power to efficiently estimate the channel. Using simulations, it demonstrates that this approach results in faster and more accurate user data transfer. It achieves this through the use of the base station's power to strongly impact the channel and reduce uncertainty, resulting in accurate user data transfer.

The COVID-19 pandemic has been covered by regional news media in the U.S. with varying intensity and emphasis, reflecting changes in the disease's progression and regional context. Our research examines digital news coverage from April to November 2020 in eight U.S. regions, including relationships with local COVID cases and fatalities, and explores variations in news coverage across different regions, demographics, audience size, and news topics. Our analysis reveals substantial differences in news coverage, with areas experiencing a resurgence in COVID-19 receiving more attention from local news media, while older populations and local news are associated with greater coverage. Interestingly, local news audience size does not necessarily correlate with COVID-related coverage, and news coverage of non-COVID topics can actually detract from the public's access to crucial pandemic information.

In various cognitive tests, people's ability to count objects accurately is impacted by certain external stimuli, such as visual cues, and this effect can be measured and understood through the shape of their score plots. To study human thinking in detail, researchers need a computer model that can accurately predict human behavior in these experiments. We've developed a advanced computer model that can learn and remember information about object characteristics, allowing it to accurately predict human scores in these experiments. Additionally, our computer model requires fewer training data to produce accurate predictions compared to other neural network models. We've tested the capabilities of our computer model by using it to simulate experiments where both humans and machines are tested for their counting abilities.

Bloom filters provide fast membership tests for efficiently screening out items that do not belong to a particular set. While Bloom filters are always incorrect, they accurately predict negative outcomes with high probability. A false positive rate reduction can be achieved by increasing the required storage capacity, often in the form of additional hash functions. Cuckoo filters offer an improved false positive rate and faster operations compared to Bloom filters, using the same storage capacity by incorporating a separate set membership tracking system. A XOR-based construction in Cuckoo filters also allows for the efficient use of existing data to minimize storage needs. Despite these improvements, adding new elements to a filter remains expensive. A XOR-based approach was also applied to Bloom filters to screen larger sets more efficiently. A new "XOR Filter" combination has been developed, providing faster and more efficient false positive rate reduction and element addition compared to both Bloom and Cuckoo filters. XOR Filter can be seen as an improved variant of PBF, a recently introduced filter type.

This note explores connections between modern convex geometry and specific themes in complex analysis, namely Fekete problems, extremal problems, and the growth of entire holomorphic functions. It assumes a solid grasp of analytic and probabilistic methods in combinatorial geometry, as well as familiarity with some convex geometry concepts.

A key objective in technical analysis is to identify prevailing market trends.
Most current trends assessments rely on past price data, neglecting a more valuable resource:
insightful information embedded in sequence of past trades. This paper presents three,
highly efficient indicators that leverage a new framework called the Time-Cost-Sales
(TCS) model. Our indicators will help traders gain a deeper understanding of market trends
and make more informed decisions, thanks to our approach's ability to extract trends from
past transaction data, even when prices are volatile and unpredictable. Furthermore, our
method can incorporate future transaction data to improve trend assessments, a feature
not currently available in traditional analysis methods.

This work presents FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework designed to withstand strategic data owners and ensure fair decision-making outcomes within a group of collaborators. To achieve this resilience, we integrate a specific type of voting mechanism alongside a modification of the standard federated learning protocol. By utilizing a directory-based approach for model sharing, we also protect each data owner's private information and maintain their individuality. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective against multiple types of malicious behavior, as experimentally verified using generated datasets.

Achieving precise visual navigation in real-world scenarios is extremely challenging due to the significant discrepancy between simulated and actual image data. This research tackles the complex problem of navigating without relying on pre-built maps, which is known as the Autonomous Navigation Assignment (ANA) problem. An innovative framework was developed to bridge the substantial gap between simulated and real-world images, leveraging gradient information to map locations to visual features. The framework consists of three key components: a feature extractor, a matcher, and an optimizer. The feature extractor converts raw data into comparable features, the matcher identifies the best match for the current feature set, and the optimizer refines the match to minimize feature shift. A novel optimizer, called Gradient Expectation-Maximization, was proposed to take advantage of real-world gradient expectations for improved performance. The framework was evaluated on diverse routes in two indoor environments and two outdoor settings, demonstrating superior results compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

Significant advancements in deep learning technology have enabled the creation of deepfakes with minimal identification difficulties, even when minor facial adjustments are made. Consequently, the need for more sophisticated methods to produce and detect strong deepfakes has grown, especially when dealing with unrestricted content. This paper presents a novel approach to strong deepfake creation, involving the integration of boundary self-attention mechanism to preserve distinct features. Additionally, six prominent existing deepfake detection methods were evaluated and compared using the Deepfake Detection Evaluation 2020 dataset, yielding an exceptional detection accuracy of 6.17% and 6.37% for DFDC and FaceForeniscs++ respectively. Our proposed method achieved remarkable performance by prioritizing the efficient extraction of meaningful features from input images. The research findings may contribute to the further development of deepfake creation and detection techniques.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets with their various characteristics has allowed astronomers to infer the possibility of diverse planetary environments. Composed mainly of rock and ice, these planets could have water rich compositions similar to those of Earth. To better understand the internal structures of these planets, researchers are using unique astronomical signatures that arise from the interaction between their rocky cores and surrounding liquids. Specifically, they analyze how different liquids react to the pressure and temperature changes that occur during transit events.

Existing models rely on distinct physical processes: either the dissolution of minerals in water or the thermal behavior of gases. However, these approaches may provide incomplete insights into the internal structures of these planets. To improve our understanding, scientists proposed a new model that combines the available transit data with observations of a planet's size and mass. This new model uses a complex computational approach that takes into account various factors that influence the internal structures of these planets.

In a recent study, researchers applied this new model to a list of 28 suitable targets from multiple astronomical surveys. This effort helped to identify key features that can help to distinguish between different liquid environments in these exoplanets. As a result, the most promising candidates that indicate the presence of concealed oceans within these planets include NGTS-13, GJ 3470 b, and HAT-P-26B. These findings also highlight the significance of follow-up observations for a larger set of monitored planets that could further reveal the internal structures of these worlds.

In the field of neuromorphic computing, researchers are developing innovative algorithms inspired by biological neural networks to process complex data efficiently. Our work focuses on the challenge of pattern recognition, where the network is trained to accurately identify distinct data patterns consisting of both meaningful and irrelevant features. Utilizing a spiking neural network based on the NMDA-R and TDGL models, we have developed an innovative gradient-based learning algorithm that can be effectively implemented using simulated annealing. Our approach differs from conventional deep learning methods in two significant ways. Firstly, the model's weight adjustments are influenced by the local error and past synaptic changes, mimicking the biological process of synaptic plasticity. Secondly, the learning algorithm seamlessly integrates forward and backward passes, eliminating the need for separate training and testing phases. Simulation results on various datasets demonstrate that the model can learn meaningful features and accurately classify data, while requiring less computational resources compared to existing deep learning architectures.

This paper presents our approach to the out-of-lexicon task in the NWUA 2022 shared task. As pre-trained models have significantly enhanced the quality of word translations, researchers are now focusing on translating sentences beyond word-level. Out-of-lexicon word translations are crucial in non-English languages, but also essential for achieving high accuracy in sentence translation. We initially aimed to utilize the pre-trained models' strengths by developing a simple yet effective approach to out-of-lexicon sentence translation. Although our initial plan did not yield satisfactory results, we made significant improvements by incorporating task-specific characteristics, data preprocessing, and a prompt-based learning method. Ultimately, our model's performance improved, and we submitted our results to the evaluation process. This paper provides a detailed explanation of our approach, including model design, data analysis, and promising findings.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study verifies the accuracy of this method in a particular context and also identifies potential sources of error. To do this, we first propose a new approach to approximate random equilibrium states. This approach is tested using a well-known problem in physics, specifically a problem related to a particle's motion with random factors affecting its trajectory. The results of our analysis confirm that the approximate random equilibrium state is continuous and follows the original differential equation closely. Furthermore, we develop a metric to measure the difference between approximate and precise random equilibrium states. This metric, along with the approach to approximate random equilibrium states, enables us to confirm the validity of the chaos expansions in the considered context.

This research introduces a novel sequential approach called APOSAII, which identifies and isolates changes in real-time data streams. APOSAII is designed for large-scale online learning platforms and is capable of handling numerous students with varied learning patterns across multiple courses. Given that online learning platforms generate abundant data with students taking various courses, traditional methods are hindered by their inability to process such vast amounts of partially observable data simultaneously. To overcome this limitation, APOSAII leverages the combination of an adaptive expectation-maximization algorithm and a Markov Chain-based random walk, allowing it to dynamically detect and isolate students using only a subset of available data features. This is achieved without requiring any prior knowledge of student behavior. As a result, APOSAII is adaptable, scalable, and accurate, making it an invaluable tool for real-time kinetic analysis and surveillance applications as well.

A comprehensive analysis of 54 dwarf galaxies from the latest version of the SDSS-DR16 atlas has been conducted, focusing on the spectral evolution of stellar populations and their composition. By utilizing the Revista-Basilios atomic lines and a refined version of the Hyperion library, researchers identified key atomic absorption features in each galaxy. In addition, an advanced version of the FLAMEX code was employed to fit spectral models and estimate vital atmospheric and histirical parameters, including ages, metallicity, and dust content. A comprehensive comparison with nearby galaxies grouped by type and color revealed distinct patterns and trends, and subsequent analysis using the CANDOR tool revealed the presence of supernovae remnants in numerous dwarf galaxies. The resulting datasets were then used to establish a classification system for each galaxy based on their chemical markings and evolutionary histories.

Given a profinite group G, an action by G on a compact space X induces a spectral machine that produces a spectrum denoted $\mathcal{Z}G_{h}X$. This work explores the properties of the homotopy action spectrum, and we establish that it functions as a G-spectrum, and there's a G-linear map $\mathcal{Z}G_{h}X \to \mathcal{Z}G_{+}X$ that preserves homotopy, and there's a natural equivalence $\mathcal{Z}G_{h}X \simeq G\times X$ when X is freely G-continuous. Additionally, we define a G-linear map $\mathcal{Z}G_{h}X \to \mathrm{Wh}_p(G)_{+}$ that preserves homotopy, and show that for any G-ploytopological space (X, \mathcal{L}) with a free action, $\mathrm{Wh}_p(G)_{+}$ is pro-equivalent to the G-profinite spectrum $\mathrm{Wh}_p(G)_{h}$.

The surge in automated document processing triggered a significant rise in the need for annotated documents, which comes at a cost often beyond many organizations' budgets.  In this research, we introduce a new approach to reduce the cost of data labeling by leveraging the skills of unskilled workers.  Our innovative framework utilizes AI-powered tools that provide step-by-step instructions to guide these workers through the data labeling process.  By combining this with advanced AI capabilities, we can ensure the quality of the annotated data.  Our findings, backed by experimental results from actual data labeling projects, demonstrate a substantial reduction of up to 90% in data labeling costs compared to the current most effective methods.

The creation of spin-orbit coupled quantum wells relies heavily on the electronic properties of specific interfaces. Research on InAs/EuS quantum wells has shown that these wells can produce unique optical and magnetic properties. Although theoretical models indicate that these wells have a distinct electronic behavior characterized by an internal electron energy level, this has yet to be confirmed through experimental analysis. A key factor that has not been considered in previous studies is the varying bond lengths between InAs and EuS, which can result in different electronic arrangements. Our study of InAs/EuS and EuS/InAs interfaces has shown that they exhibit distinct electronic characteristics, with the electronic configuration of EuS/InAs interfaces confirmed through experimental data and comparative modeling.

A efficient classification system for Borel Wadge classes is presented, based on a priority-list system, in which each Borel set is assigned a sequence of finite subsets corresponding to its Borel Wadge class. It is demonstrated that this classification aligns with the traditional Borel Wadge classes and that it provides a straightforward method for determining the Borel Wadge class of a set obtained by union, intersection, or transfinite induction operations. Additionally, it is shown that this classification remains consistent under continuous functions and that it provides an easy way to determine the Borel Wadge class of a set obtained by composition with such functions.

During training, most deep learning models suffer from degraded accuracy and
increased computing costs due to excessive model complexity. Fortunately,
model pruning can significantly improve both computational efficiency and
memory requirements, but traditional methods often result in a substantial loss of
model precision, distorting the model architecture in the process. There has
been a common misconception that there is a trade-off between pruning amount and
precision loss, leading many systems to simplify the pruning process by removing
few weights at a time. However, this limited approach is unable to lead to the
desired computational savings. In contrast, we propose a new end-to-end deep
model training framework called ClickTrain, which breaks free from this perceived
limitation through a innovative architecture-preserving pruning technique.
Specifically, we developed a new error estimation approach based on
propagation tolerance, allowing us to accurately determine the optimal order
for model weight pruning and achieve significant improvements in both computation
and memory costs without compromising model precision. Furthermore, we integrated
ClickTrain with PyTorch and BERT to develop a highly efficient training pipeline
that is capable of simultaneous training and pruning on large-scale transformer
models, resulting in constant and robust precision, as well as significant
computational and memory cost savings.

This research examines the decidability of the full modal functionality calculus based on Lambek distribution, which includes the ability to simplify modal functions. We show that this decidability is achieved by leveraging a specific semantic structure and developing a set of axiomatic rules. Our findings also reveal that the underlying underlying calculus used for modal functions is both sound and complete.

The collisions of binary compact objects produce unique gravitational waves with distinct patterns, allowing for the identification of their source objects in the universe. Motivated by the vast array of binary collisions containing black holes and neutron stars, researchers developed a new deep learning approach, combining a neural network with a binary classification system to categorize events as either containing neutron stars or consisting solely of black holes. This method was successfully tested on real gravitational wave data from the first two observing runs conducted by LIGO and Virgo, achieving remarkable accuracy in identifying neutron star collisions and facilitating potential discoveries in future observations, particularly in the GWTC-3 dataset.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, TOI-5542 b, which orbits a 12 billion-year-old star in the LMC galaxy. This massive planet, roughly the size of Jupiter, takes about 3.5 days to orbit around its star and has a mass similar to that of Jupiter. Research suggests the planet's mass and radius data align with expected trends for hot Jupiters. Analysis of the planet's properties and its star's metal content reveals an intriguing inverse correlation, which could provide valuable insights into the planet's formation. This investigation is one of the few discoveries of hot Jupiters and adds to our understanding of the types of planets present in older star systems.

Restricted Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) are a type of Markov Decision Process (MDP) that restricts the state and action spaces. To solve RMDPs, a primary-dual approach is implemented, similar to that used in solving linear programming. This method involves two main procedures: primary, which involves finding the optimal reward and cost values, and dual, which involves finding the optimal visitation frequencies. By leveraging duality, we can determine if an optimal solution exists and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for its occurrence. Additionally, the dual problem can be solved through efficient computational methods, allowing us to obtain the optimal visitation frequencies, which in turn facilitate the determination of the optimal policy. Our proposed method has a notable advantage in computational efficiency, particularly when the number of possible states is substantial.

This study addresses the challenge of Offline Handwritten Mathematical Notation Recognition. Despite significant advancements in Offline Handwriting Recognition, the recognition of mathematical notation remains a complex task due to intricate math symbols and diverse algebraic structures. To tackle this challenge, we leverage the power of context information in math recognition. Firstly, we propose a context-aware recognition approach utilizing spatial relationships among recognition results. Secondly, we develop a context-dependent algebraic structure recognition technique based on the math context. Additionally, we design a context-aware spelling checker to post-correction recognize handwritten math. A comprehensive math dataset, called MathAI, is constructed to support offline handwritten math recognition research. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed context-aware recognition approaches and the feasibility of the post-correction strategy.

We examine supersymmetric quantum systems with a focus on the evolution of wavepackets. By leveraging algebraic geometry, we expand the definition of wavepacket cohomology and its associated charge conjugation. Our approach encompasses both the time-dependent and time-independent scenarios.

When analyzing complex systems, researchers typically apply statistical methods to identify patterns and regularities, but these approaches often overlook the intricacies of interaction processes. To bridge this gap, our work delves into the realm of complex systems dynamics, focusing on the variability of interaction processes to better understand the behavior of complicated systems.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications due to its ability to learn complex decision-making strategies efficiently. However, its implementation is often hindered by the challenging exploration problem in unknown environments. One notable approach combining deep reinforcement learning with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has achieved notable results in adapting to changing environments dynamically. Building upon this idea, this research proposes an enhancement to the actor-critic model through incorporation of a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo-like exploration mechanism, specifically designed for models lacking the capability to compute gradients fully effectively. Subsequently, theoretical and experimental evaluations were conducted to assess the approach's efficacy. Experimentally, the results indicate that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in various reinforcement learning benchmark tasks.
We present an elementary proof for the twin prime hypothesis by incorporating Cai and Diamandopoulos's ideas, leveraging the polynomial equation $z^5-(x+y)^5+x^5+y^5=0$.

Mobile robots navigating complex indoor spaces with multiple levels faces a significant challenge due to limited visibility from one floor to another. Our proposed indoor localization and tracking system over different stories uses a combination of sonar and 2D laser range finders to overcome common obstacles such as interference from reflections and limited range of detection. By incorporating algorithms for sonar signal processing, motion planning, and multi-level navigation, our system enables a robot to acquire and process data, estimate positions on both floors, and make informed decisions to switch between tracking targets on the same level and across levels at 2 Hz. Our approach to switching between tracking algorithms includes statistical analysis and a 'golden target' method to optimize performance and reduce errors. Our system has successfully tested and demonstrated effective navigation capabilities across different environments.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, displays an irregular shape and orbital characteristics that make it uniquely positioned for examination. The surface of Nereid, thought to be composed of two distinct icy regions and a darker low-frequency area, presents an intriguing geological profile that demands further investigation. To better comprehend Nereid's composition and surface features, our analysis focuses on the spectral reflectance data of the object, obtained from the NICMOS and PIXXL instruments on board the Infrared Telescope Facility. Our analysis of Nereid's spectral reflectance reveals an overall pattern that fits the expectations of an icy surface, yet as we delve into the details of its spectral characteristics, discrepancies between the observed data and the predicted patterns become evident, pointing to possible surface layering or contamination by organic matter. The inherent difficulties associated with interpreting Nereid's spectral reflectance from great distances may also contribute to these discrepancies. Further exploration of this satellite is necessary to resolve these ambiguities in Nereid's composition and surface morphology.

This work explores affine and projective surfaces defined by specific zero sets of polynomials, focusing on a particular type of ring formed by lower triangular matrices with entries from a specific set of ideals in the polynomial ring $k[x,y]$ where $k$ is a two-element set. The study reveals the detailed geometric properties of these surfaces, including references to the surfaces' configurations, in the context of rational maps and minimal rational surfaces associated with these configurations.

We propose a modified version of Tukey-sequence, built upon key tenets established by Fred Galvin and Krzysztof Pawlikowski. This new framework allows us to recover the original concept of Tukey-sequence, while also yielding a distinct concept of degree of intercalation. We demonstrate that their axioms generate a significant amount of interesting cardinal combinatorics, analogous to the outcomes of forcing axioms over minimal uncountable cardinal. Our work is particularly focused on the continuous game and key axioms concerning continuous games.

In the context of dynamic treatment frameworks, pessimistic models assume an adverse treatment effect, often to guarantee asymptotic consistency in the absence of knowledge about the best possible treatment. Nevertheless, conventional pessimistic approaches may overestimate a treatment's detrimental impact, thereby potentially selecting a suboptimal treatment. To overcome this limitation, a new method grounded in Bayesian learning is proposed, aiming to mitigate excessive pessimism and identify a more realistic adverse treatment effect, thus facilitating the selection of a better treatment. The proposed approach builds on the concept of "pessimistic Bayesian learning," which incorporates prior pessimistic assumptions into its learning framework. The theoretical findings validate the reliability and consistency of the proposed strategy, demonstrating that it converges toward the optimal treatment rule. The results of numerical experiments, performed using both artificially generated data and real-world information, show that the proposed approach outperforms alternative pessimistic methods, specifically by reducing the error rate and adapting more swiftly to changing environments.

Dualities between category theory frameworks yield substantial benefits, such as exchanging algebraic and topological properties. This research demonstrates how one such duality can derive functorial properties and transformations from dual objects, thereby providing an alternative proof of their existence. Additionally, the paper illustrates how this duality can be employed to compute homological invariants by mapping dual functors to these invariants and thereby inferring their dual properties. To accomplish this, we first establish the relevant dual objects and then utilize them to map dual functors to homological invariants such as cohomology, homotopy groups, and K-theory, thereby inferring their dual properties in these invariants.

A proposed framework for a quantum computing system utilizes a complexification of a Lie algebra, embedded within a larger Hilbert space. This approach assigns values to algebraic weights and roots, which serve as indices for states and observables. When the Lie algebra is simple, it can be reconfigured into a non-simple form by increasing the number of components, albeit at the cost of losing its initial defining properties. This study explores the properties of such systems with the $E_8$ Lie algebra and examines their potential for serving as a base for quantum information processing. Despite restrictions imposed upon the weights and roots of these systems, significant degrees of freedom remain, allowing a great deal of freedom in state design and the assignment of meaning to quantum measurements. Furthermore, the study discovers the possibility of entanglement across multiple dimensions and demonstrates a connection between entanglement and the conflict between quantum measurement rules and the rules governing the preparation of states, a relationship that manifests as a form of contextuality.

In a research study, the phenomenon of superconductivity is explored within a holographic model that includes N bodies and relies on a specific potential with a strong attraction. The calculation reveals that the system exhibits a condensation of wavefunctions in the lowest energy state, resulting in a collective zero-energy state. The study further demonstrates that these condensation patterns resist small disturbances but are susceptible to larger influences. Notably, the research includes analyses of how the condensation is affected by interbody interactions and finds that these interactions play a crucial role in the overall superconducting properties of the system.

The Polish topological group scenario equates finite discrete groups with the integers. Extending this analogy, we propose that a particular type of infinite groups, which have a specific topological property, should be represented by the real numbers. Our approach to this extension involves proving a generalized version of a well-known mathematical theorem, which has a distinct duality aspect. This generalized theorem will allow us to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the cardinalities of certain infinite groups that have a specific topological structure. Our methodology in this proof involves using techniques from measurement theory, which relies on ideals in commutative topological groups. Our approach to extending the Polish group analogy also enables us to address the broader category of non-locally-compact topological groups by considering the real line as a representation of an infinite discrete group that has a specific topological property.

This research examines different clustering techniques applied to existing data sets of two types: data that can take high values of 0 or 1, or greater than 0. The analysis focuses on existing datasets from two fields: research on the characteristics of widely available species and data from experiments investigating the effects of radiation on the development of fruit flies. To compare the various clustering approaches, overall performance is assessed through metrics including overall cluster quality and metrics specific to the data at hand, followed by a focus on the characteristics that influence clustering results.

In recent years, salient object recognition has become a popular topic within computer vision research, with rapid advancements in both theory and practice. Due to the simple and straightforward approach, identifying a salient item in an image or 3D data has numerous practical applications in real-world scenarios. However, the results of current techniques are hindered by the absence of comprehensive and effective strategies. To address this issue, this paper aims to provide a clear and concise overview of the challenges and limitations in identifying a salient item using RGB and RGB-D data. Additionally, the paper introduces and explores a new set of effective strategies, which have been lacking in previous work. To ensure the fairness and comparability of the results, this paper also proposes a set of rules for evaluating salient item identification algorithms. The findings of this research reveal that certain existing algorithms are capable of accurately identifying a salient item in images and 3D data, while also providing valuable insights for future research in this area.

This paper presents our approach to the 2019 SemEval Offensive Language Detection Challenges. We submitted entries in two subtasks: detecting offensive tweets and detecting offensive comments. For subtask A, we utilized BERT and SVM models. Our BERT model took a multilingual approach, leveraging its pre-trained embeddings. Our SVM model, on the other hand, was trained on features derived from lexicons, tweets' syntactic analysis, and semantic analysis. In subtask B, we employed an SVM classifier trained on a dataset incorporating features from text edits. We experimented with both classification and ranking methods in both challenges. Our models achieved scores of 0.7426 in subtask A and 0.7941 in subtask B.

Consider a number base b greater than one. In this base, the term "palindrome" describes a number that reads the same forwards and backwards. A non-palindrome, or "antipalindrome", is a number that doesn't meet this criterion. Let's denote the count of palindromes among the numbers from 0 to (b-1) as P, and the count of antipalindromes as A. The ratio of palindromes to antipalindromes, P/A, equals either 1 or P>A. The goal of this study is to explore this ratio in bases greater than three. Specifically, we've found that both 2nd and 3rd powers will always result in the ratio being less than or equal to 2, while 1st powers may yield this ratio and are therefore worthy of further investigation.

We introduce a pioneering approach to reconstructing images, incorporating multiple levels of energy and counteracting noise in CT scans, while simultaneously accounting for the degradation of materials. This framework is initially validated through computer simulations and then applied to real-world data obtained from a prototype dual-energy CT system. The results demonstrate its capability to produce enhanced images and distinguish between varying materials without being constrained to a convex optimization formulation.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with minimal resource assistance remains an unsolved problem in the field. Traditional approaches rely on extensive annotated datasets, which are difficult to obtain for rare languages. Recent research suggests that synthetic data can effectively contribute to solving this problem, but current methods have notable limitations. They often produce synthetic data in bulk, requiring significant pre-processing time. Furthermore, their labors are often wasted if the data does not align well with the test data. By contrast, this paper proposes a new approach that generates synthetic data individually in real-time using a trained model. When a new HTR model is to be trained, this approach creates a new class by sampling individual handwritten examples from existing classes and applying them to a new label. By processing data in single-shot batches, this method eliminates the need for time-consuming data pre-processing. By adapting to data distributions in real-time, it also optimizes synthetic data for better performance. Experimental results on 9 low resource languages show that this approach surpasses previous synthetic data methods in accuracy with minimal assistance. When assistance is increased to 10k labels, this approach reaches 97.6% accuracy, comparable to that of highly trained base model.

To study heavy nuclei, researchers integrated the Barnes-Bening quantum field theory for nuclear masses and the Hartree-Fock-Fock quantum modeling for the nuclear structure. By merging these theories, extensive calculations were undertaken for nuclei ranging from light to very heavy, yielding precise mass predictions and a deeper understanding of the structure within. Notably, the analysis of measured magnetic moments in numerous nuclei revealed a common trend, with results accurate to one part in a million. To facilitate further research, the study's data, comprising 300,000 calculated nuclear masses, has been made publicly accessible through the Evaluated Atomic Data and Nuclear Mass Data platform.

We start by defining various elements associated with the SSH model topological properties, such as realization, uniqueness, independence, and complementarity. Our study further explores the model's quantum eigenstates, examining notions like localization, polynomial Heisenberg equivariance, and distinctness. Our findings demonstrate that all quantum eigenstates exhibit polynomial Heisenberg invariance and reside within a single, bounded geographic area. Additionally, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between unique eigenstates and layovers along the model's discrete spectrum. Our analysis also reveals that all eigenstates possess a distinct feature set.

Let $\Omega$ be a convex open set in $\mathbb{C}$ or an analytic disc within $\mathbb{C}^n$. The space $A^2(\Omega)$ consists of square-integrable holomorphic functions on $\Omega$. For a compact set $K\subset\Omega$, the bounded linear operators from $C(\overline{\Omega})$ to $A^2(\Omega)$ that remain bounded when restricted to $C(\overline{K})$ are investigated. In specific instances, we identify the exact compactness criteria and explore connections with weighted Lebesgue spaces, while general cases yield necessary but not sufficient conditions for compactness.

We derived the two-loop amplitude for five-dimensional supergravity in the AdS$_5$ space using an approach that translates QFT principles directly, specifically by converting QFT correlations into supergravity amplitudes via a proven theorem. In doing so, we successfully computed the two-loop supergravity amplitude, which we then verified matches the previously established two-loop Weyl anomaly in four-dimensional conformal field theory when reduced to the AdS$_5$ boundary conditions.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a highly efficient concurrent memory allocator designed for use on GPUs with multiple memory segments. It is specifically tailored to support object-based programming and includes a self-balancing algorithm that ensures even memory distribution. DynaSOAr provides user-defined memory allocation and deallocation functions, enabling easier programming on GPUs. We conducted comprehensive performance evaluations using various benchmarks and real-world applications, and our results demonstrate a significant speedup of up to 140x and an average of 21.6x over current best practice.

We investigate three Standard Model extension theories based on a $U(1)_{X}$ gauge group, which are inspired by a high-dimensional SO(10) theory. While these models can fit into the framework of a unified SO(10) theory at a high energy scale, they can also be analyzed as independent theories. To analyze the loop corrections to the beta function of the $U(1)_{X}$ gauge group, we examine the loop-level fermion interactions within the three models, specifically focusing on the additional fermions introduced in each scenario under the $U(1)_{X}$ and $U(1)_{Y}$ representations. Furthermore, the three models differ in their diagonal $U(1)_{X}$ and $U(1)_{Y}$ charges, leading to distinct phenomenological characteristics and possible paths to particle physics outcomes, as well as dark matter stabilization.

In particle physics, experimental facilities require robust straw chambers with durable electrical connections to handle high-energy collisions and maintain stability under intense conditions. Research focuses on the mechanical properties of straws made from Kapton, evaluating their structural stability under both internal pressure and external forces to ensure reliable operation over extended periods. This study utilizes finite element modeling to analyze the material's elastic behavior, considering various factors such as pressure, temperature, and mechanical loading to determine the thermal expansion coefficient. The simulation includes a detailed electrical connector model to assess its impact on the elastic behavior of the straw. The findings demonstrate that the shape memory alloy's ability to limit deformation is unnecessary as the connector's design already minimizes mechanical stress. Furthermore, the research reveals that temperature is the primary factor contributing to deformation, followed by pressure, and finally mechanical loading.

In various practical scenarios, ensuring the reliability of machine learning model predictions is of utmost importance. This is particularly the case when such models are integrated with sensitive information and their results have a direct bearing on critical decision-making processes. Although previous studies have focused on measuring the uncertainty associated with machine learning model predictions, they have largely overlooked the inherent weaknesses of the Bayesian learning framework. This research undertakes the pivotal task of quantifying the reliability of machine learning model predictions at the inference level for Bayesian learning methods. Specifically, we define a metric called "sturdiness" to quantify the reliability of belief network inference outcomes and propose an efficient computational protocol to determine this metric. Furthermore, we establish a method for integrating multiple machine learning models, each with its own strengths and weaknesses, to enhance the overall reliability of the Bayesian learning framework. This research is the first to provide a theoretical foundation for machine learning reliability assurances and offers a versatile framework that can be applied to various real-world use cases.

A general equation for dynamical density waves in supersolid states has been formulated, allowing for the inclusion of internal degrees of freedom. This approach applies to any supersolid state, and its application to the spin supersolid phase of the Bose-Hubbard model reveals distinct damped sound modes. These modes can travel long distances, and their speed is determined by the effective mass of the system. In the weak coupling limit, the system behaves as a massless fluid with sound propagation guided by the density of the underlying Bose-Einstein condensate.

In a generalized quadrilateral, distinct points $P_1, \ldots, P_6$ are used to create a partial arrangement, and we define a neighborhood transitive code as a set of vectors determined by the distances between these points. It is proven that in a particular instance, there exist linear subspaces with specific properties. Additionally, it is shown that in another instance, there do not exist linear subspaces with the same properties.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is a star cluster rich area at the heart of the Milky Way that plays a key role in understanding how a galaxy's mass is distributed. To measure the mass arrangement pattern in the CMZ, researchers used two-dimensional correlation analysis on data from the Telescopes for Image and Fast Spectroscopy of the Milky Way (TIGER). The results revealed an anisotropic mass pattern in the area and found that this pattern changes with radius. The findings provide new insights for future research on the CMZ into its origin, evolution, and growth.

To effectively analyze large datasets produced by high-intensity x-ray sources, a streamlined processing system is crucial. A proposed solution involves dividing data processing into two distinct stages: initial data filtering, and an in-depth examination using advanced modeling techniques. A specialized algorithm, inspired by rate equations used in quantum mechanics, is designed to accurately model the resonant absorption patterns observed around key energy thresholds in atoms. By simulating the absorption patterns of individual electrons within a molecule, the algorithm can efficiently handle large molecular structures and accurately account for overlapping resonant signals. A notable benefit of this approach is its computational scalability, allowing it to handle datasets produced by high-intensity x-ray sources with millions of data points. A comprehensive case study demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness using experimental data from the Linac Coherent Light Source.

This work presents a temperature sensor that operates within a wide range of voltages from 0.6V to 1.8V, utilizing a single CMOS implementation. The design leverages a binary-weighted resistor network and a fully customizable P-channel MOSFET array to achieve a high temperature resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius, along with a minimal energy consumption of 1.06 nanojoules per temperature conversion step. Furthermore, the design incorporates two configurable feedback nodes to enable precise temperature sensing as well as data retention capabilities, thereby facilitating the development of sophisticated thermal monitoring systems integrating both temperature measurement and data storage functionalities.

Quantum entanglement serves as the defining characteristic of quantum states and plays a pivotal role in quantum information and technologies. However, the majority of quantum states are parameterized entangled states, yet only a limited subset of these states possesses useful properties for practical applications. The development of entanglement purification, quantization, and polarization techniques has made vast collections of entangled states accessible and has enabled the conversion of non-polarized entangled states into valuable resources for dual use. In this context, our quantum scissors technique is introduced as an efficient method for an entanglement purification process known as polarization. This approach employs a vast collection of arbitrary pure entangled states to obtain approximately polarized entangled states of high purity, and it does so with minimal requirements for multiple control operations. The technique's efficiency is directly proportional to the number of compatible measurements in state characterization and is therefore greatest for states exhibiting high symmetry. Our findings are demonstrated through specific numerical calculations involving symmetric two-qubit and two-photon states, and our approach is shown to yield substantial results even with limited characterizations. The technique's name "quantum scissors" refers to the technique's ability to cut through complex correlations by parsing the entangled states into distinct, use-case-specific components.

We have investigated the creation of Euclidean spanners over the internet topology. Initially, we developed a simple algorithm that takes a weighted graph $G$ and a set of probabilities associated with its edges as input. The goal is to produce a probabilistic spanner $G'$ of $G$, which is also a weighted graph defined on the same vertices, and is guaranteed to have a specific weak subadditivity property. It is established that $G'$ maintains a strong approximation ratio of at most $1+\epsilon$ in expected value for every edge in $G$, and is subsequently used to construct a probabilistic $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate Euclidean spanner of the internet topology. Furthermore, we have introduced an alternative algorithm that enables the direct creation of a high-probability $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate Euclidean spanner of the standard model $S_n$, which represents the uniform distribution of $n$ points in the $d$-dimensional unit cube. The model $S_n$ is a well-known representation of the internet topology and is known to be metric space with specific properties. It is established that both algorithms used in our studies are efficient and can be completed in a polynomial time of $n$. The findings of our studies, including the algorithms, are explained in a clear and simple manner.

In the realm of IoT, extracting key features from a gadget's expense-friendly fingerprint is a critical challenge. Instead of training a model from a comprehensive dataset, we propose an innovative approach centered on expense-minimal feature extraction. By combining principles from both information theory and machine learning, our method identifies the most relevant features at the lowest possible expense, leveraging the concept of mutual information to analyze relationships between features and classes. These crucial features are then utilized to develop a cost-efficient classification model, reducing computational expenses associated with redundant features. Our approach was tested on various IoT gadgets, featuring diverse feature sets, and produced promising results, outperforming existing feature selection methods while minimizing expenses.

This study introduces algebraic and relational frameworks for Godel modal logics and several of its extensions. It demonstrates that Godel modal logic can be represented by both finitary and infinitary modal logics in the spirit of Kripke. Furthermore, this research develops an algebraic structure for Godel modal logics by refining an existing topological structure. Additionally, the paper presents modal logics based on finite Godel algebras and develops an algebraic and relational framework for finite Godel algebras.

This research presents a novel technique for translating words based on their context, which does not require pre-trained models or alignments. Instead, it relies on learning word translations from external bilingual resources and uses a self-improving process that incorporates user feedback in real-time. Unlike traditional approaches, this model can function without initial bilingual data and instead relies on external sources, such as monolingual data with bilingual information. Additionally, it utilizes a context-based model to improve the accuracy of word translations. Experimental results demonstrate that this model achieves comparable translation accuracy to existing approaches and showcases promising applications in translation and domain adaptation.

A distorted resolvent approach is introduced to establish the existence of Nash equilibria in various classes of Nash games defined on atypical spaces. It encompasses situations described by measure-valued functions in abstract Luce spaces. Our method allows for the inclusion of infinite data and distortions of all nonnegative types. The study focuses on two key scenarios: games defined on the space of probability measures (Luce spaces) and those defined on general metric spaces with infinite data. The approach is illustrated by applying it to two distinct game scenarios.

Recent breakthroughs in ground-breaking technology, such as the construction of Event Horizon Telescope, has facilitated the observation of black holes in the millisecond regime. This advancement has paved the way for a novel approach in astrophysics and cosmology, enabling us to perceive black holes near their theoretical minimum size. Furthermore, the discovery of primordial black holes may serve as a potential dark matter candidate, given their vast number density when formed in the early universe. Despite their immense potential, modeling primordial black holes is a computationally complex challenge due to their low masses. This complication has been alleviated by the integration of the codes such as Castro and CHYM, allowing us to produce high-resolution images of black holes including their thermal effects, accordion-like effects, gravitational ripples, and surrounding matter. However, a recent development features a new code, PopSyCLE, designed to produce accurate synthetic observations of massive black holes in diverse settings, including groups of multiple black holes, different types of accretion, various matter distributions, and a diverse range of black hole masses. This novel code has enabled the production of the first primordial black hole shadow matter simulations, offering a fresh outlook on shadow research. Primordial black holes exhibit distinct characteristics in their formation from the inside out or the outside in due to their homogeneous or inhomogeneous initial conditions in the early universe. This variation in their formation patterns translates to differences in their thermal effects and surrounding matter distributions, resulting in unique and diverse synthetic observations.
